questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: All of the following is seen in the terrible triad of elbow, except.
options: Fracture of the coronoid process of ulna
questions.explanation: The "Terrible Triad" of the elbow is a severe injury pattern characterized by the combination of three specific components: 1. Posterior elbow dislocation (Option A). 2. Radial head fracture (Option B). 3. Coronoid process fracture of the ulna (Option D). A fracture of the olecranon (Option C) is NOT a component of this specific triad. This injury is labeled "terrible" because it is highly unstable and notoriously difficult to manage, often leading to chronic joint instability, stiffness, and early-onset osteoarthritis. The coronoid process and radial head are critical "anterior" and "lateral" stabilizers of the elbow; their simultaneous fracture, combined with ligamentous injury during dislocation, leads to total joint incompetence. Management almost always requires surgery to repair or replace the radial head, fix the coronoid, and restore the lateral collateral ligament. Accurate knowledge of these anatomical triads is essential for orthopedic surgeons to plan complex reconstructive procedures and to counsel patients on the challenging recovery process
questions.learning: The "Terrible Triad" of the elbow is a severe injury pattern characterized by the combination of three specific components: 1. Posterior elbow dislocation (Option A).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient taking metronidazole for diarrhea consumed alcohol at a party. Subsequently, he developed red rashes, generalized itching, and a headache. What is the most likely cause of these symptoms?
questions.explanation: Several medications, most notably metronidazole, inhibit the enzyme acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, which is responsible for breaking down the toxic metabolite of alcohol. When a patient on these drugs consumes even a small amount of alcohol, acetaldehyde accumulates in the blood, leading to a highly unpleasant syndrome called a disulfiram-like reaction. Symptoms include intense flushing ("red rashes"), headache, nausea, vomiting, sweating, and palpitations. Methanol poisoning (Option A) is characterized by metabolic acidosis and visual disturbances. The "cheese reaction" (Option C) occurs when patients on MAO inhibitors eat tyramine-rich foods, leading to a hypertensive crisis. To prevent this reaction, patients prescribed metronidazole must be strictly counseled to avoid all alcohol during treatment and for at least 48-72 hours after the last dose. Other drugs causing this reaction include certain cephalosporins and sulfonylureas
questions.learning: Several medications, most notably metronidazole, inhibit the enzyme acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, which is responsible for breaking down the toxic metabolite of alcohol.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is contraindicated in PPH in a primigravida with chronic hypertension?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Methyl ergometrine

Methylergometrine is contraindicated in the management of postpartum hemorrhage in a female with chronic hypertension.

Methylergometrine is an ergot derivative, which acts directly on the myometrium. It excites uterine contractions which come so frequently one after the other with increasing intensity that the uterus passes into a state of spasm without any relaxation in between. Hence, it should be used only be used either in the late second stage of labor(after the delivery of the anterior shoulder) or following the delivery of the baby.

Indications :

• Prophylactic - Active management of the third stage of labor as prophylaxis to excess bleeding following delivery
• Therapeutic - To stop the atonic uterine bleeding, following delivery, abortion or expulsion of hydatidiform mole. It is used at a dose of 0.2mg im/iv, repeated every 2-4 hours.

Side effects :

• Nausea and vomiting.
• Because of its vasoconstrictive action, it may precipitate a rise in blood pressure, myocardial infarction, stroke and bronchospasm.
• Repeated use may lead to gangrene of the toes due to its vasoconstrictive effect.
• Repeated use in puerperium may interfere with lactation by lowering prolactin levels.

Contraindications :

• Multiple pregnancy - If given accidentally with the delivery of the first baby, the second baby is compromised by the tetanic contractions of the uterus.
• Heart disease - Results in sudden squeezing of blood from the uterine circulation into the systemic circulation causing overloading of the right heart and failure.
• Hypertensive disorders, pre-eclampsia and eclampsia
• Rh-negative mother - More risk of fetomaternal microtransfusion.
• Vascular disease

Other options :

Option B - Misoprostol is a methyl ester of PGE1, used in the induction of labor and in the management of postpartum hemorrhage. Side effects include fever, tachysystole (hyperstimulation), fetal heart rate changes and meconium passage. It should not be used for cases with previous cesarean birth because the risk of uterine rupture is high.

Option C - Oxytocin is used in the active management of the third stage of labor, augmentation of labor and control of postpartum hemorrhage. Contraindications for its use are hypovolemic states, obstructed labor and cardiac disease.

Option D - Prostaglandin F2 alpha derivative (carboprost) is used in the management of postpartum hemorrhage. Contraindications for its use are asthma, active cardiac, renal, or hepatic disease.
questions.learning: Methyl ergometrine Methylergometrine is contraindicated in the management of postpartum hemorrhage in a female with chronic hypertension. Methylergometrine is an ergot derivative, which acts directly on the myometrium.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient is brought to the casualty following a road traffic accident. On examination, the patient is conscious, BP is 90/60 mm Hg, respiratory rate is 40 breaths per minute, and pulse rate is 120 bpm. The X-ray is shown below. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chest tube insertion

The given X-ray features showing a well-demarcated area devoid of lung markings on the left side with tracheal deviation and the mediastinal shift to the right side, along with the clinical scenario is suggestive of tension pneumothorax. The next best step in the management is chest tube insertion.

Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, and treatment should never be delayed while waiting for radiological confirmation. Imaging modalities used are ultrasound–extended focused assessment with sonar for trauma (eFAST), chest x-ray, and spiral CT.

A tension pneumothorax develops when there is a tear either in the parietal or visceral pleura. This tear acts as a one-way valve i.e., air enters from the lung or chest wall through it during inspiration but has no way to escape during expiration. This ultimately leads to the collapse of the affected lung.

It usually occurs following penetrating or blunt chest trauma, iatrogenic lung injury, or mechanical positive pressure ventilation.

It is characterized by:

• Chest pain
• Tachypnea and acute dyspnea
• Sudden onset hemodynamic compromise (tachycardia, hypotension, low O2 saturation, loss of consciousness)
• Neck vein distention
• Tracheal deviation away from the side of the injury
• Decreased chest movements on the affected side
• Hyper-resonance on percussion on the affected side
• Absence or decreased breath sounds on the affected side

The X-ray below shows a left-sided tension pneumothorax. There is a large, well-demarcated area devoid of lung markings on the left side. The yellow arrows are pointing to the tracheal deviation and the mediastinal shift to the right side.

Management of tension pneumothorax:

• Immediate management- needle decompression or needle thoracostomy i.e. insertion of a wide-bore needle in the 5th ICS anterior to the midaxillary line
• Definitive management- tube thoracostomy or chest tube insertion in the 5th ICS in the triangle of safety, identified as a triangle that lies anterior to the midaxillary line above the nipple, below, and lateral to the pectoralis major muscle.

The images below show the triangle of safety and technique of chest drain insertion.

Other options:

• Pericardiocentesis is done in cases of cardiac tamponade which is characterized by the presence of hypotension, distended jugular veins, and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad). The breath sounds are absent in tension pneumothorax while they are present in cardiac tamponade.
• Surgery for pneumothorax can be performed by video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) or as an open procedure (thoracotomy) in cases of spontaneous pneumothorax failing to settle despite chest drainage. Pleural adhesion is achieved by chemical pleurodesis where talc is used and is insufflated into the chest cavity.
questions.learning: Chest tube insertion — The given X-ray features showing a well-demarcated area devoid of lung markings on the left side with tracheal deviation and the mediastinal shift to the right side, along with the clinical scenario is suggestive of tension pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A middle-aged woman presents with fissured tongue and peripheral neuropathy. Investigations showed reduced glutathione reductase activity. Which vitamin deficiency is the likely cause of this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin B2

This patient is most likely suffering from riboflavin/vitamin B2 deficiency.

Deficiency of riboflavin is characterized by cheilosis, desquamation, and inflammation of the tongue, seborrheic dermatitis, corneal vascularization, anemia, and personality changes.

Riboflavin nutritional status is assessed by measurement of the activation of erythrocyte glutathione reductase by FAD added in vitro.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which type of blood can be safely transfused to a patient with the Bombay (Oh) blood group?
questions.explanation: A patient with the Bombay blood group (Oh phenotype) lacks the H antigen, which is present in all other blood groups (A, B, AB, and O). They also have anti-A, anti-B, and anti-H antibodies. Therefore, scientifically, such patients can receive only Bombay blood, because even O negative blood contains H antigen and can trigger a severe hemolytic reaction. However, in some exam contexts or emergency situations, O negative blood is considered the best available option, especially when Bombay blood is not readily available. Hence, exam keys may mark O negative as the answer. Why other options are incorrect: (A) A blood: Contains A and H antigens → reacts with anti-A and anti-H antibodies. (B) B blood: Contains B and H antigens → reacts with anti-B and anti-H antibodies. (C) AB blood: Contains A, B, and H antigens → highly incompatible. Thus, while Bombay blood is ideal, the exam-oriented answer is O negative
questions.learning: A patient with the Bombay blood group (Oh phenotype) lacks the H antigen, which is present in all other blood groups (A, B, AB, and O). They also have anti-A, anti-B, and anti-H antibodies.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following pupillary abnormalities is most likely to be observed in a patient with primary open-angle glaucoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Marcus Gunn pupil

Primary open-angle glaucoma commonly causes bilateral and asymmetric optic nerve damage. Marcus Gunn pupil also known as relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is the earliest sign of optic nerve disease as seen in optic nerve neuritis or primary open-angle glaucoma(POAG).

RAPD is caused due to a defect in the afferent pathway (optic nerve) of the pupillary light reflex in one eye.

It is diagnosed by the swinging flashlight test where the flashlight is swung to and fro, and the pupillary response is observed. Normally, both pupils constrict when any one eye is stimulated (due to direct and consensual light reflex). In the presence of RAPD, both pupils will abnormally dilate when the affected eye is stimulated. This paradoxical response of the pupil to light is called Marcus Gunn pupil.

Causes of RAPD:

• Optic nerve lesions (e.g.All types of optic neuritis, glaucoma)
• Optic tract lesions (e.g., infarction)
• Severe retinal disease (e.g., central retinal artery occlusion, extensive retinal detachment)
• Maculopathy (macular degeneration )

Other options:

Option B: Adie tonic pupil is a unilateral dilated pupil with light-near dissociation due to postganglionic parasympathetic pupillomotor nerve supply damage. In these patients the light reflex is absent and the accomdation (near) reflex is sluggish. It is commonly seen in young females and is associated with absent knee jerk.

Option C: Argyll Robertson pupils are bilateral small pupils with light-near dissociation. It is commonly seen in patients with neurosyphilis. In these patients the pupillary reflex is absent but the accommodation reflex is present (ARP).

Option D: Hutchinson's pupil is a clinical sign where the pupil on the side of an intracranial mass lesion is dilated and unreactive to light, due to compression of the oculomotor nerve on that side.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Anti-D vaccine is not given in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intrauterine transfusion at 28 weeks

The anti-D vaccine is not given in intrauterine transfusion at 28 weeks. Intrauterine transfusion is done in alloimmunized pregnancies, where the maternal immune system (Rh negative) has already been exposed to the fetal blood (Rh positive).

The purpose of the anti-D vaccine is to prevent the development of maternal antibodies against fetal red cells, which is already occurring in alloimmunized pregnancies.

Anti-D vaccine is administered only in ICT-negative non-isoimmunized pregnancies.

Intrauterine transfusion is done when the peak systolic velocity of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) exceeds 1.5 multiples of the median or if hydrops develop or if the fetal hematocrit is <30%. This indicates that the mother already has antibodies against the fetus's red blood cells, making the administration of anti-D unnecessary.

The indications for administering anti-D are:

• Pregnancy loss: spontaneous or elective abortion (option D) and ectopic pregnancy.
• Fetal death: Regardless of the trimester.
• Procedures: Such as amniocentesis (option A), chorionic villus sampling, fetal blood sampling, and molar pregnancy evacuation.
• Other situations: Antepartum bleeding (including threatened abortion), delivery (vaginal or cesarean), external cephalic version, placental abruption, manual removal of placenta (option B), and trauma to the abdomen during pregnancy.

All Rh D-negative women should be given a single dose of 300 mcg of anti-D at 28 weeks of pregnancy (ICT should be negative).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which microorganism is most likely responsible for causing bilateral pulmonary infiltrates in an HIV-positive patient?
questions.explanation: In an HIV-positive patient with a low CD4 count, the classic cause of pneumonia presenting with bilateral, diffuse interstitial infiltrates (often described as "ground-glass" opacities) on a chest X-ray is Pneumocystis jirovecii. As discussed in Questions 54 and 100, this fungal pathogen causes an opportunistic infection that characteristically spreads through the alveolar spaces of both lungs simultaneously. Cryptococcus (Option A) more commonly causes meningitis or focal lung nodules. Histoplasmosis (Option B) can cause diffuse disease but often presents with hilar lymphadenopathy or miliary-style patterns. Aspergillus (Option D) typically causes focal consolidation or cavities in immuno compromised hosts. Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) remains a leading cause of hospitalization and death in patients who are unaware of their HIV status or who are not consistently on antiretroviral therapy. Diagnosis is confirmed by visualizing the organism in sputum or BAL fluid using specialized stains like Silver stain or by PCR testing
questions.learning: In an HIV-positive patient with a low CD4 count, the classic cause of pneumonia presenting with bilateral, diffuse interstitial infiltrates (often described as "ground-glass" opacities) on a chest X-ray is Pneumocystis jirovecii.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 36-year-old farmer came to the clinic with cough, chest pain for one week, and fatigue for a month, and his Chest X-ray was taken which is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hydatid cyst

The chronic history, the frequent exposure to animals as he is a farmer, and the chest x-ray which shows a cystic lesion in the right lung are suggestive of Hydatid disease.

* The causative organism of hydatid disease is Echinococcus granulosus and it belongs to the class cestodes.

* It is a tape-like, segmented worm. It infects man accidentally, giving rise to hydatid cysts.

* Dogs are the definitive hosts of E. granulosus.

* Sheep are the usual intermediate hosts, but humans are accidental intermediate hosts. Humans are end-stage hosts of the parasite since there is no human to human transmission

The hydatid cyst wall consists of 3 layers:

* Pericyst- the outer dense fibrous capsule that is formed as a result of host inflammatory response.

* Ectocyst- the intermediate layer consisting of acellular, chitinous, laminated hyaline material.

* Endocyst- the inner germinal layer that is cellular and consists of a number of nuclei embedded in protoplasmic mass and is extremely thin. It is the vital layer of the cyst and it is the site of asexual reproduction giving rise to brood capsules with scolices.

The clinical features of hydatid disease of the lung are breathlessness, cough, hemoptysis, and chest pain.

Treatment includes wedge resection or lobectomy and administration of albendazole.

Other options:

* Asbestosis presents as pleural plaques, irregular opacities, ground-glass appearance particularly present at the lower lung fields. HRCT will show the presence of pleural plaque, subpleural curvilinear lines 5–10 mm in length that appears to be parallel to the pleura.

* Silicosis is an occupational disease and is caused by exposure to silica. It is seen in people who work in mining, stone cutting, sandblasting, and quarrying. It presents as small rounded opacities in the upper lobe. There may be calcification of hilar lymph nodes which leads to the appearance of eggshell calcification. HRCT will show a characteristic crazy paving pattern.

* Byssinosis is an occupational disease due to chronic exposure to cotton dust as in yarns of textile and rope-making industries. In the early stage of the disease, patients complain of occasional chest tightness towards the end of the first day of the workweek termed as monday chest tightness. As the day progress, the chest tightness may recur or persist throughout the week. Chest X-ray shows hyperlucency, diaphragmatic flattening, and emphysema. A chest CT demonstrates ground glass opacities largely distributed in then basal fashion with centrilobular nodules.

Pearl PF1538: Indications and contraindications of puncture, aspiration, injection, and re-aspiration (PAIR) in hydatid cyst

Indications:

* Relapse cyst, infected cyst, cyst >5 cm in different liver segments

* Patients who refuse surgery or where surgery is contraindicated

* Pregnant women, children < 3 years of age

* WHO - type CE1 and type CE3a.

Contraindications:

* Cysts in lung

* Cysts communicating with bile duct

* Cysts with multiple septae—honeycomb cysts

* Inaccessible cysts

* Hyperechogenic cysts

* Calcified cysts

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 22-year-old boy was admitted to the casualty with a history of breathlessness following massage by his mother. He had a history of hairline ankle fracture and was on a below-knee cast which was removed recently. The most probable diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pulmonary thromboembolism

The given clinical history of immobilization after the application of the cast is a risk factor for deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Massaging the leg may dislodge the thrombus causing pulmonary embolism (PE). It is the commonest complication of DVT leading to death.

PE and DVT are part of the same spectrum of venous thromboembolism. PE occurs due to obstruction of the pulmonary arterial circulation by deep venous thrombi that detach from their site of formation and embolize to the vena cava, right atrium, and right ventricle. Virchow’s triad of venous stasis, hypercoagulability, and endothelial injury, leading to recruitment of activated platelets, provides the ideal environment for thrombus formation.

DVT presents with pain and swelling of the calf (the most common symptom), tenderness and edema. Clinical examination is unreliable and the elicitation of signs such as Homan's or Mose's signs is not recommended owing to the risk of clot dislodgement. Patients with symptoms of PE present with fever, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and hemoptysis. On examination, they can have cyanosis, jugular venous distension, fixed split-second heart sound and pleural rub, but may be subtle or absent. Some patients are asymptomatic.

Depending on the clinical presentation, patients with PE can be stratified as:

• High-risk (massive) PE is characterized by systemic hypotension. Patients can have dyspnea and syncope and may present in cardiogenic shock.
• Intermediate-risk PE is characterized by right ventricle (RV) dysfunction but normal blood pressure. RV dysfunction can be diagnosed with echocardiography and ECG.
• Low-risk PE is characterized by normal blood pressure and the absence of any RV dysfunction.

Investigations:

• Venous duplex ultrasound to look for thrombi in the leg.
• Chest x-ray in PE shows hyper lucency in an area of oligemia (Westermark sign). D-dimer levels are elevated and ECG will show sinus tachycardia (the most common ECG abnormality) and an S1Q3T3 sign (an S wave in lead I, a Q wave in lead III, and an inverted T wave in lead III).
• Definitive diagnosis of PE is by a CT-Pulmonary Angiography.

The management of PE will vary according to the risk stratification:

• A patient with high-risk PE will primarily be treated with anticoagulation and thrombolysis or catheter/surgical embolectomy.
• A patient with low-risk PE will be treated with anticoagulation alone, or an IVC filter as secondary prophylaxis.
• Patients with intermediate-risk PE require individualized treatment.

Anticoagulation can be done with the classical strategy of low-molecular-weight heparin followed by warfarin, or by low-molecular-weight heparin for 5 days, switched to novel oral anticoagulant like Dabigatran after that. Fibrinolysis, if indicated, is done with recombinant TPA administered over 2 hours. It can be done up to 14 days after the PE has occurred.

Management of DVT:

• Anticoagulation with low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) and unfractionated heparin (UFH) if renal impairment is present.
• After treatment with heparin, patients should be commenced on oral anticoagulants for at least 3 months with either factor Xa inhibitors (rivaroxaban and apixaban) or direct thrombin inhibitors (dabigatran).
• Other measures such as rest, limb elevation and compression stockings are also used.
questions.learning: Pulmonary thromboembolism — The given clinical history of immobilization after the application of the cast is a risk factor for deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents to the hospital with a history of high fever and chills. On examination, a maculopapular rash was observed over the neck, with a positive tourniquet test. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dengue haemorrhagic fever

The clinical features are suggestive of dengue haemorrhagic fever.

Dengue, also known as break-bone fever, manifests after an incubation period of 3-14 days. Dengue fever is an acute febrile illness with two or more of the following manifestations: headache, retroorbital pain, myalgia, arthralgia, and rash.

Dengue haemorrhagic fever, or dengue shock syndrome, can occur in individuals with preexisting non-neutralising heterologous dengue antibodies caused by previous infection with a different serotype of the virus or passively acquired maternal antibodies in children. Initially, symptoms simulate normal dengue; however, the patient’s condition worsens.

The virus–antibody complexes are formed within a few days of the second dengue infection, and the non-neutralising enhancing antibodies promote infection of higher numbers of mononuclear cells followed by the release of cytokines, vasoactive mediators, and procoagulants, leading to the disseminated intravascular coagulation seen in the haemorrhagic fever syndrome.

The most important pathology of dengue haemorrhagic fever is increased vascular permeability with plasma leakage into the interstitial spaces associated with increased levels of vasoactive cytokines, which can lead to life-threatening shock in some patients. The clinical criteria of dengue haemorrhagic fever are dengue fever with haemorrhagic tendencies evidenced by one b more of the following:

* Positive tourniquet test

* Petechiae, ecchymoses or purpura

* Bleeding from the mucosa, gastrointestinal tract, injection sites or other sites

* Thrombocytopenia, a more than 20% drop in haematocrit following volume replacement treatment compared to baseline

* Signs of plasma leakage (pleural effusion, ascites, hypoproteinaemia)

Dengue shock syndrome is characterised by all the above criteria for dengue haemorrhagic fever with evidence of circulatory failure manifested by rapid, weak pulse and narrow pulse pressure or hypotension for age, cold, clammy skin and restlessness.

Other options:

Option B: Quartan fever, which occurs on the first and fourth days, is typically associated with Plasmodium malariae infection.

Option C: The disease can present as classical filariasis or occult filariasis. Clinical features include:

* Classical filariasis – Fever, lymphangitis, lymphadenitis, lymphedema, lymphangiovarix, hydrocele, lymphorrhagia, elephantiasis

* Occult filariasis – Massive eosinophilia, hepatosplenomegaly, dyspnoea, arthritis, glomerulonephritis, etc.

Option D: Chikungunya fever is due to infection with the chikungunya virus, spread by mosquitos. The Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes are the most common vectors. It presents as an acute onset of fever, arthralgia, and myalgia with other flu symptoms such as headache, loss of appetite, and nausea. A progressive maculopapular rash develops, which is more pronounced on the trunk.
questions.learning: Dengue haemorrhagic fever — The clinical features are suggestive of dengue haemorrhagic fever. Dengue, also known as break-bone fever, manifests after an incubation period of 3-14 days.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following procedures has the highest risk to cause the recurrence of duodenal ulcers?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Highly selective vagotomy

Highly selective vagotomy (HSV) has the highest risk to cause the recurrence of duodenal ulcers among the given options.

HSV retains the vagal innervation to the antrum, pylorus, and the remaining abdominal viscera while cutting off the vagal nerve supply to the proximal two-thirds of the stomach, which houses nearly all of the parietal cells. As a result, the procedure reduces overall gastric acid secretion by around 75%, and GI side effects are uncommon. However, HSV has not had great success treating type II (gastric and duodenal) and type III (prepyloric) gastric ulcers, possibly as a result of hypergastrinemia brought on by prolonged antral stasis and gastric outlet obstruction.

Option A: Resective procedures like gastrectomy have the least rates of recurrence but are less preferred nowadays due to higher rates of morbidity and mortality.

Option C: Unlike HSV, vagotomy and drainage is widely accepted as a successful definitive operation for complicated PUD, with lower rates of recurrence.

Option D: Gastrojejunostomy is a good choice in patients with gastric outlet obstruction or a severely diseased proximal duodenum.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is shown in the image below (circled)?
questions.explanation: The circled area in the CT scan represents the Osteomeatal Complex (OMC), a critical anatomical region in the lateral nasal wall. It is the common drainage pathway where the frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoidal sinuses empty into the middle meatus. Obstruction of the OMC is a primary cause of chronic rhinosinusitis and is the focus of Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS). The columella (Option A) is the external fleshy tissue separating the nostrils. The nasal valve (Option C) is the narrowest internal part of the nasal airway that regulates airflow. The crest of the maxilla (Option D) is a bony ridge on the floor of the nasal cavity. Precise identification of the OMC on imaging is essential for preoperative surgical planning
questions.learning: The circled area in the CT scan represents the Osteomeatal Complex (OMC), a critical anatomical region in the lateral nasal wall. It is the common drainage pathway where the frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoidal sinuses empty into the middle meatus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: When cellular components are separated by centrifugation, in which cellular fraction is lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) most likely to be found?
questions.explanation: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is a vital metabolic enzyme that catalyzes the reversible conversion of pyruvate to lactate. This reaction is a final step in anaerobic glycolysis, a process that occurs entirely within the cytosol. Therefore, when cell components are separated via differential centrifugation, LDH is found in the supernatant representing the soluble cytoplasm or cytosol fraction. Mitochondria (Option A) contain enzymes for the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, such as succinate dehydrogenase. Lysosomes (Option B) are characterized by acid hydrolases. The Golgi complex (Option D) contains enzymes for protein modification and sorting, such as glycosyltransferases. LDH is often used in laboratory research as a marker enzyme for the cytoplasmic fraction to verify the purity of cell sub-fractions. Clinically, its release into the serum is a non-specific indicator of cell damage or lysis in various tissues
questions.learning: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is a vital metabolic enzyme that catalyzes the reversible conversion of pyruvate to lactate. This reaction is a final step in anaerobic glycolysis, a process that occurs entirely within the cytosol.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young male patient presents to ER with complaints of daytime somnolence and repeated awakening at night from sleep and his partner gives history of snoring in bed. All of the following are true except?
options: Apnea is due to fall in oxygen saturation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pharngeal muscle tone increases

Pharyngeal muscle tone decreases during snoring.

Pharyngeal muscles are relaxed during sleep and cause partial obstruction. Breathing against obstruction causes vibrations of soft palate, tonsillar pillars and base of tongue producing sound.

Types of snoring:

• Primary snoring: without association with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Primary snoring is not associated with excessive daytime sleepiness and has apnea—hypnoea index of less than five.
• Complicated snoring: associated with OSA.

Obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS) is diagnosed if the patient has either symptoms of nocturnal breathing disturbances or daytime sleepiness, and ≥5 episodes of obstructive apnea or hypopnea per hour of sleep. Each such episode should last for at least 10 seconds, resulting in ≥3% drop in oxygen saturation or a brain cortical arousal. OSA is diagnosed by overnight polysomnogram (PSG).

OSAHS is characterized by recurrent episodes of upper airway obstruction during sleep, leading to intermittent hypoxia and sleep fragmentation

Usually, there is a decline in neuromuscular output to pharyngeal dilator muscles during sleep. In predisposed individuals, this results in complete (apnea) or partial (hypopnea) pharyngeal collapse.
questions.learning: Pharngeal muscle tone increases Pharyngeal muscle tone decreases during snoring. Pharyngeal muscles are relaxed during sleep and cause partial obstruction.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn presented with chest retractions, dyspnea, and lethargy. The pediatrician diagnosed the baby with respiratory distress syndrome. This occurs due to the deficiency of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lecithin

Respiratory distress syndrome in a neonate is likely due to the deficiency of lecithin.

Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), also known as hyaline membrane disease, is due to the decreased production and secretion of the lung surfactant. Surfactant is a lipoprotein primarily made of phospholipids such as lecithin (otherwise known as dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine). The other minor components are phosphatidylglycerol, apoproteins, and cholesterol. It is synthesized in type II pneumocytes/granular pneumocytes in the endoplasmic reticulum (shown below).

RDS is commonly seen in preterm babies less than 34 weeks of gestation. Surfactant deficiency leads to an increase in the surface tension over the alveoli, causing the alveoli to collapse easily during expiration. Therefore, the baby has to put more effort to expand the lungs. Tachypnea, cyanosis, nasal flaring, prominent expiratory grunting, and intercostal and subcostal retractions are some of the common findings seen in this condition.

Chest x-ray shows features such as reticulogranular pattern, ground-glass opacity, and air bronchogram. White-out lungs can be seen on chest x-ray in severe diseases.

Management in mild to moderate RDS is with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), where the positive pressure keeps the alveoli open in a spontaneously breathing baby. Severe cases will require mechanical ventilation. Steroids increase the production of the surfactant, and therefore, steroids are administered antenatally to mothers with preterm labor.

Other options -

Option A: Dipalmitoyl inositol, or phosphatidylinositol, acts as a precursor for the secondary messenger system. It also helps in cell signaling and membrane trafficking.

Option C: Sphingomyelin is a dominant sphingolipid in the plasma membrane. The lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio in amniotic fluid helps in determining fetal lung maturity.

Option D: Dipalmitoyl ethanolamine is present in the cell membrane.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which constituent is the major determinant of serum osmolality among the given options?
questions.explanation: Sodium is the predominant cation in the extracellular fluid and the primary determinant of serum osmolality. This is evident from the standard clinical formula for estimated serum osmolality: Sodium is multiplied by two to account for its accompanying anions (mainly chloride and bicarbonate), demonstrating that it contributes the largest share to total osmolality. Potassium (Option A) is mainly an intracellular cation and is present in low serum concentrations, so its osmotic contribution is minimal. Bicarbonate (Option C) acts as a buffer but is present in much lower concentrations than sodium. Hydrogen ions (Option D) regulate pH and exist in extremely low concentrations, making their osmotic effect negligible. Therefore, sodium is the principal regulator of serum osmolality and water balance, and disturbances in serum sodium directly lead to osmotic shifts causing cerebral edema or dehydration

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of oseltamivir and zanamivir?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Neuraminidase inhibition

Oseltamivir and zanamivir are neuraminidase inhibitors.

They competitively and reversibly interact with the enzyme sites to inhibit viral neuraminidase activity. This interferes with the release of the progeny from infected host cells, halting the spread of infection.

Early administration hastens the resolution of symptoms if given within 48 h of infection. Oseltamivir is given at a dose of 75 mg, BD for 5 days for the treatment of Influenza A and B.

For prophylaxis, it is given at a dose of 75mg, OD and continued for the duration of exposure.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The most common cause of maternal mortality in India is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Obstetric haemorrhage

Obstetric haemorrhage is the leading direct cause of maternal mortality in India.

• Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) – most common
• Antepartum hemorrhage (placenta previa, abruptio placentae)
• Ruptured ectopic pregnancy

Rapid blood loss can lead to hypovolemic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and death if not managed promptly.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Obstructed labour: An important cause of maternal morbidity and mortality but less common than hemorrhage.
• C. Unsafe abortion: A significant preventable cause but contributes fewer maternal deaths than hemorrhage.
• D. Toxaemia of pregnancy (Hypertensive disorders): Includes preeclampsia and eclampsia; the second leading direct cause of maternal mortality in India.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is least likely to suggest a medical cause of her mental illness?
questions.explanation: In psychiatric evaluation, it is essential to distinguish between primary mental disorders and those secondary to a general medical condition. Auditory hallucinations (Option C) are a hallmark feature of primary psychiatric disorders like schizophrenia and are least likely to suggest an underlying medical cause. Conversely, the other options are significant "red flags" for organic (medical) brain syndromes. Elderly age (Option A) of onset for first-time psychiatric symptoms strongly suggests dementia or metabolic issues. A history of loss of consciousness (Option B) points toward trauma, epilepsy, or hypoxia. An acute onset (Option D) of confusion or behavioral changes is typical of delirium caused by infections, drug toxicity, or electrolyte imbalances. Primary psychiatric conditions usually have an insidious onset in younger adulthood and do not typically involve fluctuations in consciousness. Clinicians must always rule out these "medical" indicators before concluding that a patient's symptoms are purely functional or psychiatric in nature

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding management of hyperkalemia in a child? I. Intravenous calcium (gluconate or chloride) is given to enhance cellular uptake of potassium II. Beta adrenergic agonists (salbutamol or terbutaline) are used to stabilize myocardial cell membrane III. Regular insulin and glucose given intravenously enhance cellular uptake of potassium IV. Sodium polystyrene sulfonate enhances total body potassium elimination Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. III and IV

Hyperkalemia is a potentially life-threatening electrolyte emergency because it can cause fatal cardiac arrhythmias. Management involves three key principles:

1. Stabilize the cardiac membrane
2. Shift potassium into cells
3. Remove potassium from the body

Why is D correct?

• I. Intravenous calcium (gluconate or chloride) is given to enhance cellular uptake of potassium. ✘

• Incorrect.
• IV calcium does not lower serum potassium.
• It stabilizes the myocardial cell membrane, reducing the risk of life-threatening arrhythmias.

• II. Beta-adrenergic agonists (salbutamol or terbutaline) are used to stabilize myocardial cell membrane. ✘

• Incorrect.
• β₂-agonists shift potassium into cells by stimulating the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump.
• They do not stabilize the cardiac membrane.

• III. Regular insulin and glucose given intravenously enhance cellular uptake of potassium. ✔

• Correct.
• Insulin activates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, driving potassium into cells.
• Glucose is administered to prevent hypoglycemia.

• IV. Sodium polystyrene sulfonate enhances total body potassium elimination. ✔

• Correct.
• It is a cation-exchange resin that binds potassium in the intestine and increases fecal potassium excretion.

questions.text: What is the angle between the laparoscopic working port and telescope called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Azimuth angle

Azimuth angle is the angle between telescope and working port, ideally 15–30° for ergonomics. Elevation angle is instrument–abdominal wall angle, manipulation angle is between two working ports.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding UTI in pregnancy?
options: It is lower in people with sickle cell trait
The preferred antibiotic in pregnancy is amoxicillin
If ASB is not treated 75 % of them will develop symptomatic infection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The preferred antibiotic in pregnancy is amoxicillin

The true statement regarding UTI in pregnancy is that the preferred antibiotic in pregnancy is amoxicillin.

Asymptomatic bacteriuria(ASB) is characterized by persistent and actively multiplying bacteria in the urinary tract without any symptoms. It is defined as the presence of ≥105 colony-forming units/mL in a urine culture. Its prevalence during pregnancy is around 2-7% and it is a precursor of infection.

It is more common in patients with sickle cell anaemia/trait and diabetes. There is a high risk of developing chronic renal lesions in later life. ASB in pregnancy is associated with an increased risk of premature labour and low birth weight.

If ASB is not treated approximately 25% of the affected women will develop symptomatic infection during pregnancy

The oral antibiotics that can be used to treat asymptomatic bacteriuria are amoxicillin, ampicillin, cephalosporin, nitrofurantoin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Recurrent cases need to be treated until delivery with prophylactic doses.
questions.learning: The preferred antibiotic in pregnancy is amoxicillin The true statement regarding UTI in pregnancy is that the preferred antibiotic in pregnancy is amoxicillin.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 34-year-old man presents with chronic diarrhea, cognitive changes, and a photosensitive skin rash, with a diet mainly consisting of maize. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely causing these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The patient exhibits the classic triad of the "3 Ds": Diarrhea, Dermatitis (on sun-exposed areas), and Dementia (cognitive impairment). This is the hallmark of Pellagra, caused by a deficiency of Niacin (Vitamin B3). The dietary history of a maize-based diet is a significant clinical clue, as maize is deficient in both niacin and its precursor amino acid, tryptophan. Furthermore, the niacin in maize is often chemically bound and unabsorbable unless treated with lime. Vitamin B6 (Option B) and Biotin (Option D) deficiencies cause different skin and neurological issues but not the specific photosensitive rash of pellagra. Ascorbic acid (Option C) deficiency causes scurvy. Pellagra was historically common in populations where corn was the primary staple. Modern management involve niacin supplementation and dietary diversification. Recognizing the link between maize consumption and the "3 Ds" is a fundamental requirement for diagnosing nutritional deficiencies in clinical practice
questions.learning: The patient exhibits the classic triad of the "3 Ds": Diarrhea, Dermatitis (on sun-exposed areas), and Dementia (cognitive impairment). This is the hallmark of Pellagra, caused by a deficiency of Niacin (Vitamin B3).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with chest pain, dyspnea increasing on lying down and relieved on sitting upright. On examination, heart sounds are muffled and her lungs are clear. CXR given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cardiac Tamponade

| Finding | Significance

| ------- | ------------

| Dyspnea relieved by sitting forward | Pericardial disease

| Muffled heart sounds | Fluid around heart

| Clear lungs | Not pulmonary edema

Dyspnea worse on lying down and relieved by sitting up suggests pericardial pathology.

Muffled heart sounds with clear lung fields indicate pericardial effusion causing tamponade.

Cardiac tamponade presents with Beck’s triad:

| Feature | Mechanism

| ------- | ---------

| Hypotension | ↓ Cardiac output

| JVD | Impaired venous return

| Muffled heart sounds | Fluid around heart

Chest X-ray typically shows an enlarged, globular cardiac silhouette.

Pulmonary edema would have lung crepitations, and MI or embolism do not cause muffled heart sounds.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 38-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of spontaneous, unilateral, blood-stained discharge from a single duct of the right nipple. There is no palpable breast lump. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intraductal papilloma

Intraductal papilloma is the most common cause of spontaneous, unilateral, blood-stained nipple discharge from a single duct in women aged 35–55 years. It is a benign papillary tumor arising within a major lactiferous duct, usually located beneath the areola.

Why not the other options?

• B. Fibroadenoma: Presents as a painless, mobile breast lump; nipple discharge is uncommon.
• C. Duct ectasia: Usually occurs in perimenopausal women and causes multiduct, thick green/brown, sticky discharge with nipple retraction.
• D. Breast carcinoma: May cause bloody nipple discharge, but is usually associated with a palpable hard irregular lump, skin changes, or axillary lymphadenopathy.
questions.learning: Intraductal papilloma Intraductal papilloma is the most common cause of spontaneous, unilateral, blood-stained nipple discharge from a single duct in women aged 35–55 years.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A young woman reports a history of unprotected intercourse four days ago and requests emergency contraception. Which option is most appropriate in this situation?
questions.explanation: For a woman requesting emergency contraception up to 5 days (120 hours) after unprotected intercourse, the most effective and suitable option is the insertion of a Copper Intrauterine Contraceptive Device (IUCD). The Copper T IUCD has a failure rate of less than 0.1% and provides the added benefit of ongoing, long-term reversible contraception. Levonorgestrel (LNG) (Option A) is very effective but its efficacy drops significantly if taken more than 72 hours after intercourse. OCPs (Option C) used in the "Yuzpe regimen" are less effective and cause more side effects than LNG or IUCD. Misoprostol (Option D) is used for medical abortion, not for emergency contraception. While oral medications like Ulipristal acetate are also effective up to 5 days, the IUCD remains the "gold standard" for efficacy regardless of the timing within the 5-day window or the patient's body mass index. Clinicians must offer the IUCD to all women seeking emergency contraception as it is the only method that offers near-perfect protection
questions.learning: For a woman requesting emergency contraception up to 5 days (120 hours) after unprotected intercourse, the most effective and suitable option is the insertion of a Copper Intrauterine Contraceptive Device (IUCD).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 5-year-old girl was brought to the outpatient department by her mother saying she noted some abnormality in her genital area. On examination, there was presence of pubic and axillary hair. Which of the following is the least likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 17-Hydroxylase deficiency

The presence of pubic and axillary hair in a five-year-old girl is suggestive of precocious puberty and 17-Hydroxylase deficiency is least likely to cause it.

In 17-hydroxylase deficiency, patients are unable to synthesize sex hormones. Females are normal at birth and present with complaints of delayed puberty, primary amenorrhea, and a lack of secondary sexual characteristics in later life. The affected males are incompletely virilized and present as phenotypic females but undescended testes are usually palpable in the inguinal region.

In both 21-hydroxylase and 11β-hydroxylase deficiencies, the respective precursors to the hormones are shunted to the androgen synthesis pathway, resulting in all the signs and symptoms of androgen excess. Female babies are typically born with signs of virilization like ambiguous genitalia characterized by clitoral enlargement and labial fusion. Whereas, the males have normal-appearing genitalia at birth and present at 2 to 4 years with precocious puberty like early pubarche, a growth spurt, and adult body odour.

Since this child is having features of ambiguous genitalia and virilization, it is unlikely that she would have a 17-Hydroxylase deficiency.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the cause of the sago-grain appearance of the conjunctiva?
questions.explanation: "Sago-grain appearance" is a classic clinical description used for Bitot's spots, which are a hallmark sign of Vitamin A deficiency (Xerophthalmia). These are small, foamy, triangular-shaped white plaques that typically appear on the bulbar conjunctiva, most often on the temporal side. They are composed of keratinized epithelial cells and Corynebacterium xerosis bacteria. Option B (Pterygium) is a fleshy, fibrovascular growth. Option C (Phlyctenular conjunctivitis) presents as a small nodule near the limbus. Option D (Membranous conjunctivitis) features a thick layer of fibrin on the conjunctival surface. Vitamin A deficiency is a major cause of preventable childhood blindness worldwide. It begins with night blindness (Nyctalopia) and progresses to Bitot's spots, corneal xerosis, and finally keratomalacia (softening of the cornea). Management involves immediate high-dose oral Vitamin A supplementation according to WHO protocols to prevent permanent ocular damage and improve systemic health

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Biosafety level for culture of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. BSL III

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is handled in Biosafety Level III (BSL-III) laboratories.

• MTB is transmitted via airborne droplet nuclei, requiring strict airborne precautions
• BSL-III is designed for pathogens that can cause serious or potentially lethal disease via inhalation
• Laboratory features include:

• Negative pressure rooms
• HEPA-filtered exhaust air
• Controlled access
• Work within biosafety cabinets

Comparison:

• BSL I: non-pathogenic organisms
• BSL II: moderate-risk pathogens (e.g., Staphylococcus, Salmonella)
• BSL III: airborne pathogens (e.g., Mycobacterium tuberculosis)
• BSL IV: highly dangerous agents with no treatment (e.g., Ebola virus)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman presents with fatigue, pallor, and jaundice, and investigations show hemolytic anemia with spherocytes on peripheral smear. In which condition is elective splenectomy considered the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation: Hereditary spherocytosis (HS) is an inherited disorder of the red blood cell membrane, typically due to defects in proteins like ankyrin or spectrin. This results in the formation of rigid, spherical RBCs (spherocytes) that are selectively trapped and destroyed as they pass through the narrow splenic sinusoids. This destruction leads to the classic triad of anemia, jaundice, and splenomegaly. Elective splenectomy is the preferred and definitive treatment for symptomatic HS, as it effectively stops the premature destruction of these abnormal cells, thereby resolving the anemia and jaundice. G6PD deficiency (Option A) is an episodic condition managed by avoiding triggers. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (Option B) involves a complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis and is treated with eculizumab. Hairy cell leukemia (Option D) is a malignant lymphoproliferative disorder where splenectomy was historically used but has been replaced by chemotherapy. While splenectomy does not correct the underlying membrane defect in HS, it removes the primary site of cell death, significantly improving the patient's quality of life

questions.text: A young male patient developed abdominal pain for which he was being evaluated. CT and IVU findings are given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Horse shoe kidney

The given images show a horseshoe kidney. It is prone to obstruction, reflux, and stone formation (the likely cause of pain in this case)

Horseshoe kidney is the most common congenital anomaly of the kidneys with male preponderance

Horseshoe kidney is caused due to the fusion of the lower poles of the kidney. The lower border of the kidneys usually lies in front of the L3 vertebra due to the arrest of ascent.

The common associations of horseshoe kidney are:

* Vesicoureteral Reflux

* Wilms Tumor

* Multicystic Dysplastic Kidney

* Turner’s Syndrome

IVU findings of a Horseshoe kidney:

* Handshake sign - due to the position of the lower poles closer to the spine, and the lower calyces closer to each other

* Flower vase sign - due to medially rotated calyces

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with salicylic acid poisoning has the following arterial blood gas analysis report: pH = 7.3, pCO2 =16mmHg, HCO3-=6.3mmol/L, Na+- 135, K+- 4.5 Cl- 113.7, lactate was normal. Which of the following options correctly describes the condition?
options: Metabolic acidosis with partial compensated respiratory alkolosis with high anion gap
Respiratory acidosis with compensatory metabolic alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis with uncompensated respiratory alkalosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Metabolic acidosis with partial compensated respiratory alkolosis with high anion gap

The acid-base disorder here is a mixed disorder of metabolic acidosis with partially compensated respiratory alkalosis with high anion gap.

It should not be confused with metabolic acidosis with uncompensated respiratory alkalosis. This can be understood by the following calculation:

Step 1: The pH in this patient is 7.3 (pH <7.35) which indicates acidosis

Step 2: HCO3- is 6.3 mmol/L (Normal HCO3- - 22–30 mmol/L). In metabolic acidosis, HCO3- levels decrease.

Hence, this is a case of metabolic acidosis.

Step 3: Calculate the anion gap.

Anion gap = Na+-(Cl-+HCO3-)

= 135 – (113.7 +6.3)

= 15, which is a high anion gap (normal anion gap is between 6-12 mEq/L)

Step 4: As per Winter's formula, the expected respiratory compensation in metabolic acidosis can be calculated using,

pCO2 =( 1.5 x [HCO3-] ) +8 ± 2

In this case, Expected pCO2 = ( 1.5 x [6.3] ) +8 ± 2

= 17.5 ± 2

= 15.45 - 19.45 mmHg

The pCO2 in this patient is 16 mmHg, which implies there is an overcompensation of pCO2. This overcompensation can happen only if there is an additional component of respiratory alkalosis contributing to reduced pCO2.

Hence, this patient has a mixed disorder - metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis.
questions.learning: Metabolic acidosis with partial compensated respiratory alkolosis with high anion gap The acid-base disorder here is a mixed disorder of metabolic acidosis with partially compensated respiratory alkalosis with high anion gap.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Twin pregnancy should have ultrasound at 10–13 weeks to confirm which of the following? I. Number of foetus II. Viability of foetus III. Chorionicity of twins IV. Malformation in either foetus Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I, II, III and IV

A first-trimester ultrasound (10–13+6 weeks) is the most important scan in twin pregnancy. It establishes the diagnosis of multiple gestation, accurately determines chorionicity and amnionicity, confirms fetal viability, dates the pregnancy, and screens for major fetal anomalies. Early determination of chorionicity is essential because it is the single most important predictor of pregnancy outcome in twin gestations.

All the listed objectives are achieved by ultrasound at 10–13 weeks:

• I. Number of fetus: Confirms whether the pregnancy is singleton, twin, or higher-order multiple gestation. ⭐
• II. Viability of fetus: Demonstrates cardiac activity in each fetus and confirms viability. ⭐
• III. Chorionicity of twins: The most important purpose of the first-trimester scan is to determine chorionicity and amnionicity. This is best assessed between 11 and 13+6 weeks using:

• Lambda (Twin Peak) sign → Dichorionic twins
• T-sign → Monochorionic twins

• IV. Malformation in either fetus: A first-trimester scan includes screening for major structural anomalies and nuchal translucency assessment.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old male presented with verrucous carcinoma around the glans of the penis. Examination reveals that the inguinal lymph nodes are not enlarged. What is the appropriate management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Partial penectomy.

The most appropriate management for this patient with verrucous carcinoma around the glans of the penis is partial penectomy.

Carcinoma of the penis is commonly a squamous cell carcinoma. It arises from the skin of the glans penis or the prepuce. The lesion can be flat or warty in appearance.

• T1- confined to the skin
• T2- invades the corpus spongiosum or cavernosum.
• T3- invades the urethra
• T4- invades adjacent structures.

The first lymph node to be involved is the superficial inguinal lymph node and thus, the sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) is helpful for evaluating the spread of penile cancer.

Tumors of low-grade and low-stage are managed by Mohs’ surgery. Tumors involving the glans penis require glansectomy, and in advanced cases require partial penectomy.

Other options:

Option A: In penile carcinoma, total amputation of the penis is done if the stump is < 2cm after resection of the tumor.

Options B, and C: Topical 5-fluorouracil cream and CO2 laser ablation are preferred in case of penile intraepithelial neoplasia.
questions.learning: The most appropriate management for this patient with verrucous carcinoma around the glans of the penis is partial penectomy. Carcinoma of the penis is commonly a squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with dryness of the eyes requiring frequent use of artificial tears and dryness of the mouth requiring frequent sipping of water. She also reports pain and stiffness involving multiple joints of the hands. There is no history of skin tightening, Raynaud phenomenon, oral ulcers, or photosensitive rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sjögren syndrome

Sjögren syndrome, an autoimmune exocrinopathy characterized by lymphocytic destruction of the lacrimal and salivary glands, leading to keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes) and xerostomia (dry mouth). It may occur as a primary disorder or secondary to another autoimmune disease, most commonly rheumatoid arthritis.

• Autoantibodies: Anti-SSA (Ro) and Anti-SSB (La) are highly characteristic; ANA and RF are frequently positive.
• Diagnosis: Positive Schirmer test (↓ tear production), ocular surface staining, and minor salivary gland (lip) biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis.
• Complications: Dental caries, oral candidiasis, parotid gland enlargement, corneal damage, and a markedly increased risk of MALT (marginal zone B-cell) lymphoma.
• Treatment: Artificial tears, saliva substitutes, muscarinic agonists (pilocarpine, cevimeline), and immunomodulatory therapy for systemic disease.

Why not the other options?

• A. SLE: Typically presents with photosensitive rash, oral ulcers, nephritis, serositis, and hematologic abnormalities; sicca symptoms may occur but are not the predominant feature.
• B. Systemic sclerosis: Characterized by skin thickening, Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and internal organ fibrosis rather than isolated sicca symptoms.
• C. Rheumatoid arthritis: Causes symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis but does not cause prominent dry eyes and dry mouth unless associated with secondary Sjögren syndrome.
questions.learning: Sjögren syndrome Sjögren syndrome, an autoimmune exocrinopathy characterized by lymphocytic destruction of the lacrimal and salivary glands, leading to keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes) and xerostomia (dry mouth).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A teenager developed swelling of the face, lips, and tongue and also found it difficult to breathe within a few minutes of consumption of prawns. What is the type of hypersensitivity seen here ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Type 1

Anaphylaxis following consumption of prawns is an example of IgE-mediated reaction or Type 1 hypersensitivity.

Immediate (Type I) Hypersensitivity

* These are also called allergic reactions or allergies.

* They are induced by environmental antigens (allergens) that stimulate strong TH2 responses and IgE production in genetically susceptible individuals

* Activation of TH2 cells is mediated by IL-4 and in turn, TH2 cells produce IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13.

* These cytokines act on B cells to stimulate IgE and activation of eosinophils.

* IgE coats mast cells by binding to Fcεg receptors; reexposure to the allergen leads to cross-linking of the IgE and FcεRI, activation of mast cells, and release of mediators.

* The principal mediators are histamine, proteases, and other granule contents; prostaglandins and leukotrienes; as well as cytokines.

* The mediators are responsible for the immediate vascular and smooth muscle reactions and the late-phase reaction (inflammation).

* The clinical manifestations may be local or systemic and range from mildly annoying rhinitis to fatal anaphylaxis.

* It occurs in two phases: immediate phase and late phase.

Image: Sequence of events in immediate hypersensitivity

Pearl PF0858: Disorders Caused by Immediate Hypersensitivity

Clinical Syndrome

Clinical and Pathologic Manifestations

Anaphylaxis (may be caused by drugs, bee sting, food)

Fall in blood pressure (shock) caused by vascular dilation; airway obstruction due to laryngeal edema

Bronchial asthma

Airway obstruction caused by bronchial smooth muscle hyperactivity; inflammation and tissue injury caused by late-phase reaction

Allergic rhinitis, sinusitis (hay fever)

Increased mucus secretion; inflammation of upper airways, sinuses

Food allergies

Increased peristalsis due to contraction of intestinal muscles

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following features is not associated with superior semicircular canal dehiscence syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sensorineural hearing loss

Sensorineural hearing loss is not seen in superior semicircular canal dehiscence syndrome (SSCDS). They may experience mild to moderate hearing conductive loss.

Conductive hearing loss is due to the abnormal transmission and dissipation of acoustic energy through the defect (third window), leading to reduced conduction to the cochlea for lower frequencies. This can manifest as a low-frequency air-bone gap at multiple frequencies. There is no defect in the cochlea or the auditory pathway.

Superior semicircular canal dehiscence (SSCD) is a condition in which bone between the apex of the superior semicircular canal and the middle cranial fossa is absent. This causes endolymph in the labyrinthine system to move with sound or pressure, causing an activation of the vestibular system.

Patients may have vestibular symptoms like vertigo triggered by loud sounds (Tullio phenomenon)or pressure such as coughing and can also experience hyperacusis for bone-conducted sounds. They may perceive the sounds of their own eye movements or footsteps in the affected ear.

The patients may exhibit nystagmus when exposed to loud sounds or during the Valsalva maneuver or pressure in the ear canal (positive fistula test). The direction of the nystagmus aligns with the affected superior semicircular canal, and some patients may tilt their heads in the plane of the affected superior semicircular canal in response to loud sounds.

Noncontrast HRCT of the temporal bone can demonstrate the defect. The click-evoked VEMP (vestibular evoked myogenic potential) response and vestibuloocular reflex are pronounced in SSCD patients, in which the evoked eye movements align with the affected superior canal.

For mild symptoms, avoidance of triggers is recommended. In case of severe disabling symptoms, surgical resurfacing of the superior semicircular canal or plugging of the superior semicircular canal may be attempted.
questions.learning: Sensorineural hearing loss Sensorineural hearing loss is not seen in superior semicircular canal dehiscence syndrome (SSCDS). They may experience mild to moderate hearing conductive loss.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 38-year-old man comes to the OPD with reports of dyspnea on exertion and decreased exercise tolerance. His medical history is unremarkable, and he has no history of childhood asthma or cough. The patient has gained almost 30kg over the past 4 years due to a sedentary lifestyle. He currently has a BMI of 41 kg/m2. His respiratory rate is 22/min and pulse oximetry is 93% on room air at rest. Physical examination is notable for central obesity. Lungs are clear on auscultation bilaterally. Which of the following changes are most likely to be seen on pulmonary function testing in this patient?
options: FEV1 low, FVC low, RV normal, TLC low
FEV1 low, FVC low, RV high, TLC high
FEV1 high, FVC low, RV normal, TLC low
FEV1 low, FVC low, RV high, TLC low
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. FEV1 low, FVC low, RV normal, TLC low

Severe obesity (BMI ≥40) can cause a restrictive ventilatory defect due to reduced chest wall compliance and diaphragmatic limitation.

Pulmonary function test findings in obesity-related restriction:

• ↓ FEV₁
• ↓ FVC
• Normal or mildly reduced RV
• ↓ Total lung capacity (TLC)

Reason:

Excess abdominal and thoracic fat limits lung expansion, reducing lung volumes but preserving the FEV₁/FVC ratio (restrictive pattern).
questions.learning: FEV1 low, FVC low, RV normal, TLC low Severe obesity (BMI ≥40) can cause a restrictive ventilatory defect due to reduced chest wall compliance and diaphragmatic limitation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A woman has been using combined oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) for contraception. The use of combined OCPs is associated with a reduced risk of several cancers. Which of the following cancers does not have a reduced risk with OCP use?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cervical cancer

Use of combined oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) is associated with a reduced risk of ovarian, endometrial, and colorectal cancers due to suppression of ovulation and endometrial proliferation.

In contrast, long-term OCP use is associated with an increased risk of cervical cancer, not a protective effect.

Hence, cervical cancer does not show reduced risk with OCP use.
questions.learning: Cervical cancer Use of combined oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) is associated with a reduced risk of ovarian, endometrial, and colorectal cancers due to suppression of ovulation and endometrial proliferation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is considered to be the best for the detection of Clostridium difficile?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glutamate dehydrogenase and toxin assay

A combination of glutamate dehydrogenase and toxin assay can be used for the detection of Clostridium difficile.

Clostridium difficile is a gram-positive anaerobic bacillus that causes Clostridioides (formerly Clostridium) difficile infection after ingestion of spores of the organism. The more severe form of the condition is known as pseudomembranous colitis (PMC). Enzyme immunoassay to detect glutamate dehydrogenase is less specific compared to toxin detection for diagnosis. So a combination of the two can be used for diagnostic confirmation.

The condition is most commonly associated with prolonged antimicrobial use, which interferes with the commensal colonic microflora. The most commonly implicated antibiotics are cephalosporins, ampicillin, and clindamycin. The spores are spread by contact with the feces of affected individuals or asymptomatic carriers. It can persist on surfaces for months. Risk factors include poor hand hygiene, old age, and gastrointestinal surgery.

The spores germinate in the small intestine and produce two toxins—toxin A (enterotoxin) and toxin B (cytotoxin). These interfere with the epithelial-cell barrier function and result in diarrhea and pseudomembrane formation. The pseudomembranes appear as small whitish-yellow plaques initially which later coalesce to involve the entire colon wall. It contains necrotic leukocytes, fibrin, and cellular debris. The anamnestic IgG response determines which patients develop the disease or remain asymptomatic.

Symptoms include diarrhea, fever, and abdominal pain. The diagnosis is based on a combination of clinical criteria and detection of toxin or the organism in stool samples. This can be done by nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) methods such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or by culture.

Discontinuation of any ongoing antimicrobials and adequate hydration are general measures that are recommended. Oral fidaxomicin or vancomycin is the first-line treatment. Oral metronidazole can be used when these are not available.

Other options:

Option A: Aerobic culture of stool is the most sensitive test and is highly specific. It is not used practically as the turnaround time is slow.
questions.learning: Glutamate dehydrogenase and toxin assay — A combination of glutamate dehydrogenase and toxin assay can be used for the detection of Clostridium difficile.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which one of the following correctly denotes the inheritance pattern of cystic fibrosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Autosomal Recessive

Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator) gene located on chromosome 7. The most common mutation is ΔF508 (deletion of phenylalanine at position 508).

The defective CFTR protein results in impaired chloride and bicarbonate transport, leading to thick, viscous secretions in multiple organs, particularly the lungs, pancreas, gastrointestinal tract, and reproductive system.

Cystic fibrosis follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, meaning:

• Both parents are typically asymptomatic carriers.
• The child must inherit two mutated CFTR alleles to develop the disease.
• Each pregnancy carries:

• 25% affected
• 50% carrier
• 25% unaffected
questions.learning: Autosomal Recessive Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator) gene located on chromosome 7.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old male patient was brought to the ER after RTA, his RR is 25/min, BP is 80/45mmHg. On examination, hyper-resonance is heard over the left side of the chest. The chest X-ray performed is given below. What would be the appropriate management in this case?
options: Wide bore needle insertion in the 5th ICS
Wide bore needle insertion in the 5th ICS followed by an intercostal drain in the 5th ICS
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wide bore needle insertion in the 5th ICS followed by an intercostal drain in the 5th ICS

The given clinical scenario and the given chest radiograph are suggestive of pneumothorax. It is managed by inserting wide-bore needle in 5th ICS followed by placing an intercostal drain in the 5th ICS.

Tension pneumothorax and simple pneumothorax have similar signs, symptoms, and examination findings, but hypotension qualifies the pneumothorax as a tension pneumothorax.

Immediate management includes inserting a wide-bore needle in the 5th intercostal space in the midaxillary line.

Definitive management includes insertion of the intercostal tube in the triangle of safety. If a sucking wound is present, then it is covered with gauze pieces and taped on 3 sides.

Remember: (Acc to ATLS 10th edition)

* In adults, needle thoracotomy location changed to 5th ICS mid axillary line from 2nd ICS midclavicular line.

* In the pediatric age group, the thoracotomy location remains at the 2nd ICS midclavicular line.
questions.learning: Wide bore needle insertion in the 5th ICS followed by an intercostal drain in the 5th ICS The given clinical scenario and the given chest radiograph are suggestive of pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-year-old child presents with sudden onset of loud, abnormal breathing sounds. Based on the symptoms, a specific type of stridor is suspected. Stridor is a high-pitched sound caused by turbulent airflow in the upper airway, reflecting the phase of breathing most affected by obstruction. Which type of stridor is most likely in this child?
questions.explanation: In a 2-year-old child, acute onset of loud breathing sounds (stridor) is most commonly caused by obstructions in the extra-thoracic upper airway, such as Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) or a foreign body at the level of the glottis. This typically results in an inspiratory stridor, which is audible only during the inhalation phase. This occurs because the negative pressure within the upper airway during inspiration causes the flexible tissue above the thoracic inlet to collapse inward, narrowing the lumen further. Expiratory stridor (Option B) is associated with obstructions below the thoracic inlet, such as a foreign body in the bronchus or asthma. Biphasic stridor (Option C) indicates a fixed, severe obstruction at the level of the glottis or subglottis that affects both phases of the respiratory cycle. Given the common pediatric presentations of acute airway narrowing, inspiratory stridor is the most frequent clinical finding
questions.learning: In a 2-year-old child, acute onset of loud breathing sounds (stridor) is most commonly caused by obstructions in the extra-thoracic upper airway, such as Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) or a foreign body at the level of the glottis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements about Ciclesonide is incorrect?
options: Oral candidiasis is common with its use
It has fewer side effects than other inhalational corticosteroids.
It is a prodrug activated by bronchial esterase.
It has comparable efficacy to other inhalational corticosteroids.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Oral candidiasis is common with its use

Ciclesonide

A clever inhaled corticosteroid that behaves like a “stealth prodrug”→ Active only in the lungs

Ciclesonide is an inhaled corticosteroid prodrug activated in the lungs by bronchial esterases. Because activation occurs locally, oropharyngeal deposition is minimal and oral candidiasis is uncommon. It has fewer systemic and local side effects while maintaining efficacy comparable to other inhaled steroids. Hence stating candidiasis is common is incorrect.

| Feature | Ciclesonide | Other ICS

| ------- | ----------- | ---------

| Prodrug | ✔ Yes | ❌ No

| Activation | Lung only | Everywhere

| Oral candidiasis | ↓ Low | ↑ Higher

| Systemic effects | ↓ Minimal | ↑ More
questions.learning: Oral candidiasis is common with its use Ciclesonide — A clever inhaled corticosteroid that behaves like a “stealth prodrug”→ Active only in the lungs Ciclesonide is an inhaled corticosteroid prodrug activated in the lungs by bronchial esterases.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the pattern of inheritance in neural tube defects?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Multifactorial inheritance

The pattern of inheritance in neural tube defects(NTDs) is multifactorial inheritance.

Multifactorial inheritance refers to traits that are caused by a combination of inherited, environmental, and stochastic factors. NTDs and a number of other congenital malformations, such as cleft lip and palate, can recur in families, but inheritance for the majority of affected individuals does not occur in a straightforward, mendelian inheritance pattern. In this situation, multiple genes and environmental factors together likely contribute to the pathogenesis.

These include the following:

Children (congenital malformation)

Adults

Pyloric stenosis

Neural tube defects

Congenital heart defects

Congenital dislocation of hip

Cleft lip and cleft palate

Diabetes Mellitus

Hypertension

Coronary heart disease

Gout

Schizophrenia
