questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 47-year-old woman was brought to the casualty in an unconscious state after having suddenly collapsed. As there was no pulse, cardiopulmonary resuscitation was started and the monitor showed the following rhythm. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 mg epinephrine IV

The patient has an organized, apparently normal ECG without a pulse - i.e the patient has pulseless electrical activity (PEA). A pulseless electrical activity involves a heterogeneous group of cardiac rhythms all without a pulse.

The immediate treatment for this is giving chest compressions and 1 mg epinephrine at the earliest until more definitive therapy to the cause can be instituted.

It is essential to rule out the reversible causes of cardiac arrest because the treatment for each of them is different and PEA is likely to persist until the cause is treated.

Pearl PF1232: Reversible Causes of Cardiac Arrest

* 5 H’s:

* Hypovolemia

* Hypoxia

* Hydrogen ion (acidosis)

* Hypokalemia or hyperkalemia

* Hypothermia

* 5 T’s:

* Tension pneumothorax

* Tamponade (cardiac)

* Toxins

* Thrombosis (pulmonary)

* Thrombosis (coronary)
questions.learning: 1 mg epinephrine IV The patient has an organized, apparently normal ECG without a pulse - i.e the patient has pulseless electrical activity (PEA). A pulseless electrical activity involves a heterogeneous group of cardiac rhythms all without a pulse.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Anaplasia refers to:
options: Variation in cell size and shape
Replacement of one type of cell by other
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lack of differentiation

Anaplasia refers to a lack of differentiation.

The term anaplasia means to form backward implying a reversal of differentiation to a more primitive level. The extent to which neoplastic cells resemble normal cells, both morphologically and functionally, is called differentiation.

Anaplasia is an important morphological feature of malignant transformation.

The morphological features of malignancy include:

• Anaplasia
• Pleomorphism - variation in the size and shape of cells
• Increased N: C ratio (nucleus: cytoplasmic ratio) - around 1:4 in normal cells, increases to 1:1 in malignant cells
• Hyperchromasia - coarsely clumped and darkly stained chromatin within irregular nuclei
• Increased mitosis - atypical, bizarre mitotic figures
• Loss of polarity - sheets or large masses of tumor cells grow in an anarchic, disorganized fashion
questions.learning: Lack of differentiation Anaplasia refers to a lack of differentiation. The term anaplasia means to form backward implying a reversal of differentiation to a more primitive level.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The process of apolipoprotein B48 synthesis involves which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. RNA editing

The process of apolipoprotein B48 synthesis involves RNA editing.

RNA editing is the process by which the coding sequence of the mRNA is changed before translation. As a result, the mRNA template differs from the DNA from which it was transcribed. This leads to the formation of a different protein. This occurs by insertion of additional uracils at the 3’ end of the mRNA and proceeds in 3’ to 5’ direction.

RNA editing in apoB synthesis:

• In the liver, the apoB gene is transcribed to mRNA which is then translated to apoB 100.
• In the intestine, the same apoB gene is transcribed to the same mRNA. But now, the mRNA undergoes editing by an enzyme cytidine deaminase which converts the CAA codon in the mRNA to UAA at a single specific site. This edited mRNA translates to apoB 48.
questions.learning: RNA editing — The process of apolipoprotein B48 synthesis involves RNA editing. RNA editing is the process by which the coding sequence of the mRNA is changed before translation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old traveler was lost in the desert. He was found after 2 days. He says that he has not consumed food or water for more than 24 hours. His vitals were normal. Which of the following part of the kidney must have been the site of maximum water reabsorption in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Proximal convoluted tubule

The proximal convoluted tubule is the site of maximum water reabsorption about 67% of the filtered water.

The driving force for water reabsorption is a transtubular osmotic gradient established by reabsorption of solutes.

Based on the ultrastructure proximal tubule is divided into three segments:

* S1 segment: 1st half of PCT

* S2 segment: 2nd half of PCT and 1st half of proximal straight tubule

* S3 segment: 2nd half of proximal straight tubule

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: During the action potential, at which point in the given image are both Na⁺ and K⁺ conductance at their lowest?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A

At the resting membrane potential (Point A), both voltage-gated Na⁺ and K⁺ channels are closed, so Na⁺ and K⁺ conductance are at their lowest. The resting membrane potential is maintained primarily by K⁺ leak channels and the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, not by voltage-gated ion channels.

Why not the other options?

• B. B (Threshold): Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels begin to open, increasing Na⁺ conductance.
• C. E (Repolarization): K⁺ conductance is high due to opening of voltage-gated K⁺ channels, while Na⁺ channels are inactivated.
• D. F (After-hyperpolarization): K⁺ channels remain open longer than necessary, so K⁺ conductance is still elevated.

Exam Pearls:

• Point A (Resting membrane potential): Lowest voltage-gated Na⁺ and K⁺ conductance
• Depolarization: Rapid ↑ Na⁺ conductance due to opening of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
• Peak of action potential: Na⁺ channels become inactivated; K⁺ channels begin opening
• Repolarization & after-hyperpolarization: ↑ K⁺ conductance due to delayed closure of voltage-gated K⁺ channels
• Resting membrane potential (\~–70 mV): Maintained mainly by K⁺ leak channels and the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, not voltage-gated channels.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Injury to which part causes difficulty in dorsiflexion of the foot?
questions.explanation: In the provided image, point B identifies the common peroneal nerve as it courses superficially around the neck of the fibula. This nerve is highly susceptible to injury at this site. It branches into the deep and superficial peroneal nerves, with the deep peroneal nerve responsible for innervating the tibialis anterior muscle. This muscle is the primary driver of dorsiflexion (lifting the foot upward). An injury at point B results in "foot drop," where the patient cannot dorsiflex the foot. The sciatic nerve (Point A) would cause much more extensive leg weakness. The tibial nerve (Point C) innervates the posterior compartment, and its injury would cause difficulty in plantarflexion (pointing the foot down). While the deep peroneal nerve (Point D) also causes foot drop, the injury at the fibular head (B) is the more classic clinical site
questions.learning: In the provided image, point B identifies the common peroneal nerve as it courses superficially around the neck of the fibula. This nerve is highly susceptible to injury at this site.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient diagnosed with borderline tuberculoid leprosy presents with the given clinical findings. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is involved, and which nerve is characteristically enlarged in this condition?
questions.explanation: The patient demonstrates a visibly thickened greater auricular nerve in the neck. In borderline tuberculoid leprosy, acute inflammation of nerves and skin lesions indicates a Type 1 (reversal) reaction. This reaction is a form of delayed-type hypersensitivity (Type IV) caused by a sudden increase in the cell-mediated immune response to Mycobacterium leprae. Type 1 reactions (Option A) are immediate IgE-mediated allergies. Type 2 reactions (Option B) are antibody-mediated. Type 3 reactions (Option C) involve immune complexes, such as Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL), which is the clinical manifestation of a Type 2 leprosy reaction. Because the reversal reaction specifically involves a T-cell mediated response and commonly affects the greater auricular nerve, the pairing in Option D is correct
questions.learning: The patient demonstrates a visibly thickened greater auricular nerve in the neck. In borderline tuberculoid leprosy, acute inflammation of nerves and skin lesions indicates a Type 1 (reversal) reaction.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding the thoracolumbar fascia is incorrect?
options: In the lumbar region, it is in 4 layers
In the thoracic region, it is attached medially to the vertebrae
The anterior, posterior, and middle layers join to form the aponeurotic origin of transversus abdominis
questions.explanation: The thoracolumbar fascia is a critical structural complex in the back, but statement B is incorrect because it consists of three layers in the lumbar region, not four. These are the anterior, middle, and posterior layers which envelop the psoas major, quadratus lumborum, and erector spinae muscles. Statement A is correct; the fascia is highly innervated with nociceptive and proprioceptive nerve endings, playing a significant role in chronic low back pain. Statement C is correct, as the fascia in the thoracic region is a thin fibrous layer attached medially to the thoracic spines. Statement D is also correct, as the three layers fuse laterally to form the aponeurotic origin of the transversus abdominis and internal oblique muscles. This fascia acts as a "nature's back brace," providing stability to the spine and facilitating load transfer between the upper and lower limbs. Understanding its trilaminar structure is essential for surgical approaches to the posterior abdominal wall
questions.learning: The thoracolumbar fascia is a critical structural complex in the back, but statement B is incorrect because it consists of three layers in the lumbar region, not four.

questions.text: An employee diagnosed with TB gets extended sickness benefit for:
questions.explanation:

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Identify the neurological test being performed.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Babinski sign

The image shows extensor plantar response, which is a positive Babinski sign.

The normal response to uncomfortable or painful cutaneous stimulation of the file of the foot includes plantar flexion of the toes. This can be accompanied by flexion withdrawal of the limb. If there is an upper motor neuron lesion affecting the leg being tested, there will be an extensor plantar response, which is a positive Babinski sign. The minimum extensor response to be looked for is at least the extension of the great toe. It can be accompanied by fanning of other tows and contraction of the tensor fascia lata. Other features which may be seen in UMN lesions are spasticity of the leg, pathologically brisk reflexes, and ankle clonus.

The below image shows the positive and negative Babinski signs.

The image below shows a positive Babinski sign in an adult, which is abnormal and indicative of a UMN lesion.

In infants whose corticospinal tracts are still underdeveloped, dorsiflexion of the great toe and fanning of other toes is a normal response to scratching of the sole of the foot. The image below shows an extensor response in an infant, which is normal.
questions.learning: Babinski sign — The image shows extensor plantar response, which is a positive Babinski sign. The normal response to uncomfortable or painful cutaneous stimulation of the file of the foot includes plantar flexion of the toes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Nitric oxide is synthesized from which of the following amino acids?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Arginine

Nitric oxide is synthesized from arginine by a calcium-dependent reaction catalyzed by NO synthase.

Arginine, O2, and NADPH are substrates for cytosolic NO synthase. The co-enzymes of NO synthase include flavin mononucleotide (FMN), flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), heme, and tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4).

Functions of NO:

* It is a potent vasodilator.

* It acts as a neurotransmitter in CNS.

* Antimicrobial and cytotoxic activity of various inflammatory cells.

* Inhibitor of platelet aggregation.

* In GIT, it relaxes smooth muscle.

Pearl PF1957: Amino Acid Derivatives

Pearl PF0102: Classification of Hormones According to their Chemical Structure

Proteins and polypeptide hormones

* Pituitary hormones - GH, ACTH, FSH, LH, Prolactin, Oxytocin and ADH

* Insulin and glucagon

* Parathormone

Steroid hormones

* Cortisol, aldosterone

* Estrogen, progesterone

* Testosterone

Derivatives of a specific amino acid

* Tyrosine

* Thyroid hormones, catecholamines

* Tryptophan

* Serotonin (5-HT), melatonin

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 4-year-old child presents with easy fatiguability. The mother also complains that the child has increased hunger between meals, which is relieved after food. Liver examination revealed no glycogen. The enzyme most likely deficient is _________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glycogen synthase

The most likely enzyme deficiency in a child with fatigue, excessive hunger between meals, and absent liver glycogen is glycogen synthase deficiency.

Glycogen is a storage carbohydrate synthesized from glucose (glycogenesis) and is stored in the liver, muscles, and brain. Glycogen synthase is a regulating enzyme for glycogenesis.

Glycogen synthase exists in both phosphorylated (inactive) and dephosphorylated (active) forms. Phosphorylation is stimulated by epinephrine, norepinephrine, and glucagon via cAMP. Dephosphorylation is stimulated by insulin via phosphodiesterase.

A deficiency of glycogen synthase leads to glycogen storage disorder and presents in infancy with early morning drowsiness and fatigue, fasting hypoglycemia, pallor, emesis, and hypoglycemic convulsions. It leads to a marked decrease in liver glycogen stores. Hepatomegaly is absent.

Laboratory investigations reveal prolonged hyperglycemia, glycosuria, ketosis, lactic acidosis, low alanine levels, and normal insulin levels after glucose administration. A liver biopsy is diagnostic.

Treatment involves protein-rich frequent meals, and nighttime supplementation with cornstarch to prevent hypoglycemia and hyperketonemia.

Other options:

Option A: Glycogen phosphorylase deficiency, also known as McArdle's disease or glycogen storage disease type V, primarily affects skeletal muscle glycogen metabolism. Affected individuals experience muscle weakness, cramps, and exercise intolerance, but it doesn't typically cause the symptoms mentioned in the question.

Option C: Debranching enzyme deficiency, also known as Cori's disease or glycogen storage disease type III, presents with hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, and growth retardation. The liver would still contain glycogen, albeit with an abnormal structure.

Option D: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, known as von Gierke's disease or glycogen storage disease type I, is characterized by severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hepatomegaly. In this case, glycogen is present in the liver but cannot be broken down efficiently into glucose.
questions.learning: Glycogen synthase — The most likely enzyme deficiency in a child with fatigue, excessive hunger between meals, and absent liver glycogen is glycogen synthase deficiency.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Urine LAM is used for the diagnosis of ___________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. M. tuberculosis

Urine lipoarabinomannan (LAM) assay is used for the diagnosis of tuberculosis.

Lipoarabinomannan (LAM) antigen is a lipopolysaccharide present in mycobacterial cell wall. It is released from metabolically active cells or degenerating cells of patients having tuberculosis. Urine LAM testing is especially useful in diagnosing TB in patients with HIV and low CD 4 counts.
questions.learning: M. tuberculosis Urine lipoarabinomannan (LAM) assay is used for the diagnosis of tuberculosis. Lipoarabinomannan (LAM) antigen is a lipopolysaccharide present in mycobacterial cell wall.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: An adolescent male came with complaints of lesions all over the face and back, which were predominantly comedones. What is the most effective treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Systemic doxycycline

An adolescent with multiple co medones (open/closed) on face and back has acne vulgaris (comedonal/papulopustular type).

• Pathogenesis (4 key factors):

o    ↑ Sebum production

o    Follicular hyperkeratinization → comedone formation

o    Cutibacterium acnes proliferation

o    Inflammation
• Most effective treatment: Systemic doxycycline → for moderate inflammatory acne

Therapy approach:

• Mild (comedonal) → topical retinoids ± benzoyl peroxide
• Moderate (papulopustular) → oral antibiotics (doxycycline)
• Severe/nodulocystic → oral isotretinoin (definitive)

Why not others:

• Isotretinoin → reserved for severe/refractory cases
• Topical dapsone → mild/moderate inflammatory acne
• Azithromycin → alternative, not first-line

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient hailing from an area infested with mosquitoes presents with fever, chills, and myalgias. WBC count was 4000 cells/cu.mm, RBC was normal, and platelets were 90000 cells/cu.mm. He also had a maculopapular rash. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dengue

The given clinical scenario with a patient hailing from a mosquito-infested area with fever and decreased platelet counts is diagnostic of dengue.

Symptoms of severe dengue are headache, myalgias, retroorbital pain, end-organ damage, pleural & ascitic effusions and thrombocytopenia (<100,000/ uL). Complications include mild hepatic injury, seizures, arrythmias and acute kidney injury.

Diagnosis is made by NS1 antigen detection and IgM antibody assays. Treatment includes crystalloid infusion in mild cases and colloid infusion in severe cases, oxygen administration and close monitoring.

Dengue is classified into dengue with or without warning signs and severe dengue. Dengue is to be suspected when a high fever (40°C/104°F) is accompanied by any two of the following symptoms during the febrile phase (2-7 days) which include severe headache, retro-orbital pain, arthralgia or myalgia, nausea, vomiting and maculopapular rash.

Warning signs in dengue are:

• severe abdominal pain
• persistent vomiting
• tachypnea
• bleeding gums or nose
• fatigue
• restlessness
• hepatomegaly
• malena or hematemesis
questions.learning: Dengue — The given clinical scenario with a patient hailing from a mosquito-infested area with fever and decreased platelet counts is diagnostic of dengue.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Once the confirmation of the pregnancy is done, consider the following statements regarding the registration of pregnancy: 1. It is to be done as soon as possible, and within 12 weeks. 2. It is to be done as soon as possible, once 12 weeks are complete. 3. It is the primary responsibility of the ASHA. 4. It is the primary responsibility of the ANM. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 4

1. Registration as soon as possible and within 12 weeks: Correct

• Pregnancy should be registered at the earliest, preferably during the first trimester and within 12 weeks.

2. Registration after 12 weeks: Incorrect

• Registration should not be delayed until 12 weeks are completed.

3. Primary responsibility of ASHA: Incorrect

• ASHA plays an important role in identifying, motivating and facilitating pregnant women to access services, but she is not primarily responsible for formal pregnancy registration.

4. Primary responsibility of ANM: Correct

• The ANM is primarily responsible for registration of pregnancy and provision/coordination of antenatal care services.

Therefore, statements 1 and 4 are correct → C.
questions.learning: Registration as soon as possible and within 12 weeks: Correct • Pregnancy should be registered at the earliest, preferably during the first trimester and within 12 weeks.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which muscle is not involved in the inversion of foot?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Peroneus longus

Peroneus longus muscle is not involved in the inversion of the foot. It causes eversion and plantar flexion.

Inversion of the foot is a movement in which the medial border of the foot is elevated so that the sole faces medially.

• Tibialis anterior - Causes dorsiflexion and inversion of the foot
• Tibialis posterior - Causes plantar flexion and inversion of the foot
• Extensor hallucis longus - Causes extension of the great toe, dorsiflexion of the foot, and inversion of the foot (minimal action)

Eversion of the foot is a movement where the lateral border of the foot is elevated so that the sole faces laterally. Peroneus longus, peroneus brevis, and peroneus tertius are the muscles involved.

These movements take place, mainly at the talocalcaneal and the talocalcaneonavicular joints, and partly at the transverse tarsal joint.
questions.learning: Peroneus longus Peroneus longus muscle is not involved in the inversion of the foot. It causes eversion and plantar flexion.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presents with fever and cough and undergoes histopathological examination of a lung lesion. Which cytokine is primarily involved in the formation of this lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IFN-γ

Granuloma formation, as seen in tuberculosis, is mediated by a Th1 cell–driven immune response, with Interferon-γ (IFN-γ) serving as the key cytokine. IFN-γ activates macrophages, transforming them into epithelioid cells and Langhans giant cells, which organize into granulomas to contain intracellular pathogens such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis. This represents a Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction.

• TNF-α is essential for maintenance of granulomas; anti-TNF therapy can cause reactivation of latent tuberculosis
• Diseases with granulomatous inflammation: Tuberculosis, leprosy, sarcoidosis, Crohn disease, and certain fungal infections.

Why not the other options?

• A. IL-6: Promotes acute-phase protein synthesis, B-cell differentiation, and fever; not the principal cytokine for granuloma formation.
• C. IL-4: Produced by Th2 cells; stimulates IgE production and alternative (M2) macrophage activation, important in allergic responses.
• D. IL-10: An anti-inflammatory cytokine that suppresses macrophage activation and inhibits Th1-mediated granulomatous inflammation.
questions.learning: IFN-γ Granuloma formation, as seen in tuberculosis, is mediated by a Th1 cell–driven immune response, with Interferon-γ (IFN-γ) serving as the key cytokine.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A newborn presents with a progressively enlarging skin lesion, as shown in the image. According to the mother, the lesion has been increasing in size day by day. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?
options: Immediate Biopsy due to Malignancy Risk
questions.explanation: The clinical image shows an infantile hemangioma, which is a benign vascular tumor common in neonates. These lesions typically go through a rapid proliferative phase during the first few months of life, as described by the mother, followed by slow, spontaneous involution over several years. The standard management for uncomplicated hemangiomas is simple observation. Regarding the distractors, excision or laser therapy (Option B) is reserved for complicated cases involving the airway, eyes, or severe ulceration. An immediate biopsy (Option C) is unnecessary as the diagnosis is clinical and the risk of malignancy is extremely low. Cryotherapy (Option D) is not a first-line treatment and can cause scarring. Since most hemangiomas regress completely without intervention by age 7 to 10, a "wait and watch" approach is preferred

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A known alcoholic is brought to the emergency department in a confused and disoriented state, reporting visual hallucinations such as snakes and insects crawling over his body. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation: The patient is presenting with "Delirium Tremens" (DT), the most severe form of alcohol withdrawal, characterized by "disorientation and visual/tactile hallucinations" (e.g., zoopsia). The gold standard for managing alcohol withdrawal and preventing seizures is the administration of "benzodiazepines," such as "Lorazepam" or diazepam, which act to stabilize the overexcited nervous system. Additionally, all chronic alcoholics must receive "thiamine" (Option C) to prevent or treat Wernicke’s encephalopathy, as they are almost universally deficient. Haloperidol (Options A and D) is generally avoided as a first-line treatment because it can "lower the seizure threshold," which is dangerous during alcohol withdrawal. Lorazepam only (Option B) is insufficient because it does not address the nutritional deficiency. DT is a medical emergency with a high mortality rate if untreated. Proper management involves aggressive benzodiazepine titration, fluid resuscitation, and correction of electrolyte imbalances (such as hypomagnesemia) in an intensive care setting
questions.learning: The patient is presenting with "Delirium Tremens" (DT), the most severe form of alcohol withdrawal, characterized by "disorientation and visual/tactile hallucinations" (e.g., zoopsia).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following drugs reduce mortality in a patient with heart failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Metoprolol

Metoprolol is a beta-blocker that is found to reduce mortality in a patient with heart failure.

Beta-blockers have been shown to prolong survival, prevent arrhythmia, and improve symptoms of heart failure and left ventricular ejection fraction, especially in patients with chronic heart failure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 56-year-old patient with obstructive jaundice has a distended gall bladder and a dilated common bile duct and intrahepatic biliary radicles on ultrasound. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed the same findings with no additional findings. Which of the following will be most useful to localize the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Magnetic resonance imaging

The given clinical scenario with USG and CECT showing a distended gall bladder, dilated common bile duct, and intrahepatic biliary radicles raises suspicion of common bile duct stones (CBD stones). Among the given options, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI/MRCP) will be next most useful modality to localize the cause and level of obstruction.

Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) uses T2-weighted MRI sequences and it is highly sensitive and specific in identifying CBD stones. MRCP provides visualization of dilated bile ducts and often enables accurate assessment of the level of occlusion in the biliary tree. It is a non-invasive test and is preferred by many surgeons to assess the need for endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). ERCP is also highly effective at diagnosing CBD stones. However, due to the risks associated with the procedure, it is rarely used as a purely diagnostic modality, rather it is now used only as a therapeutic modality such as when stone extraction or sphincterotomy is planned (option D).

Ultrasonography (USG) can detect gallstones and assess the size of the common bile duct. If a patient with gallstones, jaundice, and biliary pain shows a dilated common bile duct (>8 mm in diameter) on USG, it strongly suggests the presence of CBD stones. CT scan is also a sensitive diagnostic tool for CBD stones. USG and CT will generally be the first line modalities due to their easier availability, and lower cost and time requirements.

Other options:

Option B- Endoscopic ultrasound is used for detecting CBD stones. It is considered as good as ERCP but it is invasive and requires expertise in endoscopic procedure and hence it is not done routinely.

Option C- Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography (PTC) is rarely performed in patients with CBD stones. In patients where endoscopic or surgical procedures are contraindicated, it may be used for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes.
questions.learning: Magnetic resonance imaging — The given clinical scenario with USG and CECT showing a distended gall bladder, dilated common bile duct, and intrahepatic biliary radicles raises suspicion of common bile duct stones (CBD stones).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What is the active principle of the poison shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bhilawanol

The given image shows the seeds of Semecarpus anacardium, and its active principles are bhilawanol and semicarpol. Common names are marking nut, bhilwan, bibva, bhela, and oriental cashew.

The image shows black, heart-shaped seeds with hard rinds that identify them as seeds of S. anacardium. Within the fruit is a thick fleshy pericarp that yields the active principle, which is a brown oily resinous fluid called bhilawanol.

The juice when applied locally to the skin produces irritation, painful blisters, itching, and eczematous eruption. The seeds are used to produce an artificial bruise. Symptoms such as pain, fever, and painful passage of brownish urine may be seen.

A large dose taken orally can produce blisters in the mouth and throat, with gastroenteritis. It also produces dyspnea, cyanosis, tachycardia, coma, and death. The fatal period is 12 to 24 hours.

Medicolegal importance is the use of the juice by malingerers to fabricate wounds. Instilled in the eyes it can cause conjunctivitis or ophthalmia due to its local irritant effect.

Other options:

Option A: Ricin is the active principle of Ricinus communis. It is a toxalbumin or phytotoxin that inhibits protein synthesis by affecting the ribosomal RNA polymerase. The seeds are flat to oval-shaped and have dark brown markings (shown below). It is a chemical warfare agent.

Option C: Abrin is the active principle of Abrus precatorius. The seeds are egg-shaped, scarlet in color, and have a black spot at one end (shown below). On ingestion, it causes gastroenteritis with bloody diarrhea, rectal bleeding, tachycardia, and circulatory collapse. Injecting the active substance can mimic viperine snakebite. Rarely, it may lead to tetanic convulsions.

The seeds of A. precatorius are decocted and mixed with datura, opium, onion, spirit, and water to form a paste. From this, small sharp needles called suis are made. They are used for hunting animals and even for homicide purposes.

Option D: Calotropin is one of the active principles of Calotropis. The toxic parts of the plant are the stem, branches, leaves, and milky white latex (Madar juice). When applied locally, it can mimic bruises, and form pustules and vesicles. In the eyes, it can lead to conjunctivitis. On ingestion, it causes abdominal pain, vomiting, mydriasis, and tetanic convulsions and can eventually lead to collapse and death.

It is shown in the image below.
questions.learning: Bhilawanol — The given image shows the seeds of Semecarpus anacardium, and its active principles are bhilawanol and semicarpol. Common names are marking nut, bhilwan, bibva, bhela, and oriental cashew.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pseudoexfoliation syndrome

The diagnosis based on the image given is pseudoexfoliation syndrome.

Pseudoexfoliation syndrome is an age-related degenerative disorder, more commonly seen in women. It is marked by the deposition of exfoliative material on the iris, ciliary region, and lens capsule. They appear as flakes on the anterior lens capsule and edge of the iris.

The material can get collected in the anterior chamber angle and impede the aqueous humor drainage. Patients affected by this condition are at an increased risk of developing open-angle glaucoma. Rarely, angle-closure glaucoma can also be seen. Other ocular symptoms include iris sphincter atrophy, anisocoria, and heterochromia. Systemic manifestations due to abnormal fibrillary deposition may also be seen.

Other options:

Option A - Common intraocular foreign bodies include glass particles or metal chips. It can lodge in various sites like the anterior chamber, lens, posterior chamber, and vitreous. This can lead to cataract formation, retinal hemorrhages, and tears. Organic foreign bodies can cause infection. Iron foreign bodies can cause siderosis while copper ones can result in chalcosis. An entry wound can be identified with topical fluorescein.  In cases of metallic intraocular foreign bodies, MRI is contraindicated. CT scan can be done instead.

Option C - Ocular trauma can be a closed-globe or open-globe injury. Closed-globe injury can vary from simple corneal abrasions to widespread intraocular damage. Open-globe injuries include globe rupture or laceration.

A corneal abrasion highlighted with fluorescein staining is shown below.

Option D - Vossius ring is used to describe a ring-shaped pigment dispersal observed on the anterior surface of the lens due to the deposition of brown amorphous pigment granules. It is close to the miosed pupil in diameter. The force of the blow drives the cornea and iris backward, creating an impression of the iris on the lens.
questions.learning: Pseudoexfoliation syndrome — The diagnosis based on the image given is pseudoexfoliation syndrome. Pseudoexfoliation syndrome is an age-related degenerative disorder, more commonly seen in women.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Afferent fibers from baroreceptors for blood pressure control goes to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nucleus Tractus Solitarius

Afferent fiber for blood pressure control goes to the Nucleus Tractus Solitarius (NTS).

Increased BP stimulates the baroreceptors which provide negative feedback in response to the increase in blood pressure.

Baroreceptor reflex:

• Increased BP → stimulation of baroreceptors → stimulation of NTS → excitation of CVLM → inhibition of RVLM → inhibition of sympathetic system
• Stimulation of NTS also stimulates CVC → parasympathetic stimulation
• Net effect = sympathetic inhibition and parasympathetic stimulation → decreased HR and BP

NTS - Nucleus tractus solitarius

CVC - Cardiovagal centre

CVLM - Caudal ventrolateral medulla

RVLM - Rostral ventrolateral medulla

HR - Heart rate

BP - Blood pressure
questions.learning: Nucleus Tractus Solitarius Afferent fiber for blood pressure control goes to the Nucleus Tractus Solitarius (NTS). Increased BP stimulates the baroreceptors which provide negative feedback in response to the increase in blood pressure.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic presented with abdominal pain, jaundice and weight loss. He has hypoglycemia and elevated alpha fetoprotein levels (600ng/ml) but has normal AST and ALT. Which of the following is a likely diagnosis of the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hepatocellular carcinoma

• Chronic alcoholic → chronic liver disease risk
• Abdominal pain + jaundice + weight loss → malignancy suspicion
• Hypoglycemia → paraneoplastic clue
• AFP = 600 ng/ml → tumor marker (normal: 10-25)
• Normal AST/ALT → not active hepatitis

Put together → Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)

Classic Triad of HCC:

• Weight loss
• Abdominal pain
• Liver mass

Other Paraneoplastic Features:

• Hypoglycemia
• Polycythemia (↑ EPO)
• Hypercalcemia

Imaging Hallmark:

• Arterial phase enhancement + venous washout (CT/MRI)

| Feature | HCC | Cirrhosis | Hepatitis | Cholangiocarcinoma

| ------- | --- | --------- | --------- | ------------------

| AFP | ↑↑ | Normal | Normal | Normal

| AST/ALT | Normal/slightly ↑ | Mild ↑ | ↑↑ | Mild ↑

| Hypoglycemia | Yes | No | No | No

| Cause | Cirrhosis | Alcohol, viral | Infection | Bile duct malignancy

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An 18-month-old child visited the ophthalmologist exhibiting a white eye reflex, and ultrasonography revealed an intraocular mass with calcifications. The family history indicated that the child's father had a similar condition and underwent the removal of one eye (enucleation). What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Retinoblastoma

The clinical history of leukocoria, an intraocular mass with calcifications on ultrasound, and a positive family history, the most likely diagnosis is retinoblastoma (option b).

Retinoblastoma is a malignant tumor of the retina that predominantly affects children, and early detection and treatment are crucial for better outcomes. point toward a diagnosis of retinoblastoma.

Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular malignancy in children associated with mutations in the RB1 gene at chromosome 13q14.

It most commonly presents with leukocoria followed by a squint which is usually convergent. Rarely, the child may present with nystagmus and defective vision.

Signs:

* An intraretinal tumor is a homogeneous, dome-shaped white lesion that becomes irregular, often with white flecks of calcification.

* An endophytic tumor projects into the vitreous as a white mass that may "seed" into the gel.

* An exophytic tumor forms multilobular subretinal white masses and causes an overlying retinal detachment.

Investigations:

* Red reflex testing with a direct ophthalmoscope is a simple screening test for leukocoria.

* Dilated fundus examination using indirect ophthalmoscope

* MRI of the orbit + brain is the investigation of choice.

Histopathology of the tumor shows small round cells with large nuclei. Microscopic features of a well-differentiated tumor include Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (highly specific of retinoblastoma), Homer-Wright rosettes, pseudorosettes, and fleurettes formation. Areas of necrosis and calcification can also be seen.

Treatment typically involves chemotherapy plus focal therapy.Vincristine, Carboplatin, Etoposide are the choice of drugs for chemotherapy. Focal therapy includes cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, thermotherapy, plaque radiotherapy, and external beam radiotherapy.

Enucleation is done when the tumor involves more than half of the retina, optic nerve involvement, glaucoma, and anterior chamber involvement.
questions.learning: Retinoblastoma — The clinical history of leukocoria, an intraocular mass with calcifications on ultrasound, and a positive family history, the most likely diagnosis is retinoblastoma (option b).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: When evaluating a new diagnostic test for a rare disease, which factor has the greatest influence on the positive predictive value (PPV) of the test?
questions.explanation: The Positive Predictive Value (PPV) is the probability that an individual with a positive test result truly has the disease. While PPV is mathematically related to sensitivity (Option A) and specificity (Option C), it is most profoundly influenced by the prevalence of the disease in the population being tested. In a rare disease with very low prevalence, even a highly specific test will yield more false positives than true positives, significantly lowering the PPV. Conversely, as prevalence increases, the PPV rises because a positive result becomes more likely to be a true positive. Specificity (Option C) also significantly affects PPV, but prevalence is the population-level factor that determines the clinical utility of the test result. Relative risk (Option D) is a measure of association between exposure and disease, not a metric for test accuracy. Therefore, prevalence is the most critical variable affecting the probability of disease given a positive result

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 34-year-old HIV-positive male presented with low-grade fever, cough, night sweats, and weight loss for the past 3 weeks. In view of TB investigations, the Mantoux test was negative, chest X-ray showed non-specific findings and an adequate amount of sputum could not be collected for slide examination. Which of the following is used to diagnose latent TB infection in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Interferon gamma release assay

The test used to diagnose latent TB infection in this patient is the Interferon-gamma release assay(IGRA).

TB test done on a whole blood sample is IGRA. In this test, sensitized T lymphocytes (from whole blood) of suspected individuals, are exposed to highly specific M. tuberculosis antigens such as CFP –10 and ESAT 6. This releases the cytokine IFN- gamma into the blood, which is then measured. It has been evaluated for the diagnosis of latent tuberculosis in HIV patients (who frequently have a negative Mantoux test.

IGRAs that have been approved by the US (FDA) are

* QuantiFERON-TB Gold In-Tube test (QFT-GIT): It quantitates the amount of interferon-gamma produced by CD4+ T cells in response to the antigens from Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

* T-SPOT.TB test (T-Spot): It determines the total number of individual effector T cells expressing Interferon-gamma.

* QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT- Plus)

IGRAs are more specific than Tuberculin Skin Testing (TST) because of less cross-reactivity to BCG vaccination and sensitization by nontuberculous mycobacteria.

There are 3 described methods for tuberculin skin testing (TST):

* Mantoux test, also known as the Pirquet test (preferred method)

* Heaf test

* Tine test

The TrueNat TB test is a new molecular test that can diagnose TB and resistance to rifampicin in one hour. This test uses a sputum sample and only about 0.5 ml of the sample is required.

Urine lipoarabinomannan (LAM) assay is used for the diagnosis of tuberculosis. Lipoarabinomannan (LAM) antigen is a lipopolysaccharide present in the mycobacterial cell wall, released from metabolically active cells or degenerating cells of patients having tuberculosis. Urine LAM is a useful tool in diagnosing tuberculosis, especially in patients with HIV and a low CD 4 count.

QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT- Plus) is an improved version of the QuantiFERON-TB Gold test. QuantiFERON-TB Gold detects only TB-specific CD4+ responses. However, QuantiFeron-TB Gold Plus detects both CD8+ and CD4+ T cell responses to TB specific antigens.
questions.learning: Interferon gamma release assay — The test used to diagnose latent TB infection in this patient is the Interferon-gamma release assay(IGRA). TB test done on a whole blood sample is IGRA.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: True statements about bankart lesion?
options: Avulsion of the anteroinferior glenoid labrum
Avulsion of the anterosuperior glenoid labrum
Depression in posteroinferior part of the head of the humerus
Depression in posterosuperior part of the head of the humerus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Avulsion of the anteroinferior glenoid labrum

Bankart lesion is an avulsion in the anteroinferior part of the glenoid labrum caused due to the recurrent anterior dislocation of the humeral head.

Hill-Sachs lesion is a compression fracture on the posterolateral aspect of the humeral head. It is caused by the pressure of the anterior glenoid rim on the humeral head in recurrent dislocations.

Anterior dislocation is the commonest shoulder dislocation and can be caused due to trauma from behind the shoulder pushing the head out anteriorly. It is also caused due to falling on an outstretched hand in an abducted and externally rotated shoulder. It can be diagnosed on clinical examination with flattening of the shoulder contour and ability to place a rule (Hamilton ruler test) and the inability to touch his/her opposite shoulder (Duga's test). X-ray confirms the diagnosis and may show associated Hill Sachs or bony bankart lesion. The most common complication is recurrent shoulder dislocation.

The following X-ray shows the Bankart lesion and Hill-Sachs lesion:
questions.learning: Avulsion of the anteroinferior glenoid labrum Bankart lesion is an avulsion in the anteroinferior part of the glenoid labrum caused due to the recurrent anterior dislocation of the humeral head.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding an esophageal foreign body?
options: Most common site of impaction is at level of cricopharyngeus
One of the constrictions of the esopahgus is at the level of the right bronchus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Most common site of impaction is at level of cricopharyngeus

The correct statement with regard to the oesophageal foreign body in the image is that the most common site of impaction is at the level of the cricopharyngeus.

Foreign bodies commonly ingested by children are coins, disk batteries, and small toy items. In adults, it is usually a food bolus (mostly meat) that gets lodged.

The flat surface of a coin is seen on the anteroposterior view (AP view) and the edge is seen on the lateral view. This indicates that it is oriented in the coronal plane, which is seen when it is lodged in the esophagus (and not in the trachea).

Initial symptoms are choking, gagging, and coughing followed by excessive salivation, dysphagia, food refusal, vomiting, or pain in the neck and throat. Respiratory symptoms such as stridor, wheezing, cyanosis, or dyspnea are seen if the esophageal foreign body impinges on the larynx or tracheal wall. Imaging with chest and abdominal X-rays should be performed in AP and lateral positions. Chest CT should always be performed if oesophageal perforation is suspected.

Endoscopic removal of the esophageal foreign body is the procedure of choice. It should be performed

• Immediately in esophageal obstruction, disk batteries, and sharp pointed objects.
• Within 12-24 hours in non-pointed objects, pointed objects in the stomach, and coins in the esophagus.
• Non-urgent removal in objects in stomach >2.5cm in diameter, and disk battery in the stomach (up to 48h)

Other options:

Option A: If a foreign body becomes lodged in the esophagus and causes perforation, it can lead to mediastinitis, a potentially life-threatening infection of the mediastinum.

Option C: Esophageal foreign bodies are more commonly seen in children, although they do occur in adults, particularly in those with underlying esophageal abnormalities (e.g., strictures or motility disorders).

Option D: The esophagus has several natural constrictions, including at the cricopharyngeus (C6 level), at the aortic arch, at the level of the left main bronchus and at the diaphragmatic hiatus.
questions.learning: Most common site of impaction is at level of cricopharyngeus The correct statement with regard to the oesophageal foreign body in the image is that the most common site of impaction is at the level of the cricopharyngeus.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: McLaughlin score in trauma is used to determine which of the following?
options: To know the amount of fluid that has to be used for resuscitation.
To access the extent of neurological deficit post trauma.
To predict the need of a massive blood transfusion.
To evaluate the grade of shock.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. To predict the need of a massive blood transfusion.

Trauma patients can rapidly deteriorate due to occult hemorrhage, and early identification of those who will require massive transfusion is crucial to reduce mortality. The McLaughlin score is a trauma scoring system used to predict the need for massive blood transfusion (commonly defined as ≥10 units of PRBCs within 24 hours or significant blood requirement in early hours).

It uses early clinical and physiologic parameters (such as hypotension, tachycardia, metabolic acidosis/low base excess, and laboratory markers of hypoperfusion) to estimate the likelihood of major ongoing bleeding and the need for activation of a massive transfusion protocol (MTP).

Thus, the McLaughlin score is specifically applied to Predict the need for a massive blood transfusion in trauma, enabling prompt initiation of balanced blood product resuscitation and damage control strategies.
questions.learning: To predict the need of a massive blood transfusion. Trauma patients can rapidly deteriorate due to occult hemorrhage, and early identification of those who will require massive transfusion is crucial to reduce mortality.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young man has the following hepatitis B serological profile: HBsAg positive, IgM anti- HBc negative, IgG anti-HBc positive, and HBeAg positive. Based on this serological status, what is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: The serological profile indicates chronic active Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. HBsAg positivity indicates ongoing infection, while negative IgM anti-HBc and positive IgG anti-HBc confirm that the disease is in the chronic phase rather than acute. The presence of HBeAg signifies high viral replication and increased infectivity. Antiviral therapy is required to suppress viral replication and prevent liver damage. Lamivudine is an oral nucleoside analog that inhibits HBV DNA polymerase and is an effective (though older) treatment option for chronic HBV. Ombitasvir (Option B) is used for Hepatitis C (HCV), not HBV. Ritonavir (Option C) and Abacavir (Option D) are components of antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV and are not standard treatments for HBV monoinfection. While tenofovir and entecavir are now preferred first-line due to lower resistance rates, Lamivudine is the only appropriate HBV drug listed
questions.learning: The serological profile indicates chronic active Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. HBsAg positivity indicates ongoing infection, while negative IgM anti-HBc and positive IgG anti-HBc confirm that the disease is in the chronic phase rather than acute.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A newborn baby refuses breast milk since the 2nd day of birth but accepts glucose water. He develops vomiting and severe jaundice by the 5th day. Benedict's test was positive for urine and blood glucose was low. The most likely cause is due to the deficiency of
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase

The above clinical features on ingestion of breastmilk at birth suggest classical galactosemia, a disorder of galactose metabolism. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency leads to classical galactosemia.

It is an autosomal recessive disorder. Clinical features include:

• Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the liver causes liver damage & leads to hepatomegaly, vomiting, convulsions.
• Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate depletes the liver of inorganic phosphate leading to diminished ATP synthesis which affects gluconeogenesis resulting in hypoglycemia.
• Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the nerves causes intellectual disability.
• Accumulation of galactitol in the lens causes an oil-drop cataract.

Urinary reducing sugar (Benedict's test) and the Mucic acid test are positive.

Treatment is a galactose-free diet.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A TB patient with HIV begins ART and experiences deterioration in health after 2 months. What is the likely cause?
options: Development of drug resistance to TB drugs
Drug-drug interactions between TB and ART medications
Development of drug resistance to ART
questions.explanation: The clinical deterioration seen roughly two months after initiating Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) in an HIV-TB co-infected patient is most likely due to Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS). This condition arises from immunological changes where the recovering immune system mounts an exaggerated inflammatory response against the pre-existing Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens. Symptoms typically include worsening fever and enlarging lymph nodes. Regarding the distractors, drug resistance (Options A and D) generally develops over a longer period and presents with a failure to clear the viral or bacterial load rather than an acute inflammatory flare. While drug-drug interactions (Option B) between rifampicin and certain ART drugs like protease inhibitors are common, they typically lead to therapeutic failure rather than the paradoxical clinical worsening characteristic of IRIS. Management involves continuing both treatments while managing inflammation
questions.learning: The clinical deterioration seen roughly two months after initiating Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) in an HIV-TB co-infected patient is most likely due to Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The given chest X-ray is suggestive of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tetralogy of Fallot

The given chest X-ray shows a boot-shaped cardiac silhouette which is suggestive of the Tetralogy of Fallot.

The boot-shaped (coeur en sabot) cardiac silhouette is seen due to the right ventricular hypertrophy and upward shift of the cardiac apex. The hilar areas and lung fields appear relatively clear due to reduced pulmonary blood flow or the small size of the pulmonary arteries, or both.

In Ebsteins's anomaly (Option D) box-shaped heart is seen.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 54-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and ascites presents with fever, abdominal pain, and altered sensorium. Ascitic fluid analysis shows: Total leukocyte count: 800 cells/mm³ Neutrophils: 320 cells/mm³ Protein: low Culture: pending What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is a bacterial infection of ascitic fluid without an identifiable intra-abdominal source, most commonly seen in patients with cirrhosis and ascites.

Diagnostic criterion: Ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear (PMN) count ≥250 cells/mm³

Typical findings:

• Low ascitic fluid protein
• Fever, abdominal pain, altered mental status
• Culture may be positive (commonly E. coli, Klebsiella, Streptococcus) but treatment should start even if culture results are pending.

Management:

• Empiric third-generation cephalosporin (e.g., cefotaxime)
• Albumin infusion to reduce risk of hepatorenal syndrome.
questions.learning: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is a bacterial infection of ascitic fluid without an identifiable intra-abdominal source, most commonly seen in patients with cirrhosis and ascites.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: At what pressure does the marked structure open?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 30-40 cm H2O

In the image, the marked structure is the adjustable pressure-limiting (APL) valve of Mapelson-C anaesthetic breathing system and it will open at the pressure of 30-40 cm H2O. This valve is designed to release gas when a certain pressure is exceeded to prevent excessive pressure from building up in the patient's airway.

The APL valve typically opens at pressures of 30-40 cm H₂O to allow for safe ventilation without causing barotrauma to the lungs. This range is appropriate for manual ventilation to prevent high airway pressures that could lead to lung injury.
questions.learning: 30-40 cm H2O In the image, the marked structure is the adjustable pressure-limiting (APL) valve of Mapelson-C anaesthetic breathing system and it will open at the pressure of 30-40 cm H2O.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient was admitted to the hospital with COVID-19 and died 15 days later due to the illness. His death was reported through the official health reporting system. According to surveillance definitions, this type of reporting represents which form of surveillance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Passive surveillance

Disease surveillance is the continuous systematic collection, analysis, interpretation, and dissemination of health data for public health action.

Different surveillance methods are used depending on how data are collected.

In this case, the hospital reported the case through routine reporting channels, which is characteristic of passive surveillance.

Passive surveillance involves routine reporting of diseases and deaths by healthcare facilities to health authorities without active case search.

In this scenario, the COVID-19 death was reported through the official health reporting system, fitting the definition of passive surveillance.

India uses systems such as the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP).

IDSP collects:

• Weekly disease reports
• Outbreak alerts
• Laboratory data

Most reporting in IDSP is passive surveillance.

Active surveillance requires deliberate outreach and case finding, while sentinel and syndromic surveillance serve different monitoring purposes.
questions.learning: Passive surveillance Disease surveillance is the continuous systematic collection, analysis, interpretation, and dissemination of health data for public health action.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: An industrial worker sustained burn injuries to the anterior region of his chest and abdomen, as well as burns to his right upper limb and a circumferential burn to his right thigh, as a result of a cylinder explosion. What is the percentage of total burns surface area?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 36

The affected percentage of body surface area (BSA) is calculated using Wallace's rule of 9:

• Right upper limb - 9%
• Circumferential right thigh - 9% (Anterior thigh 4.5% and Posterior thigh 4.5% in Adults)
• Anterior chest - 9%
• Anterior abdomen - 9%

Thus, totaling to 36%.

Note: According to Bailey's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th edition, the anterior thigh accounts for 4%, while according to Current Practice of Surgery, 14th edition, the anterior thigh accounts for 4.75 %. Either percentage, when totalled gives us the best possible answer to this question to be 36%.

The following image shows Wallace's rule of 9:

Lund and Browder's chart is an accurate method to measure burns if it is used correctly. In this, different proportions of body surface areas in children are taken into consideration. This chart compensates for the changes in the shape of the body with age and can accurately assess the burn area in children.

The below image shows the Lund and Browder chart.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the site of lesion in Wernicke's hemianopic pupil?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Optic tract

The site of lesion in Wernicke's hemianopic pupil is optic tract.

Wernicke hemianopic pupil is the light reflex, where, illumination of the blind half of the retina shows no pupillary reaction while stimulating the normal side of the retina shows a pupillary reaction. It is seen in lesions involving the optic tract. It is also seen in cases such as TB, syphilis and tumours of the optic thalamus.

Homonymous hemianopia (HH) involves loss of vision on the same side of the visual field in both eyes. HH is characteristically seen in lesions involving the visual pathway posterior to the optic chiasma.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A defect in which of the following aortic arches causes the defect shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 6th left

The image above shows a patent ductus arteriosus due to a defect in the left side of the 6th aortic arch.

Usually, in term infants, the ductus arteriosus closes within 72 hours of birth. Failure of the ductus arteriosus to close results in patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).

PDA usually presents with a hyperdynamic precordium, bounding peripheral pulses, wide pulse pressure, a machine-like continuous or systolic murmur, cardiomegaly, increased pulmonary vascular markings, hepatomegaly, increasing oxygen dependence, carbon dioxide retention, and renal failure.

In a majority of cases, PDA closes spontaneously. If spontaneous closure fails to occur, COX inhibitors like indomethacin or ibuprofen can be used. Surgical ligation is indicated in case of contraindications to medical management or failure of the same.

Other options

Option A: The 4th right aortic arch gives rise to the proximal part of the right subclavian artery.

Option B: The 4th left aortic arch gives rise to the arch of the aorta. Defects involving the 4th left aortic arch could cause a variety of aortic arch anomalies, such as interruption of the aortic arch, but not PDA.

Option C: The 6th right aortic arch forms the proximal part of the right pulmonary artery.
questions.learning: 6th left The image above shows a patent ductus arteriosus due to a defect in the left side of the 6th aortic arch. Usually, in term infants, the ductus arteriosus closes within 72 hours of birth.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which nerve defect causes lagophthalmos?
questions.explanation: Lagophthalmos refers to the inability to close the eyelids completely, which leads to corneal exposure and potential ulceration. This condition is primarily caused by paralysis of the orbicularis oculi muscle, which is the muscle responsible for eyelid closure. The orbicularis oculi is innervated by the 7th cranial nerve (facial nerve). Therefore, facial nerve palsy is the most common cause of lagophthalmos. The 6th nerve (Option B) innervates the lateral rectus muscle, and its palsy results in medial strabismus. The 4th nerve (Option C) supplies the superior oblique muscle, and its defect causes vertical diplopia. The 5th nerve (Option D) provides sensory innervation to the face and motor innervation to the muscles of mastication, but it does not control eyelid closure. Clinical management of lagophthalmos focuses on ocular surface protection using lubricants, moisture chambers, or surgical procedures like tarsorrhaphy to prevent exposure keratopathy and permanent vision loss

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: The tactile hallucinations seen in cases of chronic cocaine intoxication is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Formication

Formication, which refers to the sensation of insects crawling beneath the skin, is a feature of cocaine abuse. It is also referred to as Magnan's symptoms or cocaine bugs.

The symptoms of acute stimulant intoxication include agitation, irritability, aggression, and an increase in psychomotor activity. On examination, tachycardia, hypertension, and mydriasis may be seen. When psychotic symptoms such as delusions and hallucinations are present due to stimulants such as cocaine, it is referred to as stimulant-induced psychotic disorder. Paranoid delusions and hallucinations are hallmarks of stimulant-induced psychosis. Tactile hallucinations in the form of formication are seen in cocaine use. The presence of these symptoms depends on the dose and duration of the substance abuse and thus may not be seen in all patients. Cocaine-induced psychotic disorders are more frequently seen in intravenous users and those who use crack (an extremely potent and addictive form of cocaine that can be smoked).

Other options:

Option A: Oneroid state is a dream-like state which can happen because of substance use or some organic disorder.

Option C: Dipsomania refers to a compulsive urge to drink alcoholic beverages. Patients suffering from alcohol-use disorders feel a need for daily use of large amounts of alcohol for adequate functioning throughout the day.

Option D: Carphologia (also known as floccillation) refers to the action of trying to pick imaginary objects. The patient will usually be trying to pick lint from his clothes or the bedsheet. This is often seen in delirium. Datura intake can lead to a delirious state and may show carphologia.
questions.learning: Formication Formication, which refers to the sensation of insects crawling beneath the skin, is a feature of cocaine abuse. It is also referred to as Magnan's symptoms or cocaine bugs.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An adolescent girl complaints of dropping objects from hands precipitated during morning hours and exams. There is no history of loss of consciousness. One of her cousins has been diagnosed with epilepsy. EEG was suggestive of epileptic spikes. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy

The given clinical scenario describes an adolescent girl with myoclonic jerks (a history of dropping objects) with preserved consciousness. This, along with abnormal EEG findings strongly suggests juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.

Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (Janz syndrome) is the most common generalized epilepsy in young adults. It starts in early adolescence with one or more of the following features: bilateral myoclonic jerks in the morning, causing patients to drop things, generalized tonic-clonic or clonic-tonic-clonic seizures upon awakening, and juvenile absence seizure.

Consciousness is usually preserved. Precipitating factors include sleep deprivation, alcohol, and photic stimulation. EEG shows 4 to 5Hz polyspike and slow wave discharges. A family history of epilepsy is often present.

The treatment options for JME include sodium valproate, levetiracetam, and topiramate. Benzodiazepine, lamotrigine, perampanel, phenobarbital, primidone, and zonisamide can be considered as add-on drugs. Complete remission is uncommon and has a high risk of seizure recurrence, hence antiepileptics are continued lifelong in a majority of the patients.

Other options:

Option B: Atypical absence seizures have been associated with myoclonic components and head drop. They are precipitated by drowsiness and EEG shows 1 to 2 Hz spike and slow wave discharges.

Option D: In benign childhood epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes, the child typically wakes at night due to a focal seizure with preserved awareness. Buccal and throat tingling and tonic or clonic contractions on one side of the face are seen, with drooling and preserved consciousness. EEG shows typical wide-based centrotemporal spikes.
questions.learning: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy — The given clinical scenario describes an adolescent girl with myoclonic jerks (a history of dropping objects) with preserved consciousness.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are risk factors for developing pelvic inflammatory disease in females? 1. Use of oral contraception pills 2. Multiple sexual partners 3. Lower socioeconomic status 4. Genetic predisposition Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is an ascending infection of the upper female genital tract, most commonly caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Use of oral contraceptive pills: Incorrect. OCPs are not a risk factor and may even reduce the risk of ascending infection by thickening cervical mucus.
• 2. Multiple sexual partners: Correct. Increases exposure to sexually transmitted infections.
• 3. Lower socioeconomic status: Correct. Associated with a higher prevalence of STIs and reduced access to healthcare.
• 4. Genetic predisposition: Correct. Host genetic factors influencing immune response may increase susceptibility to PID and its complications.
questions.learning: 2, 3 and 4 Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is an ascending infection of the upper female genital tract, most commonly caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with elevated blood pressure and an 8-hour history of left-sided facial paralysis and weakness. CT scan is normal. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with signs of an ischemic stroke (facial paralysis and weakness). A normal CT scan in this setting is expected, as ischemic changes often take 12–24 hours to appear on non-contrast CT. The crucial factor for the next step is the timing: the symptoms have persisted for 8 hours. Intravenous thrombolysis (Option C) is strictly limited to a window of 4.5 hours from symptom onset; therefore, she is ineligible. Intravenous labetalol (Option B) is only indicated if the BP is (for thrombolysis) or (for general management). Her BP of should be allowed to remain high to maintain cerebral perfusion (permissive hypertension). Oral Nifedipine (Option D) is contraindicated due to the risk of precipitous BP drops. Therefore, because she is outside the thrombolysis window and her BP does not meet emergency thresholds, the definitive next step is supportive observation and neurological monitoring
questions.learning: The patient presents with signs of an ischemic stroke (facial paralysis and weakness). A normal CT scan in this setting is expected, as ischemic changes often take 12–24 hours to appear on non-contrast CT.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is not a potential cause of the radiological finding shown below?
questions.explanation: The chest X-ray shows a unilateral “white-out” of one hemithorax, meaning complete opacification of one side of the chest. This radiological finding is typically seen in conditions that either fill the lung or pleural space or cause complete lung collapse. Common causes of white-out: 1. Consolidation: The lung is filled with inflammatory exudate, as in severe pneumonia, producing a dense opacity. 2. Collapse (atelectasis): Loss of lung volume leads to increased density and mediastinal shift toward the affected side. 3. Pleural effusion: Accumulation of fluid in the pleural cavity causes homogeneous opacity, often with mediastinal shift away from the affected side. Why foreign body is incorrect: A foreign body aspiration usually leads to localized airway obstruction, not complete white-out. Typical findings include: 1. Segmental or lobar collapse 2. Hyperinflation due to air trapping 3. Patchy or focal opacity It rarely causes complete opacification of an entire hemithorax. Therefore, among the given options, foreign body is not a typical cause of this radiological appearance, making option (D) correct
questions.learning: The chest X-ray shows a unilateral “white-out” of one hemithorax, meaning complete opacification of one side of the chest. This radiological finding is typically seen in conditions that either fill the lung or pleural space or cause complete lung collapse.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 15-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea and breast development corresponding to Tanner stage IV. She has sparse pubic and axillary hair. On genital examination, a blind vaginal pouch is noted. Ultrasound reveals absence of the uterus and ovaries, and testosterone levels are within the normal male range. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Complete AIS

Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS) should be suspected in an adolescent with primary amenorrhea, normal breast development, sparse or absent pubic/axillary hair, a blind-ending vagina, absent uterus, and serum testosterone in the normal male range. It results from an X-linked mutation of the androgen receptor, causing complete resistance to androgens in a 46,XY individual.

Despite normal testicular production of testosterone and anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH):

• AMH causes regression of the Müllerian ducts, resulting in absence of the uterus, cervix, and fallopian tubes.
• Because tissues cannot respond to androgens, male internal genitalia (Wolffian derivatives) fail to develop, and female external genitalia are present.
• Peripheral aromatization of testosterone to estrogen leads to normal breast development, while pubic and axillary hair are sparse or absent because hair growth is androgen-dependent.

Why not the other options?

• B. Gonadal dysgenesis: Streak gonads cause poor breast development and a present uterus due to absent AMH.
• C. MRKH syndrome: 46,XX females with normal ovaries, normal pubic/axillary hair, and female-range testosterone.
• D. Turner syndrome: 45,X with short stature, streak ovaries, poor breast development, and a present uterus.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: LIFT procedure in fistula surgery stands for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ligation of intersphincteric fistula tract

LIFT (Ligation of Intersphincteric Fistula Tract) is a sphincter-preserving procedure used for the treatment of fistula-in-ano.

Principle

• The fistulous tract is identified in the intersphincteric plane.
• The tract is ligated close to the internal opening.
• The tract is divided, thereby disconnecting the internal opening from the external tract.
• This eradicates the fistula while preserving the anal sphincters.

Advantages

• Preserves continence (minimal risk of fecal incontinence).
• Suitable for complex transsphincteric fistulas.
• Less sphincter damage compared with fistulotomy.
• Good healing rates with low morbidity.

High-Yield MCQ Points

• LIFT = Ligation of Intersphincteric Fistula Tract.
• Indicated mainly for transsphincteric fistula-in-ano.
• A sphincter-saving procedure.
• Preferred when preservation of continence is important.
questions.learning: Ligation of intersphincteric fistula tract LIFT (Ligation of Intersphincteric Fistula Tract) is a sphincter-preserving procedure used for the treatment of fistula-in-ano.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old female presents to emergency following bleeding per vaginum, preceded by amenorrhea for 7 weeks. She's in hemodynamic shock with a positive serum beta hCG. On examination, a mass is palpable in the lower abdomen. What is the most likely diagnosis in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ruptured ectopic pregnancy

The given clinical scenario of amenorrhea for 7 weeks with bleeding per vaginum and palpable mass on examination is indicative of ruptured ectopic pregnancy, as suggested by:

* A positive urine/serum beta hCG test: suggestive of pregnancy.

* Bleed per vaginum: The patient experienced amenorrhea for more than four weeks before the onset of the current vaginal bleeding.

* 6 - 8 weeks post last regular menstrual cycle

* Unstable vitals: suggestive of internal blood loss.

Unstable patients with these findings should undergo urgent surgery. It involves surgical exploration(laparotomy). It reduces haemorrhage and also gives a better view of the operating field to the surgeon.

questions.text: All of the following Decreases GFR except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased Bowman Oncotic Pressure

GFR decreases with reduced Kf, increased glomerular oncotic pressure, and reduced glomerular hydrostatic pressure.

Bowman’s space normally has negligible oncotic pressure because proteins do not filter across the glomerulus.

Therefore, increased Bowman oncotic pressure does not occur physiologically and does not decrease GFR.

| B | ↓ | Opposes filtration | ❌

| C | ↓ | ↓ driving pressure | ❌

| D | ↑ | Pulls fluid into Bowman space | ✅
