questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman comes with complaints of pain and swelling in the perineal area. She also has complaints of difficulty in walking and sitting. She gives a history of multiple sexual partners. On examination, a tender swelling is seen with redness on the labia, as shown in the image given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bartholin abscess

The given clinical vignette suggests the diagnosis of Bartholin's abscess.

Bartholin glands are the homologs of the male bulbourethral or Cowper glands. They open into the vestibule at approximately the 5 and 7 o’clock positions. The function of the Bartholin gland is to secrete mucus for lubrication during coitus. Bartholin cyst is caused by obstruction of the duct due to infection, trauma, mucus changes, and congenitally narrowed ducts. If the cyst gets infected, it leads to the formation of a Bartholin abscess. Escherichia coli is the most common causative agent, however, other gram-positive and gram-negative organisms can also cause the same.

Most Bartholin gland cysts are small and asymptomatic except for minor discomfort during sexual contact. If the cyst is larger or infected, however, patients may complain of severe vulvar pain during walking, sitting, or coitus. On examination, cysts typically are unilateral, round, or ovoid, and fluctuant or tense. Infected cysts are often erythematous and tender. Most of the cysts produce labial asymmetry.

Small, asymptomatic cysts can be managed conservatively. Large, symptomatic cysts can be managed by incision and drainage, or marsupialization, or Bartholin gland excision. Bartholin abscess can be managed by incision and drainage by word catheter placement or marsupialization. In postmenopausal women with recurrent Bartholin cysts, a suspicion of Bartholin gland cancer should arise and the cyst wall should be sent for biopsy.

Other options:

Option A - Chlamydial infections typically present with vaginal discharge, dysuria, or cervicitis rather than localized pain and swelling in the perineal area. Though Chlamydia can cause infections in the Bartholin gland, the symptoms described in the question are more suggestive of a Bartholin abscess.

Option C - Genital tuberculosis primarily affects the upper genital tract, leading to menstrual irregularities, infertility, and abdominal pain. While it can also involve the vulva and perineal area, the clinical presentation described in the question is not typical for genital tuberculosis.

Option D - Genital herpes usually presents as painful ulcers or vesicles in the genital area, rather than a tender, erythematous swelling. The clinical presentation in the question is more consistent with a Bartholin abscess.
questions.learning: Bartholin abscess — The given clinical vignette suggests the diagnosis of Bartholin's abscess. Bartholin glands are the homologs of the male bulbourethral or Cowper glands.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which nerve is involved in Frey’s syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Auriculotemporal nerve

The auriculotemporal nerve (V3 nerve) is involved in Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating).

Frey’s syndrome is also known as Dupuy syndrome or auriculotemporal syndrome. It commonly develops after parotid surgery. It is caused by an aberrant regeneration of post-ganglionic parasympathetic nerve fibers crossed along the sympathetic pathways to the sweat glands near the parotid region.

Clinical features are due to the result of salivary stimulation (by the smell or taste of food) leading to the sweating and flushing of the periauricular region on the involved side of the face. A starch iodine test is used for diagnosis.

Treatment ranges from antiperspirants (in mild cases) to tympanic neurectomy or botulinum toxin injection (in severe cases). It can be prevented by incorporating careful extracapsular dissection and closure of the superficial musculoaponeurotic layer during parotidectomy.

Other options:

Option A: Facial nerve is the 7th cranial nerve that supplies the muscles of the face, and results in facial paralysis if injured during parotidectomy

Option B: Oculomotor is the 3rd cranial nerve which supplies the extraocular muscles. If injured during ophthalmic surgeries, it results in ocular paralysis and the eye pointing down and out.

Option D: Glossopharyngeal nerve is the 9th cranial nerve and its injury causes loss of taste sensation from the posterior 1/3rd of the tongue.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are the clinical features of septic abortion? 1. Persistent tachycardia ≥ 90 bpm 2. Impaired mental status 3. Hypothermia Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Septic abortion is an abortion complicated by infection of the uterus and surrounding tissues, which may progress to sepsis and septic shock. It is a medical emergency requiring prompt antibiotics, resuscitation, and uterine evacuation.

• 1. Persistent tachycardia ≥90 bpm: Correct. An early sign of systemic infection and sepsis.
• 2. Impaired mental status: Correct. Suggests severe sepsis or septic shock with organ dysfunction.
• 3. Hypothermia: Correct. Although fever is more common, hypothermia (<36°C) is a recognized feature of severe sepsis and is associated with a poorer prognosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In a patient presenting with signs suggestive of cardiac tamponade, which clinical finding is most characteristic of this condition?
options: Jugular vein column is visibly distended without pulsations
questions.explanation: In cardiac tamponade, the accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac prevents the heart chambers from filling effectively. This leads to a rise in central venous pressure, manifested clinically as a visibly distended jugular vein column that typically lacks its normal pulsations (Option D). While Pulsus Paradoxus (Option A) is a hallmark sign, it may be absent in certain cases (like ASD), so saying it is "always" present is clinically inaccurate. Kussmaul's sign (Option B) is classically associated with constrictive pericarditis, not tamponade (in tamponade, JVP usually drops with inspiration). A tall A wave (Option C) is associated with tricuspid stenosis or right heart hypertrophy. Therefore, based on the provided choices, the distended, non-pulsatile JVP is the most accurate clinical descriptor of the venous backflow. These findings form part of Beck’s Triad (hypotension, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds)

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which segment of the nephron has the lowest osmolality in the absence of the ADH hormone?
options: Descending limb of the Loop of Henle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cortical collecting duct

In the absence of antidiuretic hormone (ADH), the cortical collecting duct has the lowest osmolality.

As filtrate moves through the nephron, it changes concentration. Initially, in the proximal tubule, water and solutes are reabsorbed in equal proportions, keeping the filtrate isotonic (~300 mOsm/L). In the loop of Henle, water is removed in the descending limb, increasing osmolality, while solutes are actively reabsorbed in the ascending limb, diluting the filtrate to ~100 mOsm/L by the time it reaches the early distal convoluted tubule.

In the absence of ADH, the late distal tubule and collecting ducts remain impermeable to water, preventing reabsorption. As a result, in the cortical collecting duct, additional solutes such as sodium and chloride are reabsorbed without water, leading to further dilution of the tubular fluid.

This makes the cortical collecting duct the segment with the lowest osmolality, often reaching values as low as 50–75 mOsm/L, before the filtrate moves into the medullary collecting duct and is excreted as dilute urine.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old construction factory worker presents with dyspnoea. He has been working in this industry for the past 25 years. Which is the most specific malignancy that we can expect in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Malignant mesothelioma

Construction factory workers show an increased risk of exposure to asbestos. The most specific malignancy in a patient with asbestosis is malignant mesothelioma.

Malignant mesothelioma is a rare malignant tumour of the pleura, associated with heavy asbestos exposure. The lifetime risk of developing mesothelioma in heavily exposed individuals is as high as 7% to 10%.

Asbestosis is a diffuse interstitial fibrosing disease of the lung. Characteristic findings include:

* Irregular or linear opacities - Pleural plaques that are usually first noted in the lower lung fields are the chest radiographic hallmark of asbestosis.

* An indistinct heart border or a “ground-glass” appearance in the lung fields may be seen.

* Pulmonary function testing in asbestosis reveals a restrictive pattern with a decrease in both lung volumes and diffusing capacity along with mild airflow obstruction (due to peribronchiolar fibrosis).

* Lung cancer is the most common asbestos-related cancer.

* Mesothelioma (pleural and peritoneal) is the most specific asbestos-related cancer.

Adenocarcinoma of lung is still the most common malignancy seen in patients with asbestosis.
questions.learning: Malignant mesothelioma Construction factory workers show an increased risk of exposure to asbestos. The most specific malignancy in a patient with asbestosis is malignant mesothelioma.

questions.text: Identify the red marked area in the image given below?
questions.explanation: The third rib is a typical rib, having a head, neck, and body. It is attached posteriorly to the thoracic vertebrae and curves around the chest wall to reach the anterior side near the sternum. The posterior part of the third rib is located close to the vertebral column and is thicker and stronger, as it supports articulation with the spine. This portion includes the head, neck, and the region near the tubercle. It plays an important role in forming the rib cage, which protects the thoracic organs. Additionally, it provides attachment sites for muscles and ligaments that are essential for breathing movements and maintaining the stability of the upper body

questions.text: Which of the following bands will increase in serum electrophoresis in Nephrotic syndrome?

Correct answer: B. Alpha 2 globulin

• Some immunoglobulins

Liver response:

• Compensatory ↑ synthesis of larger proteins:

In nephrotic syndrome, there is urinary loss of low–molecular weight proteins like albumin and gamma globulins.

The liver compensatorily increases synthesis of α₂-macroglobulin, a large protein that is not lost in urine.

Hence, α₂-globulin band is increased on serum protein electrophoresis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following antidepressant drugs act by inhibiting the reuptake of both serotonin and noradrenaline?
questions.explanation: Venlafaxine belongs to the class of Serotonin-Noradrenaline Reuptake Inhibitors (SNRIs). As its name suggests, it works by inhibiting the reuptake transporters for both serotonin and norepinephrine in the synaptic cleft, thereby increasing the concentrations of these neurotransmitters to alleviate depressive symptoms. Fluoxetine (Option A) and Paroxetine (Option C) are Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs), which primarily target only the serotonin transporter. Dapoxetine (Option D) is a short-acting SSRI specifically used for the treatment of premature ejaculation rather than major depression. SNRIs like Venlafaxine or Duloxetine are often chosen for patients who have not responded to SSRIs or for those who also have chronic pain conditions, as noradrenaline modulation can help in pain processing. Common side effects of SNRIs include hypertension due to the increased noradrenergic tone. Understanding these pharmacological categories is essential for managing psychiatric disorders and predicting drug-specific adverse effects

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Certain new vaccines are being studied in the market and their efficacies are compared and presented in the image as shown below. Which of the newer vaccines can be used with the same efficacy as compared to the previous vaccine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. C, D and E

Vaccines C, D, and E can be used with the same efficacy as compared to the previous vaccine, as their confidence interval lies within the zone of equivalence.

In a classical randomized controlled trial (RCT), the aim is to evaluate a difference between two drugs by proving the superiority of the new drug over the standard drug. However, an equivalence study is carried out with the aim of showing there are no significant differences in the efficacy between the new drug and the standard drug.

To define 'no significant differences' the limit of equivalence (δ) must be defined first. δ must be set as superiority margin (+δ) and non-inferiority margin (-δ), so that they are clinically appropriate and the differences can be tolerated as clinically irrelevant. To conclude equivalence the confidence interval (CI), i.e., the whisker (tail) of the box-whisker plot must lie within the zone of equivalence.

Therefore in the given question, vaccines C, D, and E have CI in the zone of equivalence and thus have the same efficacy as the previous vaccine. Vaccines F and G lie outside the zone of equivalence but well within +δ, making them superior to the previous vaccine. Vaccines A and B lie outside the zone of equivalence but well within -δ, making them non-equivalent and at the same time non-inferior to the previous vaccine. If the CI of any vaccine includes or crosses the -δ limit, they will be considered inferior to the standard vaccine.

Note: A superiority trial is done to show that the new drug is superior to the standard drug. A non-inferiority trial is done to show that the new drug is not worse than the standard drug. This is done for newer interventions or drugs that may be less costly, less invasive, and have fewer side effects.
questions.learning: C, D and E Vaccines C, D, and E can be used with the same efficacy as compared to the previous vaccine, as their confidence interval lies within the zone of equivalence.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which type of epithelium lines the trachea?
questions.explanation: The trachea is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, often referred to as respiratory epithelium. Although it appears layered (stratified) because cell nuclei are at different heights, every cell is actually in contact with the basement membrane, making it a "pseudo" stratified tissue. This epithelium contains goblet cells that secrete mucus to trap inhaled particles and cilia that move the mucus upward toward the pharynx (the mucociliary escalator). Simple squamous epithelium (Option A) lines the alveoli for gas exchange. Transitional epithelium (Option B) is characteristic of the urinary tract, such as the bladder, allowing for distension. Stratified squamous epithelium (Option C) is found in areas prone to abrasion, like the esophagus and skin. In chronic smokers, the tracheal epithelium may undergo metaplasia, changing to stratified squamous epithelium to survive the irritation, which unfortunately destroys the protective ciliary mechanism, leading to a persistent "smoker's cough."

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a patient who underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy, what is the ideal urine output?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 0.5-1.5 ml/kg/hour

The ideal urine output in that patient following laparoscopic cholecystectomy is 0.5-1.5 ml/kg/hour.

Normal urine output is expected in the postoperative period of a patient who underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The average normal urine output in an adult is 0.5-1.5 ml/kg/hour (Option B) or approximately 1500 mL/day (Option A).  A minimum urine output of 400 mL/day is essential to excrete the end products of protein metabolism.

Option D: Normal urine output in ml/kg would be 0.5 - 1.5 ml/kg/hour multiplied by 24 which is 12-36 ml/kg per day.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following ions is involved in peripheral oxygen sensing chemoreceptors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Potassium

Potassium is involved in peripheral oxygen sensing chemoreceptors.

Type I glomus cells (carotid and aortic body) have O2-sensitive K+ channels, whose conductance is reduced in proportion to the degree of hypoxia.

This reduces the K+ efflux, depolarizing the cell and causing Ca2+ inﬂux.

The Ca2+ influx triggers action potentials and consequent excitation of the afferent nerve endings.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman on antidiabetic therapy for the last 10 years has experienced three episodes of vaginal candida infection in the past 2 years. Which of the following drugs should be avoided in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Canagliflozin

In this case of a 50-year-old diabetic patient with recurrent episodes of candidiasis, Canagliflozin must be avoided as it is a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor, can increase the risk of genital fungal infections, including vaginal candida infections, as it promotes glycosuria (increased glucose in the urine), which can create a favourable environment for yeast growth.

Canagliflozin is a sodium-glucose transporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitor. Other SGLT-2 inhibitors include dapagliflozin and empagliflozin. They act by inhibiting the SGLT-2 transporter which is present on the proximal segment of the renal tubule. It is responsible for the reabsorption of 80-90% of filtered glucose. It inhibits glucose reabsorption resulting in glycosuria and a change in the renal threshold.

Other options

Option A : Acarbose: Acarbose is an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor that delays the digestion and absorption of carbohydrates in the intestines. It does not directly affect glucose excretion in the urine or fluid removal from the body. Common side effects of acarbose include gastrointestinal disturbances such as flatulence, diarrhea, and abdominal discomfort.

Option B: Metformin is a biguanide that acts by activation of AMP-dependent protein kinase activation. It mediates a series of actions that help in reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis. It does not affect the blood glucose levels in normoglycemic states and hence does not cause hypoglycemia.

Option D: Pioglitazone is an activator of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ), which is involved in the regulation of genes related to glucose and lipid metabolism. Its adverse effects include increased incidence of heart failure, peripheral edema, weight gain, macular edema, and osteoporosis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the structure marked in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Genioglossus

The structure marked 'A' in the image is the Genioglossus muscle.

Genioglossus is one of the extrinsic muscles of the tongue which brings about the forward traction of the tongue to protrude its apex from the mouth. Hence, it is also called the safety muscle of the tongue.

Acting bilaterally, the two muscles depress the central part of the tongue, making it concave from side to side. Acting unilaterally, the tongue diverges to the opposite side.

Other options:

Hyoglossus: Depresses and retracts the tongue, pulling it downward and backward.

Styloglossus: Elevates and retracts the tongue, drawing it upward and backward.

Palatoglossus: Elevates the posterior portion of the tongue and narrows the fauces during swallowing.

Note:

* All the muscles of the tongue except palatoglossus (cranial accessory nerve through pharyngeal plexus) are supplied by hypoglossal nerve.

* All the muscles of pharynx except stylopharyngeus (glossopharyngeal nerve) are supplied by pharyngeal plexus.

* All muscles of soft palate except tensor veli palatini (nerve to medial pterygoid from mandibular nerve) are supplied by pharyngeal plexus.

* All muscles of larynx except cricothyroid (external laryngeal nerve) are supplied by recurrent laryngeal nerve.

All intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of tongue are derived from occipital myotomes, hence innervated by hypoglossal nerve, except palatoglossus which is derived from the pharyngeal arch and is supplied by vago-accessory nerve.
questions.learning: Genioglossus — The structure marked 'A' in the image is the Genioglossus muscle. Genioglossus is one of the extrinsic muscles of the tongue which brings about the forward traction of the tongue to protrude its apex from the mouth.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old man presents with acute, severe abdominal pain radiating to the back, associated with nausea and multiple episodes of vomiting over the past 24 hours. The pain is partially relieved by leaning forward and is most intense in the upper abdomen on examination. Laboratory investigations show elevated serum amylase and lipase levels. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, which is partially relieved by leaning forward (tripod position), is classic for "Acute Pancreatitis". The definitive diagnostic criteria are satisfied here by the clinical history combined with "elevated levels of lipase and amylase" (typically >3x the upper limit of normal). Acute appendicitis (Option A) typically begins with periumbilical pain shifting to the right lower quadrant. Acute cholecystitis (Option B) usually presents with right upper quadrant pain and a positive Murphy's sign. Liver damage or hepatitis (Option D) often involves jaundice and elevated transaminases rather than severe radiating pain and high lipase. The most common causes of pancreatitis are gallstones and excessive alcohol consumption. Management requires aggressive fluid resuscitation, pain control, and monitoring for systemic complications such as SIRS or pseudocyst formation
questions.learning: The patient’s presentation of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, which is partially relieved by leaning forward (tripod position), is classic for "Acute Pancreatitis".

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with deep-seated retro-orbital pain consistent with a cluster headache. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?
questions.explanation: High-flow 100% oxygen (12–15 L/min) administered via a non-rebreather mask is the gold standard for the acute abortive treatment of a cluster headache attack. It typically provides rapid relief within 15–20 minutes and is highly effective with a superior safety profile. Verapamil (Option A) is the first-line choice for long-term prophylaxis to prevent future attacks but is ineffective for stopping an acute episode once it has started. Lithium (Option C) and Topiramate (Option D) are also used as prophylactic agents in chronic or refractory cases rather than for acute relief. Cluster headaches are characterized by severe, unilateral, retro-orbital pain accompanied by autonomic symptoms like lacrimation or nasal congestion. Because the attacks are short-lived but excruciating, rapid-acting treatments like oxygen or subcutaneous sumatriptan are prioritized. Therefore, high-flow oxygen is the most appropriate immediate intervention
questions.learning: High-flow 100% oxygen (12–15 L/min) administered via a non-rebreather mask is the gold standard for the acute abortive treatment of a cluster headache attack.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is responsible for maintaining data about births and deaths in India?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sample registration system

The Sample Registration System is responsible for maintaining data about births and deaths in India.

SRS was initiated in the mid-1960s to provide reliable estimates of birth and death rates at the National and State levels. It is a dual-record system where there is continuous registration of births and deaths and a 6-month independent survey by an investigator-supervisor. It provides reliable health information, age-specific fertility and mortality rates, infant mortality,under-five and adult mortality.

Other options:

Lay reporting is defined as the collection of information, its use, and its transmission to other levels of the health system by non-professional health workers.
questions.learning: Sample registration system — The Sample Registration System is responsible for maintaining data about births and deaths in India. SRS was initiated in the mid-1960s to provide reliable estimates of birth and death rates at the National and State levels.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the following instrument used by obstetricians:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Outlet forceps

The image shows Wrigley's forceps, which is an outlet forceps.

The instrument is light, about a third of the weight of ordinary long-curved forceps. The instrument is short which is due to a reduction in the length of the shanks and handles. It has a marked cephalic curve with a slight pelvic curve.

Pearl PF1918: Obstetrics forceps

Commonly used forceps:

1) Simpson forceps

* The most commonly used types of forceps in outlet delivery.

* Has elongated cephalic curve.

* These are used when there is substantial molding of the fetal head.

2) Elliot forceps

* Has an adjustable pin for regulating the lateral pressure on the handles.

* They are used most often when there is minimal molding.

* More suitable for outlet delivery.

3) Kielland forceps

* Has small pelvic curve and a sliding lock.

* Suitable for head with little molding.

* The most common forceps used for rotational delivery.

* Helps correct asynclitism.

4) Piper forceps

* Distinct perineal curve.

* Allows for application to the after-coming head in breech delivery.

5) Tucker-McLane forceps

* Suitable for fetal head with little molding.

* Used in rotational delivery.

6) Barton forceps and traction handle

* Used in rotational delivery.

* Most importantly used for delivery of occipitotransverse positions in a platypelloid pelvis.

* It is an obsolete procedure.

Pearl PF1868: Criteria for forceps delivery

Procedure
Criteria

Outlet forceps

• Scalp is visible at the introitus without separating the labia
• Fetal skull has reached pelvic floor
• Fetal head is at or on perineum
• Sagittal suture is in anteroposteriordiameter or right or left occiput anterior or posterior position
• Rotation does not exceed 45 degrees

Low forceps
Leading point of fetal skull is at station > +2 cm and not on the pelvic floor:
a) Rotation is 45 degrees or less, or
b) Rotation is greater than 45 degrees

Mid forceps
Station of fetal head is between 0 and +2 cm.

High forceps

Not included in classification. Not used anymore.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of sodium nitroprusside?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stimulation of guanylyl cyclase

Sodium nitroprusside acts by stimulation of guanylyl cyclase.

Sodium nitroprusside releases nitric oxide which in turn stimulates guanyl cyclase. This activates cGMP secondary messenger which results in the relaxation of the smooth muscle.
questions.learning: Stimulation of guanylyl cyclase Sodium nitroprusside acts by stimulation of guanylyl cyclase. Sodium nitroprusside releases nitric oxide which in turn stimulates guanyl cyclase.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 40-year-old man with raised intracranial pressure develops horizontal diplopia. On examination, the right eye shows failure of abduction, suggesting involvement of the nerve which is particularly vulnerable to stretching as it bends over the petrous apex beneath the petrosphenoidal ligament. Compression of this nerve occurs in a small osteofibrous tunnel before it enters the cavernous sinus. Which of the following structures transmits this nerve?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dorello’s canal

The nerve described is the abducens nerve (CN VI).

Key clues in the question:

• Failure of abduction of eye → Lateral rectus palsy → CN VI
• Passes over petrous apex under petrosphenoidal (Gruber’s) ligament

This segment of the nerve passes through Dorello’s canal before entering the cavernous sinus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for management of severe hypercalcemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intravenous infusion of normal saline

Severe hypercalcemia (serum calcium >14 mg/dL or symptomatic hypercalcemia) is a medical emergency. The initial treatment is aggressive intravenous hydration with isotonic normal saline, which corrects volume depletion and enhances renal calcium excretion (calciuresis). Definitive therapies are added after adequate hydration.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Intravenous pamidronate: A bisphosphonate that inhibits bone resorption, but its effect begins only after 24–48 hours. It is given after adequate hydration.
• B. Oral phosphate supplementation: Not used routinely because of the risk of metastatic calcification and other adverse effects.
• D. Hemodialysis: Reserved for refractory severe hypercalcemia, especially in patients with renal failure, heart failure, or inability to tolerate aggressive hydration.
questions.learning: Intravenous infusion of normal saline Severe hypercalcemia (serum calcium >14 mg/dL or symptomatic hypercalcemia) is a medical emergency. The initial treatment is aggressive intravenous hydration with isotonic normal saline, which corrects volume depletion…

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following local anaesthetic causes hypertension?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cocaine

The local anesthetic that causes hypertension is cocaine. This is due to the inhibition of norepinephrine at the adrenergic terminals leading to increased sympathetic stimulation. This effect occurs at all concentrations of cocaine and causes hypertension and ventricular ectopies.

Treatment is with the help of benzodiazepines, α-adrenergic antagonists and amiodarone.

All local anesthetics are mainly cardiodepressants causing reduced contractility and vasodilation. However, at low concentrations, all local anesthetics cause vasoconstriction due to the inhibition of nitric oxide. Only cocaine produces vasoconstriction and hypertension at all concentrations.

Accidental intravascular injection of local anesthetic like bupivacaine results in bupivacaine-induced cardiotoxicity. Management is by resuscitation followed by intralipid therapy. A rapid bolus of intralipid 20% IV is administered without delay.

Other adverse effects of local anesthetics include neurologic toxicity, respiratory depression, and hypersensitivity reactions. Nervous system manifestations are circumoral numbness, tongue paresthesia, dizziness, tinnitus, and disorientation. Finally, respiratory depression can lead to respiratory arrest.
questions.learning: Cocaine — The local anesthetic that causes hypertension is cocaine. This is due to the inhibition of norepinephrine at the adrenergic terminals leading to increased sympathetic stimulation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Up to what time after delivery can an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) be safely inserted in the postpartum period??
questions.explanation: Postpartum Intrauterine Contraceptive Device (PPIUCD) insertion is a highly effective strategy for preventing unintended pregnancies. According to standard protocols, the device can be inserted immediately after the delivery of the placenta (within 10 minutes) or up to 48 hours following delivery. After this 48-hour window, the risk of device expulsion and infection increases significantly due to the rapid involution of the uterus. If insertion does not occur within the first 48 hours, the patient is usually advised to wait at least 6 weeks (Option C) until the puerperium is complete and the uterus has returned to its normal size. Options A, C, and D are either incomplete or describe intervals outside the specific "immediate postpartum" window. PPIUCD provides long-term, reversible contraception that does not interfere with breastfeeding, making it an ideal choice for many women during the hospital stay following delivery

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The following appearance in IVP is caused by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Retroperitoneal fibrosis

Key Finding in this IVP:

The image shows medial deviation of the ureters — the classic hallmark of retroperitoneal fibrosis (RPF)

Classic IVP Findings in Retroperitoneal Fibrosis:

| Feature | Description

| ------- | -----------

| Medial deviation of ureters | Most characteristic — ureters pulled medially at L4-L5 level

| Hydronephrosis | Due to ureteric obstruction

| Tapering obstruction | Smooth extrinsic compression of ureters

| Level of obstruction | Typically at L4-L5 (mid-ureter)

| Bilateral involvement | Common

Causes of RPF:

• Idiopathic (most common — Ormond's disease)
• Methysergide use
• Aortic aneurysm
• Malignancy
• Radiation fibrosis

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A vital layer, also known as “Schmutzdecke”, is seen in which one of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Slow sand filter

The Schmutzdecke (German for “dirty layer” or “vital layer”) is a biologically active layer that develops on the surface of a slow sand filter. It consists of algae, bacteria, protozoa, fungi, and organic matter and is responsible for the major purification of water by removing microorganisms and organic impurities.

• A. Air filter ✗

• Does not contain a Schmutzdecke.

• B. Rapid sand filter ✗

• Purification occurs mainly by physical filtration after coagulation and sedimentation.
• No biological layer (Schmutzdecke) is formed.

• C. Slow sand filter ✓

• The Schmutzdecke is its characteristic feature and provides biological purification.

• D. Reverse osmosis filter ✗

• Uses a semipermeable membrane under pressure; no biological layer is involved.
questions.learning: Slow sand filter — The Schmutzdecke (German for “dirty layer” or “vital layer”) is a biologically active layer that develops on the surface of a slow sand filter.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which anatomical structure is represented by the label “C” in the given image?.
questions.explanation: The label “C” in the CT scan corresponds to the lentiform nucleus, which is a wedge-shaped structure located lateral to the internal capsule. The lentiform nucleus is composed of two parts: the putamen (laterally) and the globus pallidus (medially). On axial CT images, it appears as a relatively dense, lens-shaped gray matter structure in the basal ganglia region, matching the position indicated by label “C”. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Globus pallidus : This is only the medial component of the lentiform nucleus. It lies closer to the internal capsule and appears smaller and more medial than the structure marked “C”. Since “C” points to the entire lens-shaped area, it cannot represent just the globus pallidus. (B) Putamen : The putamen is the lateral part of the lentiform nucleus. While it forms a major portion, the label “C” includes both medial and lateral parts, indicating the complete structure rather than just the putamen. (D) None : This is incorrect because the labeled structure clearly corresponds anatomically to the lentiform nucleus. Thus, the correct answer is (C) Lentiform nucleus
questions.learning: The label “C” in the CT scan corresponds to the lentiform nucleus, which is a wedge-shaped structure located lateral to the internal capsule. The lentiform nucleus is composed of two parts: the putamen (laterally) and the globus pallidus (medially).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In this scenario, what is the mode of transmission by which the condition was passed from the grandmother to the father and then to the boy?
options: Autosomal recessive AAns AAns AAns AAns AAns AAns AAns
questions.explanation: The inheritance pattern described involves the direct transmission of a trait from a grandmother to her son (the father) and then to his son (the grandson). This vertical transmission across three generations, including male-to-male transmission, is the hallmark of Autosomal Dominant inheritance. In X-linked dominant (Option A) and X-linked recessive (Option B) patterns, a father cannot pass the trait to his son because he only contributes his Y chromosome to male offspring. Autosomal recessive inheritance (Option D) typically presents as a horizontal pattern (skipping generations) and requires both parents to be carriers, which is inconsistent with the direct lineage shown here. Therefore, because the condition is passed directly from father to son through consecutive generations, it excludes X-linked and recessive possibilities, confirming that the gene is located on an autosome and is dominant in expression
questions.learning: The inheritance pattern described involves the direct transmission of a trait from a grandmother to her son (the father) and then to his son (the grandson).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the ESI act, beneficiaries getting 70 % of the wages for 3 months is under which benefit?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sickness benefit

In the ESI act, sickness Benefit is given at 70% of daily wage for a duration of 91 days (3 months) in one year.

* Extended sickness benefit – 80% of the daily wages for a duration of 2 years for 34 specified diseases

* Enhanced sickness benefit – at full wages for sterilization procedure for a duration of 7 days post-vasectomy and 14 days post tubectomy.

Note: The ESI act has been revised which is in effect from 01.07.19

Pearl PF0292: ESI ACT, 1948

Employees State Insurance Act, 1948 (Revised)

Scope: It is applicable to all factories in India excluding

* Defense

* Railway

Finance Contribution

* Employee – 0.75% of his daily wage

* Employer – 3.25% of the employees' daily wage

* Medical benefit – 1/8th by the state government and 7/8th by the ESI Corporation.

Benefits

To the Employees

* Medical Benefit- no cash benefit, full medical care is provided.

* Sickness Benefit- is given at 70% of daily wage for a duration of 91 days in one year

* Dependance Benefit– is at 90% daily wages, lifelong for the spouse and parents and till the age of 18 years for any dependant's child, however, the benefit is withdrawn if the daughter is married earlier.

* Funeral Benefit – Rs.15,000/-

To the Employers

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old male had an episode of loss of consciousness subsequent to a head injury from a bike accident. Upon awakening, he began experiencing severe headache and nausea. He appears drowsy with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 10. One of his pupils is dilated and unresponsive. CT head given. What is the management?
options: Anticoagulants to prevent further clotting of blood
Observe and serial monitoring in the ICU
Osmotic diuresis to decrease intracranial pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Urgent surgical evacuation

The given scenario of a man with a head injury, unconsciousness, nausea, dilated and fixed pupils, and the CT finding of a lenticular hemorrhage also showing a mid-line shift is characteristic of an extradural or epidural hemorrhage. Urgent surgical evacuation of heamatoma by craniotomy is the management.

Epidural hemorrhage/hematoma is an intracranial hemorrhage in which the hemorrhage is between the dura and the skull. It classically occurs due to a tear of the middle meningeal artery, following a fracture of the temporal bone. Management is by surgical evacuation of the hematoma or by ligation of the damaged middle meningeal artery

Clinically, patients with extradural hemorrhage typically present with an initial transient loss of consciousness. A lucid interval is then seen, which may be minutes to hours during which the patient usually presents. Neurological deterioration then occurs following the lucid interval as the hematoma expands.

As the hematoma expands, compensation is exhausted with rapid deterioration. There is contralateral hemiparesis, a reduced conscious level, and ipsilateral pupillary dilatation, the cardinal signs of brain compression and herniation. The prognosis for promptly evacuated extradural hematoma, without associated primary brain injury is excellent.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with severe cardiogenic shock is placed on mechanical circulatory support. During a teaching round, the cardiologist explains that if the heart suddenly stops pumping and blood flow throughout the circulation ceases, the pressure in the entire vascular system will eventually equalize to a single value determined by the volume of blood and the compliance of the vessels. Which of the following terms describes this pressure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mean circulatory filling pressure

Mean circulatory filling pressure (MCFP) is the pressure that exists throughout the entire cardiovascular system when cardiac output is zero and blood flow has ceased, allowing pressures in all vessels to equalize. It is determined by the total blood volume and the compliance (capacitance) of the vasculature, especially the venous system.

MCFP is an important determinant of venous return, as the gradient between MCFP and right atrial pressure drives blood back to the heart.

Why not the other options?

• A. Pulse pressure – the difference between systolic and diastolic arterial pressure.
• B. Critical closing pressure – the pressure below which blood vessels collapse and blood flow stops.
• D. Perfusion pressure – the pressure gradient driving blood flow through an organ (arterial pressure − venous pressure).
questions.learning: Mean circulatory filling pressure Mean circulatory filling pressure (MCFP) is the pressure that exists throughout the entire cardiovascular system when cardiac output is zero and blood flow has ceased, allowing pressures in all vessels to equalize.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What term is used to describe the complete and systematic study of death in all its aspects?
questions.explanation: Thanatology is the scientific and comprehensive study of death in all its aspects, including the physical, psychological, and social changes that accompany it. In a medical and forensic context, it focuses on the mechanism, cause, and timing of death, as well as the various post-mortem changes the body undergoes. Forensic anthropology (Option B) is a specialized subfield focused on identifying human remains, especially skeletal remains. Toxicology (Option C) is the study of poisons and their effects on the body. Molecular death (Option D) refers to the final stage of death when all individual cells and tissues have permanently ceased their metabolic activities, typically occurring several hours after clinical death. Understanding thanatology is essential for forensic pathologists to accurately perform autopsies and establish the medico-legal "Time Since Death." It encompasses the study of the "signs of death" and is a foundational discipline within forensic medicine, aiming to provide scientific certainty regarding the end of human life
questions.learning: Thanatology is the scientific and comprehensive study of death in all its aspects, including the physical, psychological, and social changes that accompany it.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with reduced visual acuity after cataract surgery and is found to have posterior capsular opacification on examination. Which type of laser is used for its treatment?
questions.explanation: Posterior capsular opacification (PCO), often referred to as "after-cataract," is the most common late complication following successful cataract surgery. It occurs when remaining lens epithelial cells migrate and proliferate across the posterior capsule, causing blurred vision and glare. The Neodymium-doped Yttrium Aluminum Garnet (Nd:YAG) laser is the gold standard for treating this condition through a procedure called a YAG laser capsulotomy. This laser uses photodisruption to create a small, clear opening in the center of the clouded capsule, instantly restoring visual clarity without the need for invasive surgery. Femto lasers (Option A) are used for precision incisions during the initial cataract surgery but not for PCO. Argon lasers (Option D) and Argon fluoride (Option C) produce thermal or photoablative effects used in retinal photocoagulation or refractive surgery (LASIK), respectively, but they lack the photodisruptive properties required to "punch" a hole in the posterior capsule. Consequently, the Nd:YAG laser remains the primary and most effective non-invasive treatment for secondary opacification
questions.learning: Posterior capsular opacification (PCO), often referred to as "after-cataract," is the most common late complication following successful cataract surgery.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · Basics Of Cell Cytoskeleton
questions.text: A 25-year-old patient presents with a history of recurrent sinusitis, bronchiectasis, and chronic cough. He also mentions that he has had several ear infections and episodes of pneumonia over the past few years. On physical examination, you note digital clubbing. A chest X-ray is obtained. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Kartagener syndrome

Recurrent sinusitis, bronchiectasis, chronic cough, and ear infections suggest primary ciliary dyskinesia. Kartagener syndrome is the classic triad of bronchiectasis, sinusitis, and situs inversus due to defective dynein arms. Impaired mucociliary clearance causes repeated respiratory infections and clubbing. The other options do not explain chronic sinopulmonary disease from ciliary dysfunction.

Dynein arm defect in cilia

↓

Impaired ciliary movement

↓

↓ Mucociliary clearance

↓

Mucus + pathogens accumulate

↓

Recurrent infections

↓

Chronic inflammation

↓

Bronchiectasis + lung damageSignet-Ring Sign, Bronchiectasis. The bronchi (red arrows) are larger than their corresponding arteries (white arrows), the reverse of the normal pattern in which the bronchus is smaller than its corresponding vessel.

| Feature | Kartagener | Cystic Fibrosis

| ------- | ---------- | ---------------

| Defect | Ciliary movement | CFTR chloride channel

| Mucus | Normal but not cleared | Thick, sticky

| Situs inversus | Common | Rare

| Fertility | ↓ (immotile sperm) | ↓ (thick secretions)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 3-day-old neonate presents with abdominal distension and bilious vomiting. Among the following, which is the most appropriate investigation to diagnose the condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. CECT abdomen

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of jejunoileal atresia, and among the options CECT abdomen is the most appropriate investigation to diagnose the condition.

Small bowel atresias present with intestinal obstruction soon after birth. Bilious vomiting is the dominant feature in proximal bowel atresia such as duodenal atresia whereas abdominal distension with bilious vomiting is more with distal small bowel atresia such as jejuno-ileal atresia. Jejuno-ileal atresia is the most GI atresia.

Plain abdominal radiographs show a variable number of dilated loops of bowel and fluid levels according to the level of obstruction.

* Jejunal/ileal atresia - Triple bubble appearance

* Duodenal atresia - Double bubble appearance

A contrast study is the next best investigation to exclude other bowel anomalies.

In jejunal/ileal atresia, the distal end of the dilated proximal small bowel is resected and a primary end-to-end anastomosis is possible. If the proximal bowel is extremely dilated, it may need to be tapered to the distal bowel before anastomosis.

Classification of Jejunoileal atresia:

Type

Feature

Type 1

Mucosal web or diaphragm

Type 2

With an atretic cord between two blind ends of bowel with intact mesentery

Type 3 a

Complete separation of the blind ends of the bowel by a V-shaped mesenteric gap

Type 3 b

An apple peel or Christmas tree deformity with a large mesenteric gap

Type 4

Multiple atresias, with a string of sausage appearance

An erect X-ray of the abdomen showing ileal atresia. The image shows a triple bubble appearance and associated finding of apple-peel bowel with loss of dorsal mesentery is a feature of ileal atresia.
questions.learning: CECT abdomen — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of jejunoileal atresia, and among the options CECT abdomen is the most appropriate investigation to diagnose the condition.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman presents with a history suggestive of hyperthyroidism at 8 weeks of POG. What is the drug of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Propylthiouracil

The drug of choice for the treatment of thyrotoxicosis during the first trimester of pregnancy is propylthiouracil (PTU). It is because it has lower teratogenic effects than carbimazole or methimazole.

Carbimazole and methimazole are associated with teratogenic effects such as:

• Aplasia cutis congenita
• Choanal atresia
• Treacheosopageal fistula
• Fetal goiter

However, propylthiouracil use is limited to the first trimester due to the risk of hepatotoxicity. It is replaced with carbimazole or methimazole in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters of the pregnancy.

The lowest effective antithyroid drug dose should be used throughout gestation. This is to maintain the maternal serum-free T4 level in the upper limit of the non-pregnant normal reference range.

Propranolol is a non-selective beta blocker. It is used in thyroid storm preferentially as it blocks the peripheral conversion of inactive T4 to active form T3.
questions.learning: Propylthiouracil — The drug of choice for the treatment of thyrotoxicosis during the first trimester of pregnancy is propylthiouracil (PTU). It is because it has lower teratogenic effects than carbimazole or methimazole.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: If a sample is cultured in LJ media, what would be the staining characteristic of the organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acid fast

Mycobacterium tuberculosis exhibits an acid-fast property when stained with a differential stain such as the Ziehl-Neelsen method. Lowenstein-Jenson medium is a selective medium used for Mycobacterium tuberculosis culture. The presence of malachite green imparts a green colour and makes Lowenstein Jenson medium a selective media by inhibiting other bacteria.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis resists decolorisation by 20% sulphuric acid and is therefore called acid-fast.

Colony characteristics on LJ Medium:

Mycobacterium tuberculosis colonies on LJ medium are dry, rough, raised, irregular colonies with a wrinkled surface, tenacious, difficult to emulsify, creamy white and buff-colored (rough, tough, buff).

Mycobacterium bovis forms moist, smooth, flat, white colonies on LJ media that break up easily when touched.

Components of LJ medium:

* Egg: Provide fatty acids and protein required for the metabolism.

* Malachite green: Prevents growth of contaminants.

* Mineral salt solution: Buffer.

* Glycerol: Source of carbon, Favours growth of M. tuberculosis, but not M. bovis.

* L-asparagine: Source of Nitrogen.
questions.learning: Acid fast Mycobacterium tuberculosis exhibits an acid-fast property when stained with a differential stain such as the Ziehl-Neelsen method. Lowenstein-Jenson medium is a selective medium used for Mycobacterium tuberculosis culture.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the fracture:
questions.explanation: The radiograph shows a classic depressed skull fracture, where a localized fragment of the skull vault is displaced inward toward the brain parenchyma. This is typically the result of high-energy impact from a blunt object with a small surface area, such as a hammer or brick. Regarding the distractors, a linear or fissured fracture (Option B) appears as a simple crack or radiolucent line without any displacement of the bone. A hinge fracture (Option C) is a base-of-skull fracture that runs transversely from one side to the other, usually not visible in this vault view. A gutter fracture (Option D) is a specific type of groove in the bone typically caused by an oblique gunshot wound. Because the image clearly shows the "stepping" of the bone inward, it is categorized as a depressed fracture
questions.learning: The radiograph shows a classic depressed skull fracture, where a localized fragment of the skull vault is displaced inward toward the brain parenchyma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the most common electrolyte imbalance observed in pyloric stenosis?
questions.explanation: In pyloric stenosis, repeated projectile vomiting leads to loss of gastric contents, resulting in a characteristic hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Among electrolyte abnormalities, hypokalemia is considered the most consistent and prominent finding in exam context. Mechanism: 1. Vomiting causes loss of H⁺ and Cl⁻, leading to metabolic alkalosis 2. Alkalosis causes shift of K⁺ into cells, lowering serum potassium 3. Volume depletion activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system 4. Aldosterone increases renal potassium loss, worsening hypokalemia Why other options are incorrect: (A) Hyponatremia: May occur due to dehydration, but not the most consistent finding (C) Hypochloremia: Common due to HCl loss, but hypokalemia is more consistently emphasized as the key metabolic disturbance (D) Hypophosphatemia: Not typically associated Thus, the most common electrolyte imbalance (exam answer) is hypokalemia
questions.learning: In pyloric stenosis, repeated projectile vomiting leads to loss of gastric contents, resulting in a characteristic hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden vision loss and painful eye movements. Examination reveals a relative afferent pupillary defect in the affected eye, a normal-appearing optic disc, and a central scotoma on visual field testing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of sudden vision loss, pain with eye movements, and a central scotoma (blind spot in the center of the field) is highly characteristic of optic neuritis. The presence of a Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) confirms a lesion of the optic nerve. Crucially, the finding that the optic disk appears normal points specifically to retrobulbar neuritis, a form of optic neuritis where the inflammation occurs behind the globe, leaving the visible disk margin sharp and healthy. Optic nerve glioma (Option A) causes progressive, painless proptosis in children. Eale's disease (Option C) is a peripheral retinal vasculitis causing vitreous hemorrhage. Neuroretinitis (Option D) would show visible disk swelling accompanied by a macular star. Optic neuritis is frequently the presenting symptom of Multiple Sclerosis. Therefore, because the symptoms localize to the nerve without visible disk edema, Option B is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical triad of sudden vision loss, pain with eye movements, and a central scotoma (blind spot in the center of the field) is highly characteristic of optic neuritis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
A boys' hostel has an outbreak of fever cases with headache, followed by the development of pleomorphic rashes sparing palms and soles. What is the next best step in the management of suspected cases?

VZIG- Varicella zoster immunoglobulin
options: Isolate for 6 days after giving acyclovir, followed by VZIG within 72 hours of exposure
Isolate for 12 days after giving acyclovir, followed by VZIG within 48 hours of exposure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Isolate for 6 days

The scenario describes an outbreak of fever cases with headache followed by the development of pleomorphic rashes sparing palms and soles, which points to the diagnosis of chickenpox. In a boys' hostel, it is reasonable to assume that the majority of the affected individuals are not in the high-risk groups for severe varicella infection. For the management of suspected cases in this situation, isolation for 6 days from the onset of the rash is the appropriate measure to prevent further spread of the infection. Acyclovir and VZIG are not necessary for healthy individuals.

Varicella zoster immunoglobulin (VZIG) is not indicated for everyone. VZIG is a passive immunization used as post-exposure prophylaxis for individuals at high risk of developing severe varicella (chickenpox) infection after being exposed to the varicella-zoster virus. It should be administered within 72 hours of exposure to provide the best protection, although it may still be effective if given up to 10 days after exposure.

High-risk individuals who may benefit from VZIG include

1. Immunocompromised individuals, such as those receiving immunosuppressive therapy, those with congenital cellular immunodeficiency, and those with acquired immunodeficiency, including HIV/AIDS.
2. Pregnant women who have been exposed to the virus and have no history of chickenpox or vaccination, as varicella infection during pregnancy can lead to congenital varicella syndrome or severe neonatal varicella infection.
3. Newborns whose mothers developed chickenpox within five days before delivery or within 48 hours after delivery, as they are at risk of severe neonatal varicella infection.

For healthy individuals who have been exposed to the varicella-zoster virus, the varicella vaccine is usually recommended as post-exposure prophylaxis, rather than VZIG. The vaccine should be administered within 3 to 5 days of exposure to help prevent or reduce the severity of the disease.

Live attenuated vaccine is administered to children who have not had chickenpox between the age of 12 to 18 months.

The below image shows multiple vesicular lesions on the trunk is suggestive of chickenpox.
questions.learning: Isolate for 6 days — The scenario describes an outbreak of fever cases with headache followed by the development of pleomorphic rashes sparing palms and soles, which points to the diagnosis of chickenpox.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient develops postoperative ileus after abdominal surgery. Which of the following is the drug used for management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alvimopan

Postoperative ileus is worsened by opioid analgesics, which act on peripheral µ-opioid receptors in the gut myenteric plexus to suppress motility. Alvimopan is a peripherally-acting µ-opioid receptor antagonist (PAMORA) with negligible CNS penetration — it reverses opioid-induced gut stasis and accelerates return of bowel function without antagonizing central analgesia. It is FDA-approved specifically for accelerating GI recovery after bowel resection (short-term, in-hospital use only, due to MI risk with long-term use).

Other options:

• Atropine (B) and Glycopyrrolate (D) are antimuscarinics → block M₃ receptors → further ↓ motility; they would aggravate ileus.
• Loperamide (C) is a peripheral µ-opioid agonist → ↓ motility — used for diarrhea, exactly the wrong direction.
• Octreotide also ↓ GI secretions and motility → not useful.
questions.learning: Alvimopan Postoperative ileus is worsened by opioid analgesics, which act on peripheral µ-opioid receptors in the gut myenteric plexus to suppress motility.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with brown-colored urine and oliguria for the last 3 days. He has mild facial and pedal edema. His blood pressure is 126/90. He has 2+ proteinuria with >100 red cells/HPF and a few granular casts. His creatinine is 0.9, urea is 56. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. PSGN

A child presenting with acute onset (3 days) gross hematuria, hypertension, edema, oliguria, and mild to moderate proteinuria is suggestive of a nephritic syndrome picture. The only disease which causes this out of the given options is post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN).

PSGN is primarily caused by Group A β-hemolytic streptococcal infections in children aged 5 to 12 years. It is caused by immune complexes containing streptococcal antigens (M protein of cell wall) and specific antibodies. PSGN typically manifests as an acute nephritic syndrome, appearing either 1 to 2 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis or 3 to 6 weeks after streptococcal pyoderma. The severity of kidney involvement can vary, ranging from asymptomatic microscopic hematuria with normal renal function to gross hematuria with acute renal failure. Edema, hypertension, and oliguria may be present depending on the extent of renal involvement.

Laboratory findings commonly include a significant decrease in serum C3 levels during the acute phase, with values returning to normal within 6 to 8 weeks. To confirm the diagnosis, evidence of a preceding streptococcal infection is necessary. The antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer often increases following pharyngitis, while the anti-deoxyribonuclease B level is a reliable indicator of cutaneous streptococcal infection.

Light microscopic examination reveals enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with diffuse mesangial and endothelial proliferation, as well as leukocyte infiltration. Immunofluorescence analysis demonstrates granular deposits of IgG and complement C3 along the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) and in the mesangium. Electron microscopy primarily shows subepithelial humps, with subendothelial deposits observed in early stages of the disease.

Managing the acute effects of renal insufficiency (sodium restriction and diuretics) and hypertension is the mainstay. Antibiotic therapy with a 10-day course of penicillin is recommended to limit the spread of nephritogenic pathogens. But antibiotics do not alter the natural course of PSGN. Complete resolution of the hematuria and proteinuria in the majority of children occurs within 3–6 weeks of the onset of nephritis but 3–10% of children may have persistent microscopic hematuria, non-nephrotic proteinuria, or hypertension.
