questions.learning: PSGN — A child presenting with acute onset (3 days) gross hematuria, hypertension, edema, oliguria, and mild to moderate proteinuria is suggestive of a nephritic syndrome picture.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Fructosamine is obtained by glycation of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Albumin

Fructosamine is obtained by the glycation of albumin.

Fructosamine is a measure of non-enzymatic glycation of circulating proteins including albumin, globulins, and lipoproteins. It is now used as a  reasonable alternative to HbA1c measurement when it is not reliable. Since albumin is the most abundant of the serum proteins, fructosamine is predominantly a measure of glycated albumin.

Fructosamine is used as a short-term marker of glucose control. It reflects the average glycemia over the preceding 2 to 3 weeks. HbA1c reflects glucose control over a period of the preceding 8 to 12 weeks.
questions.learning: Albumin Fructosamine is obtained by the glycation of albumin. Fructosamine is a measure of non-enzymatic glycation of circulating proteins including albumin, globulins, and lipoproteins.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What condition is likely in a newborn presenting with dry, rough skin, a big tongue, and rough hair?
questions.explanation: A newborn presenting with a "big tongue" (macroglossia), dry and rough skin, coarse or "rough" hair, and a hoarse cry is highly suspicious for congenital hypothyroidism (cretinism). Other common signs include prolonged neonatal jaundice, umbilical hernia, and a large posterior fontanelle. Macroglossia occurs due to the accumulation of glycosaminoglycans in the tongue tissue. Prader-Willi syndrome (Option B) typically presents with profound neonatal hypotonia and feeding difficulties, but not the specific cutaneous and lingual findings of hypothyroidism. Edward syndrome (Trisomy 18) (Option C) involves severe growth retardation, clenched fists, and "rocker-bottom" feet. Galactosemia (Option D) presents with jaundice, liver failure, and cataracts, but does not cause macroglossia or the classic coarse features of thyroid deficiency. Screening newborns for TSH levels is standard practice because early thyroxine replacement is essential to prevent permanent, irreversible intellectual disability and ensure normal growth and development
questions.learning: A newborn presenting with a "big tongue" (macroglossia), dry and rough skin, coarse or "rough" hair, and a hoarse cry is highly suspicious for congenital hypothyroidism (cretinism).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following conditions leads to a leftward shift of the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve?
questions.explanation: The oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve describes the relationship between oxygen partial pressure and hemoglobin saturation. A leftward shift indicates an increased affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen, meaning oxygen is bound more tightly and released less easily to tissues. Alkalosis (Option C), which is an increase in blood pH, is a classic cause of this leftward shift. Hypoxia (Option A) does not directly shift the curve but triggers physiological responses. Hypercarbia (increased ) (Option B), an increase in temperature, and an increase in 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) (Option D) all cause a rightward shift in the curve, decreasing oxygen affinity to facilitate delivery to tissues during high metabolic demand. This rightward movement is known as the Bohr effect. Because alkalosis increases the attraction between hemoglobin and oxygen, it is the only factor listed that definitively causes a leftward shift in the curve
questions.learning: The oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve describes the relationship between oxygen partial pressure and hemoglobin saturation. A leftward shift indicates an increased affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen, meaning oxygen is bound more tightly and released less…

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A housewife presents with complaints of a blocked nose, loss of smell, and dry, greenish crusty nasal discharge. On examination, nasal cavities appear roomy and turbinates are atrophied. Which of the following surgeries can be done on this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Young’s operation

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of atrophic rhinitis. Young’s and modified Young’s operations are done for the treatment of atrophic rhinitis.

In Young’s operation, both the nostrils are closed completely just within the nasal vestibule by raising flaps. They are opened after 6 months or later when the mucosa may revert to normal and crusting will be reduced.

Modified Young’s operation aims at partially closing the nostrils.

Other options:

Options A and C: Submucous resection and septoplasty are done for deviated nasal septum.

Option D: Vidian neurectomy is done for vasomotor rhinitis.
questions.learning: Young’s operation — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of atrophic rhinitis. Young’s and modified Young’s operations are done for the treatment of atrophic rhinitis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An infant is brought with complaints of excessive watering of the eyes and photophobia. The image is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Congenital glaucoma

The clinical scenario of excessive watering and photophobia in an infant and the given image with corneal enlargement and haze suggest a likely diagnosis of congenital glaucoma.

Primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) is caused by impaired aqueous outflow due to a maldeveloped anterior chamber angle.

It can be classified as

• True congenital glaucoma - IOP is elevated during intrauterine life.
• Infantile glaucoma - manifests before 3 years of age.
• Juvenile glaucoma (least common) - IOP rises between 3 and 16 years of age.

Clinically, the child presents with lacrimation, photophobia, and blepharospasm.

PCG may also present with:

• Corneal haze (due to diffuse edema secondary to raised IOP)
• Buphthalmos (a large eye that results from stretching due to raised IOP before 3 years of age). The thin sclera appears blue due to underlying uveal tissue.
• Haab striae (curvilinear healed breaks in Descemet's membrane)
• Corneal scarring
• Optic disc cupping

Evaluation is done under general anesthesia. Initially, IOP measurement is performed (10–12  mmHg is normal). A corneal diameter measuring greater than 12 mm is highly suggestive of an infant under the age of 1 year.

Management is essentially surgical and goniotomy and/or trabeculectomy may be done.

Other options:

Option B: Congenital cataract occurs due to disturbance in lens growth leading to the development of opaque lens fibers. It can be idiopathic, hereditary, or secondary to metabolic disorders and infections. It presents with leukocoria (white reflex in the pupillary area), wandering eye movement, squint, and nystagmus.

Option C: Mucopolysaccharidoses are inherited metabolic disorders presenting with corneal opacification, pigmentary retinopathy, glaucoma, and optic atrophy.

Option D: Ophthalmia neonatorum presents in neonates with conjunctival discharge and chemosis, and tenderness of the eyeball secondary to infections.
questions.learning: Congenital glaucoma — The clinical scenario of excessive watering and photophobia in an infant and the given image with corneal enlargement and haze suggest a likely diagnosis of congenital glaucoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child presents with recurrent chest infections and abdominal pain. There is a history of 1 blood transfusion in the past. On examination, he had icterus and mild splenomegaly. Electrophoresis shows increased HbA2, HbF, and S spike. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sickle cell disease

The given scenario with electrophoresis showing increased HbA2, HbF, and S spike is suggestive of sickle cell disease.

Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to the point mutation in the β-globin gene which results in the replacement of glutamate residue with valine. This causes the production of sickle-shaped red blood cells due to the polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbS).

Factors that predispose to sickling are infection, dehydration, and acidosis.

The clinical features of sickle cell disease are due to the tendency of HbS molecules to stack into polymers when deoxygenated. The features are:

• Moderately severe hemolytic anemia with jaundice.
• Painful bone crisis- hand-foot syndrome or dactylitis of the bones of hands and feet.
• Acute chest syndrome typically presents with fever, cough, chest pain, and pulmonary infiltrates.
• Hyposthenuria- inability to concentrate urine.
• Aplastic crisis stems from the infection of red cell progenitors by parvovirus B19, which causes a transient cessation of erythropoiesis and a sudden worsening of the anemia.
• Spleen

• In children- splenic sequestration crises occur which results in splenomegaly due to red pulp congestion.
• Adolescence or early adulthood- autosplenectomy occurs due to splenic infarction, fibrosis, and progressive shrinkage.
• Increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated organisms like pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenza septicemia, but can be reduced by vaccination and prophylactic antibiotics.

• Other clinical features- priapism, leg ulcers, stroke, retinopathy, pigment gallstones, and growth retardation.

The diagnosis is suggested by the clinical findings, the presence of irreversibly sickled red cells on peripheral smear, and hemoglobin electrophoresis showing increased levels of HbA2, HbF, and S spike. The changes in the skull resemble a crewcut in radiographic studies as a result of compensatory erythroid hyperplasia.

The image given below shows the sickling of RBCs in sickle cell disease.

The image given below shows Howell-Jolly bodies seen in asplenia.

Note: The sickle cell trait protects against falciparum malaria in certain African populations.

Other options:

Option A: Beta-thalassemia is an autosomal codominant disorder, caused by mutations in alpha or beta globin that reduce hemoglobin synthesis. Peripheral smear shows microcytic, hypochromic cells with anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, target cells, and basophilic stippling. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows increased HbF and HbA2.

Option B: HbC disease is caused by mutation in the beta-globin chain in which glutamate is replaced by lysine in the sixth position of the beta-globin chain. Patients usually present with very mild anemia and microcytosis. Peripheral smear shows hexagonal HbC crystals. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows increased HbC levels.

Option D: Acute coronary syndrome is very rare in children and may be associated with Kawasaki disease. Children with Kawasaki disease present with fever, conjunctival ingestion, strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash, cervical lymphadenopathy, and hand and foot changes. They are treated with intravenous immunoglobulin and aspirin.
questions.learning: Sickle cell disease — The given scenario with electrophoresis showing increased HbA2, HbF, and S spike is suggestive of sickle cell disease. Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to the point mutation in the β-globin gene…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The Epstein-Barr virus interacts with B cells via which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CD21

The Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) binds to CD21 and acts as a B-cell mitogen.

It affects adolescents and younger adults more frequently but may occur from childhood to old age. It is transmitted primarily through close contact with oropharyngeal secretions. The incubation period of EBV infectious mononucleosis is 4-6 weeks.

Pathogenesis of Epstein Barr virus infection:

• The virus infects nasopharyngeal epithelial cells, salivary tissues, and lymphoid tissues.
• Lymphocytosis is caused by a proliferation of these EBV-infected B lymphocytes.
• There is a production of atypical reactive T cells which are CD8+ cytotoxic T cells, that are also called Downey cells.
• Heterophile antibodies are also produced due to B cell mitogenesis.

Clinically, patients may present with

• Fever, malaise, nausea, and anorexia.
• Lymphadenopathy- bilateral and symmetrical. Bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy is characteristic.
• Pharyngitis.
• Tonsillar enlargement.
• Hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Splenic rupture may occur even with minor trauma and is highly fatal.
• A drug-induced rash may develop on using beta-lactam antibiotics.
questions.learning: CD21 — The Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) binds to CD21 and acts as a B-cell mitogen. It affects adolescents and younger adults more frequently but may occur from childhood to old age.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: When is cord clamping ideally done?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Within 1-3 minutes

As per the AMTSL guidelines, cord clamping is practised within 1-3 minutes of the delivery of the fetus.

Delayed cord clamping is done 30 to 60 seconds after birth in all the babies. This increases the amount of blood flowing from mother to baby which decreases the risk of anaemia in later life, improves hemodynamic stability, decreases the risk of necrotizing enterocolitis,intraventricular hemorrhage in preterm infants, and also decreases the need for transfusions and inotropic support.

AMTSL guidelines recommended by WHO :

* Immediate administration of prophylactic uterotonics (Oxytocin). Oxytocin (10 IU) is given IM or IV.

* Controlled cord traction during placental delivery (in cesarean section and in vaginal birth where skilled birth attendants are present)

* Delayed cord clamping

* Postpartum abdominal uterine tonus assessment for early identification of uterine atony is recommended for all women. Continuous monitoring of uterine tone is done every 15 minutes for 2 hours. If uterine atony is detected, a fundal massage is performed.

Recent update: Uterine massage is not recommended routinely.

The goal of this is to prevent postpartum haemorrhage (PPH). Hence, uterotonics are the most important factor in decreasing PPH. Delayed cord clamping is a less important component in this direction and similarly, cord traction is not as critical. Uterine massage does not form the main component of AMTSL.
questions.learning: Within 1-3 minutes As per the AMTSL guidelines, cord clamping is practised within 1-3 minutes of the delivery of the fetus. Delayed cord clamping is done 30 to 60 seconds after birth in all the babies.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is correct regarding arginine vasopressin antagonist Tolvaptan?
options: It is useful in hypovolemic hyponatremia
It should be used for at least 1 year
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It is an oral drug

Tolvaptan is a selective vasopressin V₂ receptor antagonist that promotes free water excretion (aquaresis) without significant sodium loss. It is administered orally and is primarily used in the treatment of euvolemic and hypervolemic hyponatremia, particularly in patients with SIADH, heart failure, and cirrhosis.

Why not the other options?

• A. It is useful in hypovolemic hyponatremia: Incorrect. Tolvaptan is contraindicated in hypovolemic hyponatremia because it can worsen volume depletion.
• B. It antagonises the V₁ receptor: Incorrect. Tolvaptan selectively blocks V₂ receptors in the renal collecting ducts. (Conivaptan blocks both V₁a and V₂ receptors.)
• C. It should be used for at least 1 year: Incorrect. Therapy is generally short-term for hyponatremia due to the risk of hepatotoxicity. In SIADH, treatment duration depends on the underlying cause. In autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), it may be used long-term under close monitoring, but this is not a general recommendation.
questions.learning: It is an oral drug Tolvaptan is a selective vasopressin V₂ receptor antagonist that promotes free water excretion (aquaresis) without significant sodium loss.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-month-old infant presents with feeding difficulties, recurrent vomiting, poor growth, jaundice, and hepatomegaly. Examination also reveals oil drop cataracts, and laboratory tests show elevated galactose in blood and urine. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible for this infant’s condition?
questions.explanation: The combination of neonatal jaundice, hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, and the pathognomonic finding of oil drop cataracts is diagnostic for classic galactosemia. This autosomal recessive metabolic disorder is caused by a profound deficiency of the enzyme Galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT). Without GALT, the infant cannot metabolize galactose (derived from lactose in milk), leading to the toxic accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the liver, brain, and lens of the eye. G6PD deficiency (Option A) results in hemolytic anemia but not cataracts. ALDH (Option C) is involved in alcohol metabolism. PKU (Option D) results from phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency and leads to intellectual disability rather than acute liver failure and cataracts. Diagnosis is confirmed by elevated galactose levels in the blood and urine. The immediate treatment is the strict, lifelong removal of lactose and galactose from the diet to prevent irreversible liver damage and developmental delay
questions.learning: The combination of neonatal jaundice, hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, and the pathognomonic finding of oil drop cataracts is diagnostic for classic galactosemia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are criteria for opting Le Fort’s operation for surgical correction of pelvic organ prolapse? I. Procidentia in old age II. Unfit for long duration surgery III. Associated uterine pathology IV. Coital function no longer required Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I, II and IV

Le Fort’s operation (Le Fort’s partial colpocleisis) is an obliterative surgery performed for advanced pelvic organ prolapse (procidentia) in elderly women who no longer desire vaginal intercourse and are poor candidates for prolonged reconstructive surgery. The procedure closes most of the vaginal canal while leaving lateral channels for drainage of cervical and uterine secretions if the uterus is retained. The following are indications for Le Fort’s operation:

• I. Procidentia in old age: It is commonly performed in elderly women with complete uterovaginal prolapse (procidentia).
• II. Unfit for long-duration surgery: It is a short, relatively simple operation with minimal blood loss, making it suitable for women with significant medical comorbidities.
• IV. Coital function no longer required: Since the vagina is obliterated, future vaginal intercourse is not possible. Therefore, it is performed only in women who no longer desire sexual activity.

Why is III incorrect?

• III. Associated uterine pathology: Le Fort’s operation is contraindicated if there is suspected or confirmed uterine, cervical, or endometrial pathology, because the uterus becomes inaccessible for future evaluation. Such patients generally require hysterectomy or another appropriate procedure.
questions.learning: I, II and IV Le Fort’s operation (Le Fort’s partial colpocleisis) is an obliterative surgery performed for advanced pelvic organ prolapse (procidentia) in elderly women who no longer desire vaginal intercourse and are poor candidates for prolonged…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 36-year-old woman (P2L2) with severe endometriosis is found to have pelvic adhesions on laparoscopy. She has a history of prior tubal ligation and adhesiolysis. What is the most appropriate management option during the current laparoscopic procedure?
options: Total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo- oophorectomy
questions.explanation: Total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy For a 36-year-old patient with severe, recurrent endometriosis and pelvic adhesions who has already completed her family (P2L2, tubal ligation), the gold standard for definitive treatment is a total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TH-BSO). This procedure is chosen because it removes the diseased tissue and eliminates the main source of estrogen (the ovaries), which is the primary driver of endometrial tissue growth. Observation (Option A) is inappropriate for severe, symptomatic disease. Hysterectomy alone (Option B) leaves the ovaries intact, leading to a high rate of disease recurrence. Oophorectomy alone (Option C) leaves the uterus and potentially diseased tissue behind and induces premature menopause without fully addressing the uterine pathology. Therefore, TH-BSO provides the highest probability of permanent symptom relief in women without a desire for future fertility.
questions.learning: Total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy For a 36-year-old patient with severe, recurrent endometriosis and pelvic adhesions who has already completed her family (P2L2, tubal ligation), the gold standard for definitive treatment is a total…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: While assessing the quality of drinking water, which of the following parameters falls outside the acceptable limits for safe potable water?
questions.explanation: According to the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) guidelines for drinking water, the acceptable limit for Cadmium is 0.003 mg/L. The value provided in Option A (0.03 mg/L) is exactly ten times the safe limit, making it highly toxic and unsafe for consumption. Cadmium is a heavy metal that primarily damages the kidneys and bones. The other parameters provided are all within safe ranges: the limit for Fluoride is up to 1.0 mg/L, making 0.8 mg/L acceptable (Option B). Total Dissolved Solids (TDS) have an acceptable limit of 500 mg/L, so 300 mg/L is well within range (Option C). Nitrate levels should remain below 45 mg/L; therefore, 20 mg/L is considered safe (Option D). Maintaining these standards is crucial to prevent long-term health complications such as fluorosis or methemoglobinemia. Consequently, only the cadmium level in Option A exceeds the established safety threshold
questions.learning: According to the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) guidelines for drinking water, the acceptable limit for Cadmium is 0.003 mg/L. The value provided in Option A (0.03 mg/L) is exactly ten times the safe limit, making it highly toxic and unsafe for consumption.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 17-year-old tall male presents for a routine check-up. He has long limbs, arachnodactyly, hypermobile joints, a high-arched palate, and an increased arm span. Genetic testing reveals a defect in the FBN1 gene. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Marfan Syndrome

Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by a mutation in the FBN1 gene, which encodes fibrillin-1, an important structural component of elastic fibers in connective tissue. Defective fibrillin leads to weakness of connective tissues, particularly affecting the skeletal system, eyes, and cardiovascular system.

• Tall stature with long limbs (dolichostenomelia)
• Arachnodactyly (long, slender fingers)
• Increased arm span compared to height
• Hypermobile joints and high-arched palate
• Ocular abnormalities such as ectopia lentis
• Cardiovascular complications such as aortic root dilation and aortic aneurysm

Why other options are incorrect:

• Ehlers–Danlos syndrome: Caused by defects in collagen, presenting mainly with hyperextensible skin and joint hypermobility.
• Osteogenesis imperfecta: Due to type I collagen defect, characterized by brittle bones and blue sclera.
• Heritable disorders of connective tissue: This is a broad category, not a specific diagnosis.
questions.learning: Marfan Syndrome Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by a mutation in the FBN1 gene, which encodes fibrillin-1, an important structural component of elastic fibers in connective tissue.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which vitamin as a coenzyme required for Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase?
questions.explanation: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) is the first enzyme of the HMP shunt. It catalyzes an oxidation-reduction reaction that requires as an electron acceptor to produce NADPH. and are coenzymes derived from Niacin (Vitamin B3). Riboflavin (Vitamin B2, Option A) is the precursor for FAD and FMN coenzymes. Thiamine (Vitamin B1, Option B) is the precursor for thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), required for decarboxylation reactions. Biotin (Vitamin B7, Option D) is a cofactor for carboxylation enzymes like pyruvate carboxylase. The NADPH produced via G6PD is essential for reductive biosynthesis (like fatty acid synthesis) and for maintaining the antioxidant defense system in red blood cells. A deficiency in niacin can lead to pellagra, but its biochemical role as the backbone of is what enables critical redox reactions throughout the body. Linking vitamins to their specific metabolic co-factors and the enzymes they support is a core theme in medical biochemistry and clinical nutrition
questions.learning: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) is the first enzyme of the HMP shunt. It catalyzes an oxidation-reduction reaction that requires as an electron acceptor to produce NADPH. and are coenzymes derived from Niacin (Vitamin B3).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Diphtheria vaccine is a:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Toxoid

Diptheria vaccine is a toxoid.

Toxoids: Certain organisms like diphtheria and tetanus bacilli produce exotoxins. The toxins produced by these organisms are detoxicated and used in the preparation of vaccines. The antibodies produced to neutralize the toxic moiety produced during infection, rather than acting upon the organisms. In general, toxoid preparations are highly efficacious and safe immunizing agents.
questions.learning: Toxoid Diptheria vaccine is a toxoid. Toxoids: Certain organisms like diphtheria and tetanus bacilli produce exotoxins.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following would help in explaining the mechanism of action of ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. cGMP

Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) increases intracellular cGMP by activating the enzyme guanylyl cyclase.

ANP is secreted by the heart from atrial storage granules in response to an increase in intravascular volume. It decreases aldosterone secretion and decreases blood pressure.

Option A: cAMP is increased by activation of adenyl cyclase. Norepinephrine is a hormone that acts on intracellular adenylyl cyclase.

Option C: Gi of G-protein coupled receptors (GPCR) act via the IP3-DAG (phospholipase C) pathway.

Option D: Tyrosine kinase receptors act via the JAK/STAT pathway.

Pearl PF1611: Mechanisms of Action of Hormones

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman presents with gradually progressive difficulty in swallowing both solids and liquids for the past six months. She also complains of intermittent regurgitation of undigested food and a feeling of food getting stuck in the chest after meals. A barium swallow study has been performed and is shown below. Based on these features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Hypertensive lower (A) Achalasia cardia The barium swallow image displays the classic "bird's beak" sign—a dilated proximal esophagus with smooth, symmetric tapering at the lower esophageal sphincter (LES). This is diagnostic of "Achalasia Cardia," a motility disorder caused by the loss of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus, leading to a failure of the LES to relax and an absence of esophageal peristalsis. The clinical history of "progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids" is highly characteristic of achalasia, distinguishing it from mechanical obstructions like cancer which initially cause dysphagia only for solids. Diffuse esophageal spasm (Option B) shows a "corkscrew" appearance on barium swallow. Nutcracker esophagus (Option C) and hypertensive LES (Option D) typically require esophageal manometry for diagnosis and do not show this degree of proximal dilation and distal tapering. Treatment options for achalasia include pneumatic dilation, botulinum toxin injection, or surgical Heller myotomy.
questions.explanation: Ankylosing spondylitis. The combination of chronic inflammatory back pain (worse in the morning, improves with exercise) and a history of inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis) is highly suggestive of a seronegative spondyloarthropathy. The provided X-ray provides the definitive diagnosis, showing vertical syndesmophytes fusing the vertebral bodies, creating the classic "bamboo spine" appearance of Ankylosing Spondylitis (Option C). Pott’s spine (Option A) is spinal tuberculosis, which causes vertebral destruction and angulation (gibbus) rather than smooth fusion. Psoriatic arthritis (Option B) can cause sacroiliitis but usually presents with asymmetric large syndesmophytes. Rheumatoid arthritis (Option D) primarily affects the small joints of the hands and the cervical spine, not the lumbar spine in this manner. Therefore, the inspiratory efforts against a closed glottis, a high negative intrathoracic pressure is generated. This pressure draws fluid from the pulmonary capillaries into the alveoli, leading to rapid onset "desaturation and crepitations". ARDS (Option A) takes longer to develop and is associated with sepsis or major trauma. Pleural effusion (Option B) is a slower accumulation of fluid. Atelectasis (Option D) is common post-operatively but usually causes localized findings rather than diffuse acute pulmonary edema symptoms. NPPE is a medical emergency but usually resolves quickly with supplemental oxygen, CPAP, or brief mechanical ventilation once the airway obstruction is relieved. Clinicians must be vigilant for laryngospasm to prevent this sudden respiratory deterioration. What is the standard treatment for empyema thoracis? (A) Antibiotics alone (B) Chest tube drainage and antibiotics (C) Intercostal drain (ICD) alone (D) Wait and watch

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) reduce gastric acid secretion by acting on which specific target?
questions.explanation: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) such as omeprazole and pantoprazole suppress gastric acid secretion by irreversibly inhibiting the H⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump, also known as the gastric proton pump. This pump is located on the apical membrane of parietal cells and represents the final common pathway for hydrochloric acid secretion in the stomach. The H⁺/K⁺ ATPase exchanges intracellular hydrogen ions (H⁺) for extracellular potassium ions (K⁺). By blocking this exchange, PPIs effectively shut down acid production regardless of the stimulus (histamine, acetylcholine, or gastrin). Why the other options are incorrect: 1. H⁺/Cl⁻ ATPase: No such pump exists. 2. Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase: Maintains membrane potential in all cells; not involved in acid secretion. 3. Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ cotransporter: Found in the loop of Henle; target of loop diuretics. Thus, H⁺/K⁺ ATPase is the specific molecular target of PPIs
questions.learning: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) such as omeprazole and pantoprazole suppress gastric acid secretion by irreversibly inhibiting the H⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump, also known as the gastric proton pump.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following dimorphic fungi is most commonly responsible for subcutaneous mycosis?
questions.explanation: Dimorphic fungi are those that can exist as both molds (at room temperature) and yeasts (at body temperature). Among the options, Sporothrix schenckii is the classic cause of a subcutaneous mycosis known as "Rose Gardener's disease." The infection typically follows traumatic inoculation of the fungus from soil or vegetation (like rose thorns) into the skin. It presents with a primary nodule that ulcerates, followed by a series of secondary nodules tracking along the draining lymphatic vessels (sporotrichoid spread). Histoplasma capsulatum (Option A), Blastomyces dermatitidis (Option C), and Penicilliosis marneffei (Option D) are all dimorphic fungi, but they are primarily associated with systemic (deep) mycoses that start in the lungs rather than primary subcutaneous infection. Sporotrichosis is diagnosed by identifying "cigar-shaped" budding yeasts in tissue or culture. Treatment typically involve oral itraconazole or, historically, potassium iodide. Understanding these fungal niches is essential for diagnosing skin lesions based on the patient's occupational and environmental exposures

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A girl with a history of schizophrenia presents to a Primary Health Centre (PHC). Which of the following online government portals should the doctor use to book an appointment with a psychiatrist?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tele - MANAS

Tele-MANAS (Tele Mental Health Assistance and Networking Across States) is the flagship online platform that provides access to mental health services, enabling doctors and frontline health workers to connect patients directly to psychiatrists and trained mental health professionals for consultation.

Tele MANAS, a 24/7 mental health support helpline, launched its mobile app and video consultation services to enhance access to mental health support.

The Tele MANAS app is a user-friendly platform that offers a range of mental health resources. Users can access self-care tips, stress management techniques, and tools for recognizing early signs of distress. The app also features interactive activities, including mind challenges, games, and mindfulness practices. Additionally, Tele MANAS provides free, confidential counseling with trained mental health professionals from across India.

Video consultations enhance the already existing audio call services, enabling mental health professionals to conduct thorough assessments through direct observation. This feature facilitates history taking, clarification of concerns, and brief physical or Mental State Examinations (MSE) when needed. The service is initially available in Karnataka, Jammu & Kashmir, and Tamil Nadu, with plans for nationwide expansion.

Tele MANAS services include:

* Immediate tele-counselling by trained professionals.

* Referral support to psychiatrists for severe cases.

* Mental health awareness campaigns via digital platforms.

* Mobile-based mental health interventions ensure accessibility in rural and remote areas.

Other Options:

Option A: NIKSHAY is a digital platform for the management of tuberculosis cases.

Option C: U-WIN is a digital platform for recording all vaccination-related activities and tracking the administration of vaccines under Universal Immunization Programme (UIP).

Option D: Nikusth is the web-based solution for monitoring of Leprosy patients

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient comes to the casualty with organophosphate poisoning. He was started on atropine infusion and pralidoxime. After 2 hours, the patient had a sudden rise in temperature. What is the likely cause of fever?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Atropine toxicity

The most likely cause of fever in this patient is atropine toxicity.

The clinical scenario is suggestive of organophosphate consumption and atropine is used for its management. Atropine is a muscarinic receptor antagonist, and it competitively blocks the acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors.

Organophosphates are powerful acetylcholinesterase inhibitors. It is absorbed by inhalation or through the skin. Mucous membranes and the gastrointestinal tract are also the sites for absorption.

The predominant initial signs are of muscarinic excess which includes: (DUMBBELSS)

• Diarrhoea
• Urination
• Miosis
• Bronchospasm
• Bradycardia
• Emesis
• Lacrimation
• Salivation
• Sweating

Nicotinic manifestations include twitching of eyelids, tongue, and facial muscles which then leads to paralysis. CNS stimulation results in headache, tremors, ataxia, coma, and death.

Atropine in larger doses can lead to atropine toxicity. The features are depicted in the following image:

questions.text: Which of the following stains are used in the cervical smear below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Papanicolau stain

The cervical smear shown above is stained with Papanicolau stain. Pap stain is the most commonly used stain for cervical smears. It is a polychrome stain that stains different cell types different colors, making it easy to identify abnormal cells.

Type of cell
Identification feature

Basal & Para Basal
Cells are small, rounded, basophilic with large nuclei

Middle layer (Intermediate)
Cells are squamous cells, transparent and basophilic (Blue/Green) with vesicular nuclei

Superficial layer
Cells are acidophilic (Pink), with pyknotic nuclei

Malignant cells
Hyperchromatic, nuclei vary in size, small cytoplasm in undifferentiated malignant cells

The above image shows superficial cells (arrow mark) along with other basophilic cells.

Toluidine blue stain: Toluidine blue stain is a metachromatic stain that stains acidic and basic substances different colors. It is commonly used to stain mast cells and other cells that contain acidic and basic granules.

Hematoxylin and eosin stain (H&E stain): H&E stain is a polychrome stain that stains nuclei blue and cytoplasm pink. It is commonly used to stain tissue sections for histological examination.

Giemsa stain: Giemsa stain is a polychrome stain that stains nuclei blue and cytoplasm pink. It is commonly used to stain blood smears and bone marrow aspirates.

Stain
Uses

Papanicolaou stain (Pap stain)
Screening for cervical cancer and precancerous lesions, diagnosis of other gynecological conditions such as endometrial cancer and vulvar cancer, diagnosis of urinary tract infections and other conditions of the bladder and urethra

Toluidine blue stain
Diagnosis of mast cell disorders, detection of acidic and basic granules in cells, diagnosis of certain fungal infections

Hematoxylin and eosin stain (H&E stain)
Histological examination of tissue sections for a wide variety of diagnostic purposes

Giemsa stain
Staining blood smears and bone marrow aspirates for the diagnosis of blood disorders, diagnosis of parasitic infections, diagnosis of certain fungal infections

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old man with a history of chronic smoking came with complaints of ulcerative lesions on his lower lip for a year. On examination, there is a presence of a palpable ipsilateral submental node approximately 5*5 cm. Biopsy from the lesion was suggestive of squamous cell cancer. What is the next step in the management of this patient? MRND-Modified radical neck dissection
options: Resection of primary lesion with lip reconstruction and MRND
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Resection of primary lesion with lip reconstruction and MRND

The given patient has a squamous cell carcinoma of the lip with a primary lesion on the lower lip with ipsilateral lymph node metastasis to the submental node. This patient will need resection of the primary lesion with reconstruction and modified radical neck dissection (MRND).

Lip cancer most commonly occurs in men from 50 to 70 years old but can be seen in younger patients. Risk factors include sunlight exposure, smoking, and tobacco use. Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common type of lip cancer. But commonly occurring cancer in the upper lip is basal cell carcinoma.

Most lip cancers occur in the lower lip followed by the upper lip and commissure. The most common site is the vermilion border of the lower lip. Ulcerative lesion on the vermilion border of the lower lip is the most common clinical manifestation. Mass can extend and fix on the underlying bone. Loss of sensation over the chin indicates mental nerve involvement. The most frequently involved nodes are the submental and submandibular nodes.

Surgical resection (wide local excision with negative margins) is the preferred treatment modality. The typical lip length is 6 to 7 cm. For defects of <1/3rd of the lip, resection with primary closure is the preferred treatment.

For defects of more than 1/3rd of the lip, require local flaps for reconstruction after resection:

* Johansen step technique- local flap for large central defects

* Lip-switch (Abbe-Estlander) flap- based on the sublabial or superior labial artery. When the defect involves only the commissure, the Estlander flap is used, and the Abbé flap is used for midline defects. Abbe-Estlander Flap is used for mixed defects. The markings of the Abbe-Estlander flap are shown below.

* Karapandzic flap - circumoral advancement flap. It is a neuromuscular flap that includes the remaining orbicularis oris muscle with its innervation.

In the presence of neck metastasis, neck dissection is indicated. Postoperative radiation is administered to patients with positive margins, lymph node metastases, tumor thickness >4mm, or perineural invasion. If the mandible is involved, mandibulectomy and free flap reconstruction is required.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old female patient presents with a painless firm abdominal swelling of size 10 × 8 cm near the umbilicus. The swelling can be moved freely in a plane at right angle to the line of attachment of the mesentery. The most probable clinical diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mesenteric cyst

A mesenteric cyst classically presents as a painless, freely mobile intra-abdominal swelling. It exhibits Tillaux’s sign—the swelling is mobile at right angles to the line of attachment of the mesentery but has restricted mobility parallel to it.

Why not the other options?

• A. Dermoid cyst: Usually ovarian/sacrococcygeal; does not show Tillaux’s sign.
• B. Ovarian cyst: Arises from the pelvis and is not characteristically mobile perpendicular to the mesenteric attachment.
• D. Hydatid cyst: Commonly occurs in the liver and is relatively fixed.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In which intracellular structures are lysosomal enzymes normally found?
questions.explanation: Lysosomal enzymes (hydrolases) are synthesized by ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) and undergo initial glycosylation within the ER lumen. They are then transported to the Golgi apparatus, where they receive the mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag — the critical signal that directs them to lysosomes rather than being secreted extracellularly. This entire process follows the classical secretory pathway, meaning these enzymes are always kept within membrane-bound compartments from the moment of synthesis. Why other options are wrong: (A) Cytosol is incorrect because the cytosol lacks a membrane boundary. If lysosomal enzymes were released freely into the cytosol, they would cause catastrophic self-digestion of cellular proteins. They must always remain membrane-enclosed to protect the cell. (B) Mitochondria is incorrect because mitochondria have their own distinct enzyme sets dedicated to oxidative phosphorylation and the TCA cycle. They play absolutely no role in lysosomal enzyme synthesis or storage. (D) Nucleus is incorrect because the nucleus houses genetic material and transcription machinery. Lysosomal enzymes are never trafficked there, as they exclusively follow the ER → Golgi → Lysosome secretory pathway from the point of synthesis onward
questions.learning: Lysosomal enzymes (hydrolases) are synthesized by ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) and undergo initial glycosylation within the ER lumen.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The fourth heart sound is caused by:
options: Closure of aortic and pulmonary valves
Vibrations in the ventricular wall during systole
Closure of mitral and tricuspid valves
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ventricular filling

The fourth heart sound is caused by ventricular filling.

A fourth sound is heard immediately before the first sound when atrial pressure is high or the ventricle is stiff in conditions such as ventricular hypertrophy. It is due to ventricular filling and is rarely heard in normal adults.
questions.learning: Ventricular filling — The fourth heart sound is caused by ventricular filling. A fourth sound is heard immediately before the first sound when atrial pressure is high or the ventricle is stiff in conditions such as ventricular hypertrophy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text:
A 30-year-old patient presents with progressive difficulty in swallowing both solids and liquids for 8 months. A barium swallow was done and is shown in the image below. What other investigations should be done to confirm the diagnosis in this patient?

UGIE- Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy

PET- Positron emission tomography
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. UGIE + manometry

The given clinical scenario and the barium swallow showing bird beak sign are suggestive of achalasia cardia. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (UGIE) and manometry should be done to confirm the diagnosis.

Achalasia is a motility disorder and is less common. It typically presents as dysphagia for solids and liquids. Other features such as regurgitation and chest pain are also present.

On fluoroscopy, a grossly dilated esophagus with tapering end towards the gastroesophageal junction is seen. This is called the bird beak sign.

Barium is retained in the esophagus for more than 5 minutes and is a significant finding.

Diagnosis is confirmed with endoscopy and manometry.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman, gravida 4 para 2 with two miscarriages, presents with foul-smelling vaginal discharge and vaginal bleeding. She is diagnosed with stage IIIB carcinoma of the cervix as per FIGO staging. What is the recommended first-line treatment for this stage of cervical cancer?
options: Radical hysterectomy + pelvic lymph node dissection
questions.explanation: According to the FIGO staging and management guidelines for cervical cancer, the treatment approach depends heavily on the stage. Stage IIIB signifies advanced local disease where the tumor has extended to the pelvic wall and/or causes hydronephrosis or a non-functioning kidney. For advanced stages (Stage IIB through IVA), surgery is no longer the primary treatment modality because it cannot achieve clear margins. Instead, the gold standard is "concurrent chemoradiation" (Option A), which involves external beam radiation therapy combined with platinum-based chemotherapy (usually cisplatin) followed by brachytherapy. Radical hysterectomy (Options B, C, and D) is the treatment of choice for "early-stage" cervical cancer (Stage IA2 to IIA), where the disease is confined to the cervix or upper vagina. For a patient with Stage IIIB, surgery would be technically difficult and associated with high morbidity without offering a survival benefit over radiotherapy. Thus, chemoradiation is the definitive management aimed at local control and improved survival

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following provides attachment to the muscle responsible for extension at the hip and at the knee?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1

The muscle responsible for extension of the hip and indirectly aiding in extension of the knee is the gluteus maximus. This muscle is attached to the structure labeled 1 in the image.

The gluteus maximus originates from the posterior part of the dorsal ilium (behind the posterior gluteal line), the posterior superior iliac spine, and the posterior surfaces of the sacrum and coccyx, along with the sacrotuberous ligament.

It inserts mainly into the iliotibial tract (fascia lata) and partly into the gluteal tuberosity of the femur.

Its primary actions include extension and lateral rotation of the hip joint. By tightening the iliotibial band, it helps maintain the knee in an extended position, thus contributing indirectly to knee extension.

The gluteus medius arises from the external surface of the ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines and inserts on the lateral aspect of the greater trochanter. It functions in hip abduction and internal rotation.

The ischial tuberosity provides origin to the hamstring muscles—including semitendinosus, semimembranosus, long head of biceps femoris, and the hamstring portion of adductor magnus. These muscles assist in hip extension and produce flexion at the knee joint.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient complains of neck stiffness and severe headache. The CT image shown below is suggestive of which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Subarachnoid hemorrhage

The clinical manifestations of neck stiffness and severe headache with CT revealing blood in the basal cistern points out to the diagnosis of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is the bleeding into the subarachnoid space, which is the area between the arachnoid membrane and the pia mater surrounding the brain. The diagnosis is suspected when a hyperattenuating material is seen filling the subarachnoid space. Most commonly this is apparent around the circle of Willis, on account of the majority of berry aneurysms occurring in this region (65%), or in the Sylvian fissure (30%).

The modified Fisher scale is a method for grading SAH as seen on non-contrast CT (NCCT). The Hunt and Hess scale describes the severity of SAH and is used as a predictor of survival.

Xanthochromia on CSF is indicative of SAH in case of a negative CT scan.
questions.learning: Subarachnoid hemorrhage — The clinical manifestations of neck stiffness and severe headache with CT revealing blood in the basal cistern points out to the diagnosis of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child presents with recurrent infections. Laboratory investigations reveal low levels of both B and T lymphocytes. Genetic testing demonstrates a mutation in the adenosine deaminase (ADA) gene. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID)

A mutation in adenosine deaminase (ADA) leading to low B and T lymphocytes is characteristic of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID).

• ADA deficiency → accumulation of deoxyadenosine and dATP
• These metabolites are toxic to lymphocytes
• Inhibit DNA synthesis → failure of lymphocyte proliferation

Immunological consequence:

• ↓ T cells + ↓ B cells → combined immunodeficiency
• Leads to severe, recurrent infections early in life

Clinical features:

• Recurrent bacterial, viral, and fungal infections
• Failure to thrive
• Absent lymphoid tissue (e.g., tonsils)

Why other options are incorrect:

• X-linked agammaglobulinemia: Only B-cell deficiency
• CVID: Primarily B-cell dysfunction, later onset
• DiGeorge syndrome: T-cell deficiency due to thymic aplasia (not ADA defect)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure marked below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pons

The structure marked in the given image is pons.

Pons houses the motor nucleus of the facial nerve, and also the vestibulocochlear nuclei and abducens nuclei.

The pneumotaxic center is located in the upper pons.

Neural regulation of respiration:

It involves set of neurons located in pons and medulla:

* Pons: Pneumotaxic centre and apneustic centre (mnemonic PAP: Pons Pneumotaxic center Apneustic center)

* Medulla: Pre-Botzinger complex

* Dorsal respiratory group

* Ventral respiratory group

5th nerve nuclei: the motor nucleus is situated medially and sensory nucleus laterally in the pons. The spinal trigeminal nucleus is a caudal continuation of the main sensory nucleus, extending from the mid pons through the medulla to the cervical spinal cord.

The 6th nerve nucleus is found near the midline in the floor of the fourth ventricle just lateral to the medial longitudinal fasciculus in the pons.
