questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which malarial plasmodium vivax drug is used to prevent relapse in the post-partum period?
questions.explanation: Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale have a unique dormant liver stage known as hypnozoites. These can reactivate months later, causing clinical relapse. Primaquine is the only available drug capable of eradicating these liver stages (radical cure) to prevent relapse. While primaquine is strictly contraindicated during pregnancy due to the risk of fetal hemolysis (as fetal G6PD status is unknown), it is safe and indicated in the post-partum period once the infant's G6PD status is confirmed if breastfeeding. Artemether (Option A), Quinine (Option C), and Artesunate (Option D) are schizonticidal drugs used to treat the acute erythrocytic (blood) phase of malaria but have no effect on the hypnozoites. Therefore, they cannot prevent a relapse on their own. Primaquine remains the cornerstone for the elimination of P. vivax malaria, provided the patient is screened for G6PD deficiency before administration to prevent severe acute hemolytic anemia
questions.learning: Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale have a unique dormant liver stage known as hypnozoites. These can reactivate months later, causing clinical relapse.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the subsequent medications can lead to the development of gynecomastia?
questions.explanation: Gynecomastia is the benign enlargement of male breast tissue due to an imbalance between estrogen and androgen action. Spironolactone (Option C) is a potassium-sparing diuretic well-known for causing gynecomastia as a side effect . It works as a direct androgen receptor antagonist and also inhibits testosterone synthesis, effectively tilting the hormonal balance in favor of estrogen. Tamoxifen (Option A) is actually a Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM) used to treat painful gynecomastia in men. Oxytocin (Option B) is a reproductive hormone without significant effects on breast tissue growth in males. Clomiphene citrate (Option D) is an ovulation-inducing agent that can occasionally cause breast symptoms but is not a primary recognized cause of clinical gynecomastia compared to spironolactone. Therefore, due to its potent anti-androgenic activity, Spironolactone is the definitive answer. Patients on long-term therapy are often monitored for this bothersome but reversible side effect
questions.learning: Gynecomastia is the benign enlargement of male breast tissue due to an imbalance between estrogen and androgen action. Spironolactone (Option C) is a potassium-sparing diuretic well-known for causing gynecomastia as a side effect .

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During the assessment of an immunization program in a rural district, it was observed that vaccine potency loss was more common at the peripheral point of vaccine storage and use. At which level of the health system is the highest likelihood of cold chain failure expected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. At the village level

Cold chain failure is most likely to occur at the peripheral end of the immunization system.

Why the village level is highest risk:

• Vaccines are handled at subcentres / outreach sessions
• Longer exposure time outside cold chain during transport and sessions
• Intermittent electricity or no power supply
• Limited supervision and monitoring
• Greater dependence on ice packs and vaccine carriers

Hence, vaccine potency loss is most common at the village level.
questions.learning: At the village level Cold chain failure is most likely to occur at the peripheral end of the immunization system. Why the village level is highest risk: • Vaccines are handled at subcentres / outreach sessions • Longer exposure time outside cold chain…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
False statement regarding rabies immunoglobin is:

RIG- Rabies immunoglobulin
options: It is exclusively given in the deltoid
Not given after 7 days of the 1st dose of the vaccine
If human RIG is unavailable, equine is preferred
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is exclusively given in the deltoid

The false statement regarding rabies immunoglobulin is it is exclusively given in the deltoid. Rabies immunoglobulin is given as much as possible into the wound site or around it.

Rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) is passive immunization. It is administered only once, preferably within 24 hours of the exposure, ie, on day 0 of the anti-rabies vaccine (ARV). If RIG was not given with the ARV 1st dose, it can be given up to the 7th day after the first dose of ARV. It is not given after 7 days of receiving the 1st dose of ARV.

The dose is 20 IU/kg body weight for human rabies immunoglobulin (HRIG) and for equine rabies immunoglobulin (ERIG), the dose is 40 IU/kg body weight. When HRIG is not available, ERIG can be used. They are potent, safe, and less expensive.

The entire RIG dose or as much as anatomically possible should be infiltrated into the wound or as close as possible. If it is likely that there are additional small wounds, the remaining RIG should be given IM as close as possible to the site of wound or exposure.

All patients with category III exposures should be given RIG. This includes:

• single/multiple transdermal bites/scratches
• licks on broken skin
• contamination of mucous membranes with saliva
• contact with bats

In immunocompromised patients, RIG should be given to both category II and III exposures.
questions.learning: It is exclusively given in the deltoid — The false statement regarding rabies immunoglobulin is it is exclusively given in the deltoid. Rabies immunoglobulin is given as much as possible into the wound site or around it.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An elderly patient weighing about 70 kg is brought to the emergency department in a comatose state. Laboratory evaluation shows severe hyperglycemia (serum glucose 500 mg/ dL), arterial pH of 7.33, elevated plasma ketone levels, and normal serum potassium. While initiating treatment with intravenous saline, which additional substance should be included in the infusion for appropriate management?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with features of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): severe hyperglycemia (500 mg/dL), mild acidosis (pH 7.33), and elevated ketones. Initial management includes intravenous fluids (normal saline) followed by insulin therapy. However, an important principle in DKA management is potassium balance. Even though the serum potassium appears normal, total body potassium is actually depleted due to osmotic diuresis and insulin deficiency. Once insulin therapy is started, potassium shifts into cells, which can rapidly lead to dangerous hypokalemia, potentially causing arrhythmias. Therefore, potassium must be added to IV fluids early, provided serum potassium is not elevated. Why other options are wrong: (A) Insulin → necessary, but not added directly to saline infusion initially without addressing potassium (B) Bicarbonate → only in severe acidosis (pH < 6.9) (D) 14 units insulin IV → incorrect fixed dosing; insulin is given as infusion
questions.learning: The patient presents with features of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): severe hyperglycemia (500 mg/dL), mild acidosis (pH 7.33), and elevated ketones. Initial management includes intravenous fluids (normal saline) followed by insulin therapy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 33-year-old man is referred from the infertility clinic to the surgery OPD. On examination, the scrotum shows the appearance illustrated in the image, and palpation reveals a characteristic “bag of worms” sensation. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical description of a "bag of worms" sensation on palpation is pathognomonic for a Varicocele. A varicocele is an abnormal dilation and tortuosity of the veins within the pampiniform plexus of the spermatic cord. It is a very common cause of correctable male infertility, as the pooled blood increases scrotal temperature, impairing spermatogenesis. A hydrocele (Option A) presents as a smooth, cystic swelling that transilluminates. Testicular torsion (Option C) is a surgical emergency characterized by sudden, excruciating pain and a high-riding testis, not chronic dilated veins. Epididymo-orchitis (Option D) involves acute inflammation and pain, often with fever. Because the physical finding specifically matches the dilated venous plexus shown in the image and described by the "bag of worms" sign, varicocele is the definitive diagnosis. It most frequently occurs on the left side due to the vertical drainage of the left spermatic vein into the renal vein
questions.learning: The clinical description of a "bag of worms" sensation on palpation is pathognomonic for a Varicocele. A varicocele is an abnormal dilation and tortuosity of the veins within the pampiniform plexus of the spermatic cord.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 68-year-old male admitted to the ICU for acute exacerbation of COPD develops a sudden onset of palpitations. The following ECG changes are seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Multifocal atrial tachycardia

The given clinical scenario of a COPD patient in ICU developing palpitations and the ECG showing narrow QRS complex (<0.12 s) tachycardia with more than three different P wave morphologies, points to the diagnosis of multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT).

Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT) is characterized by at least 3 distinct P wave morphologies (shown by arrows in the image) with rates typically between 100 and 150 beats/min.

It is usually encountered in patients with chronic pulmonary disease and acute illness. The clinical features are most commonly related to the underlying precipitating illness (COPD in this case). Unlike atrial fibrillation, there are clear isoelectric intervals between P waves.

Treating the underlying disease and correcting any metabolic abnormalities is the mainstay of treatment. Electrical cardioversion has no effect.

The calcium-channel blockers verapamil or diltiazem may slow the atrial and ventricular rate. MAT may respond to amiodarone, but long-term therapy with this agent is usually avoided due to its toxicities, particularly in pulmonary fibrosis.
questions.learning: Multifocal atrial tachycardia — The given clinical scenario of a COPD patient in ICU developing palpitations and the ECG showing narrow QRS complex (<0.12 s) tachycardia with more than three different P wave morphologies, points to the diagnosis of…

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify pancreas, liver, and spleen?
questions.explanation: On a standard axial CT scan of the upper abdomen, the organs are identified by their characteristic positions: 1. A (Liver): The largest solid organ, occupying the right upper quadrant. 2. B (Pancreas): A lobulated, retroperitoneal organ that lies transversely across the midline, posterior to the stomach. 3. C (Spleen): A smaller, solid organ located in the left upper quadrant, lateral to the tail of the pancreas. Options B, C, and D provide incorrect assignments for these anatomical landmarks. Accurately identifying these organs is the first step in abdominal CT interpretation. The liver is typically on the left side of the image (the patient's right). The pancreas is often identified by its proximity to the splenic vein and the superior mesenteric artery. The spleen's location in the far left is a reliable marker. This anatomical spatial reasoning is a fundamental skill for medical board exams and clinical radiology practice
questions.learning: On a standard axial CT scan of the upper abdomen, the organs are identified by their characteristic positions: 1. A (Liver): The largest solid organ, occupying the right upper quadrant.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with complaints of chest pain for 1 hour and perspiration. He also appears anxious. ECG image is given below. What is the possible diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Posterior wall MI

The patient's presentation of chest pain for 1 hour, perspiration, and anxiety, combined with ECG findings showing ST depressions in leads V2 and V3, suggests a possible diagnosis of posterior wall MI. Posterior wall MI can present with ST depressions in the anterior leads (V1-V3) due to the reciprocal changes associated with ischemia in the posterior wall of the heart. These depressions indicate that the infarction is not directly visible in the standard ECG leads but is affecting the posterior part of the heart.

Posterior wall MI is typically caused by occlusion of the circumflex artery or the posterior descending artery, which supplies the posterior aspect of the heart. Management of posterior wall MI involves immediate medical intervention, including the administration of antiplatelet agents, anticoagulants, nitrates, beta-blockers, and, in many cases, reperfusion therapy through percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or thrombolysis to restore blood flow to the affected area of the heart.

Other options:

Option A and B: NSTEMI (Non-ST segment elevation myocardial infarction) could present with ST depression, but it typically affects a wider range of leads and is less likely to present with such a specific pattern of depression isolated to V2 and V3. Unstable angina, characterized by chest pain at rest or with minimal exertion, can cause ST depression, but it usually does not present with the level of severity and specific pattern seen in this case, particularly without elevation in cardiac biomarkers.

Option D: Acute myocarditis, while it can present with chest pain and ECG changes, usually shows diffuse changes, not isolated to specific leads like V2 and V3. It typically involves diffuse ST elevation or PR depression across multiple leads. Therefore, the combination of acute symptoms and specific ECG changes in leads V2 and V3 strongly suggests that a posterior wall MI is the most likely diagnosis for this patient.
questions.learning: Posterior wall MI — The patient's presentation of chest pain for 1 hour, perspiration, and anxiety, combined with ECG findings showing ST depressions in leads V2 and V3, suggests a possible diagnosis of posterior wall MI.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 22-year-old primigravida at 10weeks gestation comes to the ER with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Nausea and vomiting began one day back and now the patient is unable to tolerate fluids. She complains of pain in the right upper quadrant which started a few hours back. On examination, her temperature is 100.2 F, the pulse is 118 bpm and her BP is 110/70 mm of Hg. She has swelling of her lower limbs up to the ankles bilaterally. Abdominal examination shows a gravid uterus corresponding to 10 weeks of gestation and tenderness in the right upper quadrant, with mild guarding and is diagnosed as acute appendicitis. What is the next step of management? Complete blood count * Hemoglobin: 11g/dL * Leukocytes: 13,000 cells/μL * Platelets: 150,000 cells/μL Liver function tests * Aspartate transaminase (AST): 40U/L * Alanine transaminase (ALT): 48U/L Urinalysis * Protein: negative * Pus cells: 1-2/HPF * Bacteria: none USG Abdomen: Reveals a 7mm diameter, aperistaltic, non-compressible, dilated, blind-ending structure arising from the base of the caecum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Do appendicectomy

Based on the given clinical vignette, the next step of management is Laparoscopic appendicectomy at the earliest. Laparoscopic appendicectomy can be done before 28 weeks of gestation.

Acute appendicitis is the most common surgical non-gynecological cause of acute abdomen in pregnancy.

The diagnosis of acute appendicitis in pregnancy is difficult due to

* Nausea and vomiting may be considered normal, especially in the first trimester of pregnancy

* Leukocytosis is a physiological finding in pregnancy

* A gravid enlarging uterus can push the appendix upward and outward, causing the pain to localize in the right flank or right upper quadrant.

Acute appendicitis in pregnancy is associated with miscarriage, preterm delivery, increased risk of peritonitis, perinatal and maternal mortality.

USG abdomen is used to confirm. MRI abdomen can be done if USG is inconclusive.USG Abdomen would reveal a >6mm diameter, aperistaltic, non-compressible, dilated appendix seen as a blind-ending structure arising from the base of the caecum

Other options:

Option B,C,D are not appropriate because they do not treat the urgent cause of the pathology.
questions.learning: Do appendicectomy — Based on the given clinical vignette, the next step of management is Laparoscopic appendicectomy at the earliest. Laparoscopic appendicectomy can be done before 28 weeks of gestation.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Blood during autopsy is preserved in?
questions.explanation: During a forensic autopsy, blood samples collected for toxicological analysis must be preserved to prevent the degradation of certain substances or the post-mortem production of alcohol. Sodium fluoride (NaF) is the standard preservative used. As established in Question 54, it acts as an antiglycolytic and an enzyme inhibitor, specifically preventing bacteria and yeast from fermenting glucose into ethanol, which would lead to a falsely elevated blood alcohol level. Sodium chloride (Option B) is simple table salt and has no preservative value in toxicology. Formalin (Option C) is used to preserve tissues for histology but would invalidate chemical testing. Rectified spirit (Option D) is concentrated ethanol and is used to preserve viscera for certain poisons but would obviously invalidate any alcohol measurement. Using NaF-preserved tubes is a mandatory forensic step to ensure the scientific validity of the autopsy's toxicological findings in legal proceedings
questions.learning: During a forensic autopsy, blood samples collected for toxicological analysis must be preserved to prevent the degradation of certain substances or the post-mortem production of alcohol.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient in a gynecology clinic presents with a cystic lesion diagnosed as condition X, for which marsupialization is considered the treatment of choice. Where is this lesion located?
questions.explanation: The surgical procedure known as marsupialization is the "gold standard" and optimal treatment for a symptomatic Bartholin gland cyst or abscess (Condition X) . The Bartholin glands are located at the 4 o’clock and 8 o’clock positions in the posterior third of the labia majora. When the duct becomes blocked, a cyst forms; if this becomes infected, it develops into an abscess. Marsupialization involves making an incision into the cyst and suturing the edges of the cyst wall to the surrounding skin, effectively creating a permanent "pouch" that allows for continuous drainage and prevents recurrence. The perineal body (Option A), vagina (Option C), and cervix (Option D) are not the sites for this specific procedure. Therefore, because marsupialization is the definitive treatment for chronic Bartholin duct pathology, the Bartholin gland is the precise anatomical location of the lesion. This procedure preserves the function of the gland for lubrication
questions.learning: The surgical procedure known as marsupialization is the "gold standard" and optimal treatment for a symptomatic Bartholin gland cyst or abscess (Condition X) .

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 34-year-old man presents with abdominal pain, poor appetite, and chronic diarrhea over several weeks, with a history of a maize-based diet. Clinical examination reveals glossitis, a pigmented rash on sun-exposed areas, and a lesion around the neck. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation: The patient's clinical presentation—characterized by diarrhea, glossitis, and a pigmented rash in sun-exposed areas (photosensitivity)—is classic for pellagra. The lesion on his neck is likely Casal's necklace, a pathognomonic finding for this condition. Pellagra is caused by a deficiency of niacin (Vitamin B3) or its precursor amino acid, tryptophan. The history of a diet predominantly consisting of maize is a significant risk factor because maize is low in bioavailable niacin and tryptophan. Scurvy (Option B) results from Vitamin C deficiency and presents with bleeding gums and petechiae. Megaloblastic anemia (Option C) is caused by B12 or folate deficiency and presents with fatigue. Beriberi (Option D) is a thiamine (B1) deficiency affecting the cardiovascular or nervous systems. Given the "3 Ds" of pellagra (Dermatitis, Diarrhea, and eventually Dementia), this niacin deficiency is the only diagnosis that fits the described symptoms
questions.learning: The patient's clinical presentation—characterized by diarrhea, glossitis, and a pigmented rash in sun-exposed areas (photosensitivity)—is classic for pellagra.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which form of anesthesia is most appropriate for dental procedures carried out in a daycare (outpatient) setting?
questions.explanation: For minor dental surgery in a daycare setting, Infiltration Anesthesia (Option D) is the preferred method. This involves injecting a local anesthetic directly into the tissue at the surgical site to block the terminal nerve branches. It is safe, effective, and allows the patient to remain fully conscious and mobile, facilitating immediate discharge. General anesthesia (Option A) is reserved for very complex surgeries, uncooperative children, or severe dental anxiety, but it carries higher risks and requires a longer recovery period. Spinal (Option B) and Epidural (Option C) anesthesia are used for procedures involving the lower half of the body (e.g., legs or lower abdomen) and have no anatomical application for dental work in the mouth. Infiltration anesthesia, often supplemented by a nerve block (like the inferior alveolar nerve block), remains the mainstay of pain control in clinical dentistry due to its localized effect and safety profile
questions.learning: For minor dental surgery in a daycare setting, Infiltration Anesthesia (Option D) is the preferred method. This involves injecting a local anesthetic directly into the tissue at the surgical site to block the terminal nerve branches.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A pregnant woman comes for an antenatal check-up. She has a history of stillbirth at 28 weeks in her previous pregnancy. She also has a history of multiple sexual partners and vaguely remembers having a painless ulcer on her vulva prior to her last pregnancy. What would be the first step of investigation for this lady?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. VDRL

Venereal disease research laboratory test (VDRL test) is the first investigation in this patient with a history of stillbirth and painless genital ulcer, which is likely suggestive of syphilis.

Syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum, a spirochete that is actively motile. It exhibits characteristic corkscrew-like motility.

Primary syphilis occurs subsequent to inoculation of treponema pallidum following sexual contact. It manifests as a painless, non-tender, single papule over the genitalia, that rapidly becomes eroded and usually becomes indurated, and is called a hard chancre. It can be accompanied by lymphadenopathy. The chancre generally heals within 10-40 days even without treatment, leaving a scar.

The obstetric history in an untreated syphilitic woman typically gets better with subsequent pregnancies. Initial few pregnancies can result in abortions and stillbirths, subsequent pregnancies can result in live births of infants with stigmata of syphilis. Finally, after a few pregnancies, healthy infants are born.

It can be diagnosed using VDRL, and RPR tests. It can be confirmed by FTA – ABS testing or TPHA, TPI testing.

Dark ground microscopy is the most specific and sensitive technique to diagnose syphilis when an active chancre or condyloma lata is present. Since the ulcer is not active in this patient, it is not useful in this scenario.

Smear specimens can be stained using Fontana stain and pathological tissues are stained using Levaditi stain. Silver impregnation technique can also be used.
questions.learning: VDRL Venereal disease research laboratory test (VDRL test) is the first investigation in this patient with a history of stillbirth and painless genital ulcer, which is likely suggestive of syphilis.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 56-year-old female presents with generalized body pain and proximal muscle weakness. Laboratory investigations reveal: • Calcium – Normal • Phosphate – Low • ALP – High • PTH – High What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Hyperparathyroidism secondary to vitamin D deficiency
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Osteomalacia

Osteomalacia is a disorder of defective mineralization of osteoid in adults, most commonly caused by vitamin D deficiency. It presents with diffuse bone pain, proximal muscle weakness, and fragility fractures. The characteristic biochemical profile is normal or low calcium, low phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and secondary hyperparathyroidism (elevated PTH).

Why not the other options?

• A. Paget disease of bone: Characterized by markedly elevated ALP with normal calcium and phosphate; proximal muscle weakness and hypophosphatemia are not typical.
• B. Primary hyperparathyroidism: Usually presents with hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and elevated PTH.
• C. Hyperparathyroidism secondary to vitamin D deficiency: Although secondary hyperparathyroidism is present, the overall clinical diagnosis is osteomalacia, which is the disease caused by vitamin D deficiency.

| Condition | Calcium | Phosphate | ALP | PTH

| --------- | ------- | --------- | --- | ---

| Osteomalacia | Normal/↓ | ↓ | ↑ | ↑ (secondary)

| Primary Hyperparathyroidism | ↑ | ↓ | Mild ↑ | ↑

| Paget Disease | Normal | Normal | ↑↑ | Normal
questions.learning: Osteomalacia Osteomalacia is a disorder of defective mineralization of osteoid in adults, most commonly caused by vitamin D deficiency. It presents with diffuse bone pain, proximal muscle weakness, and fragility fractures.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a town of 20,000 populations, total 456 births were there in a year out of which 56 were dead born. The total death were 247 out of which 56 deaths were within 28 days of life and another 34 had dies after 28 days and before completing the first birthday. Calculate the infant mortality rate of the area?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 225

The infant mortality rate is 225 per 1000 live births.

Infant mortality rate (IMR) is defined as the ratio of infant deaths registered in a given year to the total number of live births in the same year. IMR is usually expressed as a rate per 1000 live births. Infants include those under the age of 1 year.

Calculation:

• IMR = (Number of deaths of children under 1 year of age in a year x 1000)/(Number of live births in the same year).
• In the given question, Out of total 456 births, 56 were dead born. Therefore, the number of live births= 456-56 = 400.
• In the same year, it is given that the number of deaths before 28 days is 56, and the number of deaths after 28 days but before 1 year. Therefore, the total number of deaths of children under the age of 1 year is 56 + 34 = 90
• IMR = (90x1000)/400 = 900/4 = 225
• Hence, the IMR is 225 per 1000 live births.
questions.learning: 225 The infant mortality rate is 225 per 1000 live births. Infant mortality rate (IMR) is defined as the ratio of infant deaths registered in a given year to the total number of live births in the same year.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: “Objectives are set forth for different units and subunits, each of which prepares its own plan of action, usually on a short-term basis.” The definition best sums up which one among the following terms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Management by objectives

Management by Objectives (MBO) is a participative management approach developed by Peter F. Drucker in which organizational goals are translated into specific objectives for departments, units, and individual employees. Each unit develops its own action plan to achieve these predefined objectives, usually over a short-term period, with periodic review of performance.

Why not the other options?

• A. Input-Output analysis: An economic and planning tool used to study relationships between inputs and outputs in production systems.
• B. Personnel management: Deals with recruitment, training, appraisal, and welfare of employees; it is not based on objective-setting.
• D. Work sampling: A work measurement technique used to estimate how workers spend their time through random observations.
questions.learning: Management by objectives Management by Objectives (MBO) is a participative management approach developed by Peter F. Drucker in which organizational goals are translated into specific objectives for departments, units, and individual employees.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the given structure:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pancreatic islet cells

The above image shows pancreatic islet cells. Islet of Langerhans makes up the endocrine part of the pancreas.

Islets are characterized by secretory cells supported by reticulin fibers, and containing numerous fenestrated capillaries. There is a delicate capsule around each islet. They are paler than the surrounding exocrine cells, as they have less rough endoplasmic reticulum.

The image given below shows the histology of the pancreas.

The islets of Langerhans contain four major and two minor cell types:

• Four main types are β, α, δ, and PP (pancreatic polypeptide) cells:

• α or A cells- located peripherally and secrete glucagon
• β or B cells- located centrally and produce insulin
• δ or D cells- scattered between beta cells and secrete somatostatin
• PP cells- are present in islets and also in the exocrine pancreas. They secrete a pancreatic polypeptide, which exerts several gastrointestinal effects, such as stimulation of secretion of gastric and intestinal enzymes and inhibition of intestinal motility.

• Minor cell types:

• D1 cells secrete vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), a hormone that induces glycogenolysis and hyperglycemia. It also stimulates gastrointestinal fluid secretion and causes secretory diarrhea.
• Enterochromaffin cells synthesize serotonin and are the source of pancreatic tumors that cause carcinoid syndrome.

Other options:

Option A: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs. The structure of lymph nodes consists of an outer cortex and inner medulla. The cortex contains an aggregation of B-lymphocytes (primary follicles) and quiescent secondary follicles with a pale central germinal center.

The inner medulla consists of medullary cords (lymphocytes and plasma cells) and medullary sinuses. Between the cortex and medulla, there is an ill-defined zone called the paracortex, which contains T lymphocytes.

The image given below shows the histology of the lymph node.

Option B: Glomerulus is a rounded tuft of anastomosing capillaries. The glomerular capillary wall is the filtering membrane and consists of fenestrated endothelial cells, basement membrane, and visceral epithelial cells called podocytes, which contain foot processes.

The glomerular tuft is supported by the mesangium containing mesangial cells and a non-cellular mesangial matrix.

The image given below shows the histology of the glomerulus.

Option C: Spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ. It contains round white pulp surrounded by red pulp. The white pulp is made up of aggregations of lymphocytes that surround a small artery or arterioles. Lymphocytes surrounding the arteriole are called peri-arterial lymphatic sheath (PALS) and contain T cells. Follicles in white pulp contain B cells.

The red pulp is a modified lymphoid tissue infiltrated with all the cells of circulating blood. It is like a sponge permeated by spaces (splenic sinusoids) lined by reticular cells. The zone of red pulp immediately surrounding white pulp is the marginal zone. This zone has a rich network of sinusoids.

The image given below shows the histology of the spleen.
questions.learning: Pancreatic islet cells — The above image shows pancreatic islet cells. Islet of Langerhans makes up the endocrine part of the pancreas.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The amount of iron lost per 28-day cycle in menstruating women is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 12.5 mg

Menstruating women lose approximately 12.5 mg of iron during each normal 28-day menstrual cycle, corresponding to an average menstrual blood loss of 30–40 mL. This increased iron loss explains the higher daily iron requirement in women of reproductive age compared to men.

• A. 5.5 mg ✗: Lower than the average iron loss during a normal menstrual cycle.
• B. 8.5 mg ✗: Incorrect; underestimates menstrual iron loss.
• C. 12.5 mg ✓: Average iron loss in a 28-day menstrual cycle.
• D. 15.5 mg ✗: Higher than the average; may occur in women with menorrhagia but is not the normal value.
questions.learning: 12.5 mg Menstruating women lose approximately 12.5 mg of iron during each normal 28-day menstrual cycle, corresponding to an average menstrual blood loss of 30–40 mL.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 62-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of syncope. His ECG shows regular P waves occurring independently, with normal- duration QRS complexes at a ventricular rate of 35 beats per minute. Based on these findings, what is the most likely clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient is presenting with recurrent fainting (syncope) and an ECG showing a complete mismatch between the atrial rate (75 bpm) and the ventricular rate (35 bpm). This defines complete (3rd-degree) heart block. When sudden syncope occurs due to the abrupt onset of complete heart block or an asystolic pause, it is clinically termed Stokes-Adams syndrome. 2nd-degree block (Option A) would show some P waves followed by QRS complexes and some dropped. Atrial tachycardia (Option B) involves a very high atrial rate (typically bpm). First-degree block (Option C) only involves a prolonged PR interval with a 1:1 P-to-QRS ratio. Complete heart block leads to dangerously low cardiac output, requiring an emergency temporary pacemaker followed by a permanent one. The term Stokes-Adams specifically links the physiological arrhythmia to the symptomatic neurological outcome of fainting. This is a life-threatening cardiac emergency common in the elderly with degenerative conduction system disease
questions.learning: The patient is presenting with recurrent fainting (syncope) and an ECG showing a complete mismatch between the atrial rate (75 bpm) and the ventricular rate (35 bpm).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Sour taste is mediated by which of the following receptors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. TRPV1 channel

Sour taste is mediated by the TRPV1 channel. The TRPV1 (Transient Receptor Potential Vanilloid 1) channel is involved in detecting the acidity of foods, which contributes to the perception of sour taste.

It is a cation channel that allows the influx of various cations, including sodium (Na⁺), calcium (Ca²⁺), and magnesium (Mg²⁺), in response to changes in temperature and the presence of acidic conditions or capsaicin

Taste Receptors

• Humans have five established basic tastes: sweet, salt, sour, bitter and umami.
• The taste receptors for these five basic tastes are of two major types:

• Ligand-gated channels (ionotropic receptors): for salt and sour taste
• G-Protein Coupled Receptors (metabotropic receptors): for sweet, bitter and umami

• Salt and sour taste are mediated through epithelial sodium channels (ENaC)

• Na+ movement through ENaC → salt taste
• H+ movement through ENaC → sour taste

• Sweet, bitter, and umami are sensed via GPCRs

• T1R2 and T1R3 families→ sweet taste
• T2R family → bitter taste
• T1R1, T1R3, and Metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR4) → Umami (Option A and C)
questions.learning: TRPV1 channel Sour taste is mediated by the TRPV1 channel. The TRPV1 (Transient Receptor Potential Vanilloid 1) channel is involved in detecting the acidity of foods, which contributes to the perception of sour taste.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A woman underwent surgery, but the surgeon discovered a cyst and removed her ovaries. She is of reproductive age with an incomplete family. What consent was violated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Informed consent

This kind of consent is informed consent since the patient has been made aware of the benefits and complications and has agreed to the procedure.

Informed consent is one given by the patient after understanding the nature of the condition, proposed treatment, outcomes of the recommended treatment, alternative options to treatment, and the risks and benefits involved. The patient can accept or reject the procedure. This is also called the rule of full disclosure.

"Consent" refers to a voluntary agreement, compliance, or permission. It can be expressed or implied. Expressed consent can be oral or written and refers to consent in which the terms are clearly stated in distinct and explicit language.

"Opt out" refers to a patient's refusal of the procedure, test, or treatment. It is the physician's duty to disclose the risks or consequences of refusal adequately and appropriately to the patient.

Option B: Implied consent is that which is not written or expressly stated. It is implied that the patient is giving consent to examination in a general sense. For example, when a patient visits the hospital with an illness, it implies that he has given consent to a physical examination to find out the nature of his illness. Another example of implied consent is when a patient exposes his arm for injection. It is legally effective.

Option C: The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur (the thing or the act speaks for itself) is a situation whereby an obvious gross act of negligence leads to damage to the patient. For example, prescribing high doses of NSAIDs to a patient with a history of perforated peptic ulcer. The negligent act is so obvious that the patient need not prove the negligence.

Option D: According to BNS Section 30 (IPC 92), a doctor is permitted to perform life-saving procedures on a patient with life-threatening injuries. For example, in a case where conservative measures have failed to control intractable postpartum haemorrhage, an emergency hysterectomy can be performed without obtaining consent in order to save the patient's life. The guiding principle is whether the delay in treatment in order to obtain consent would result in harm to the patient. This is the doctrine of anticipation. Under some circumstances, like emergencies, informed consent may be neither possible nor necessary.
questions.learning: Informed consent — This kind of consent is informed consent since the patient has been made aware of the benefits and complications and has agreed to the procedure.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-year-old child presents for a routine well- child visit. Examination reveals a systolic murmur and a widely split second heart sound that is fixed and does not vary with respiration. There is no family history of heart disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The physical finding of a widely split second heart sound (S2) that does not vary with respiration (fixed split S2) is pathognomonic for an Atrial Septal Defect (ASD) (Option C) . This occurs because the left-to-right shunt causes a constant volume overload of the right ventricle, delaying the closure of the pulmonic valve regardless of the phase of breathing. The associated systolic murmur is usually due to increased flow across the pulmonic valve. Ventricular septal defect (Option B) typically presents with a loud pansystolic murmur and a variable S2. Pulmonic stenosis (Option D) features a mid-systolic click and a widely split S2, but the split usually does vary with respiration. TAPVC (Option A) is a more severe cyanotic lesion that would present earlier with significant distress. Because the "fixed split S2" is the quintessential physical hallmark of an ASD, it is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The physical finding of a widely split second heart sound (S2) that does not vary with respiration (fixed split S2) is pathognomonic for an Atrial Septal Defect (ASD) (Option C) .

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: An image of a mascot is shown below. Identify the national health programme associated with this mascot.
questions.explanation: The mascot "Sapna" is the official symbol of the National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP) in India. She is central to the "Sparsh" Leprosy Awareness Campaign, which aims to reduce social stigma and encourage the early detection of leprosy at the community level. Regarding the distractors, the National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (Option B) uses symbols like the "TB Champion" or the Nikshay logo. The Malaria (Option C) and Polio (Option D) programs have their own distinct campaign materials, such as the "Do Boond" icons for polio. Sapna was specifically designed to educate children and villagers about the signs of leprosy, such as skin patches and loss of sensation. Therefore, identifying this mascot is crucial for community medicine practitioners in India

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In an HIV-positive patient with chronic persistent diarrhea, microscopic examination of the stool reveals characteristic findings. Based on these observations, which organism is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: Cryptosporidium parvum is the most common cause of persistent, life-threatening watery diarrhea in patients with HIV/AIDS, especially when CD4 counts fall below 200 cells/mm3. Under a microscope, after modified acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelsen) staining, they appear as small (4-6 m), red-colored, spherical oocysts. Cyclospora (Option B) is larger (8-10 m) and also acid-fast, but it is less common in HIV patients. Microspora (Option C) are much smaller (1-3 m) and require specialized staining like trichrome to be seen. Cystoisospora (Option D), formerly Isospora, are large (20-30 m) and oval-shaped oocysts that are also acid-fast. Cryptosporidiosis is notoriously difficult to treat in immunocompromised hosts; while Nitazoxanide is the drug of choice, clinical improvement depends primarily on restoring the patient's immune function through Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy (HAART). Accurate identification of the specific oocyst size and shape is essential for appropriate diagnosis in chronic diarrhea workups
questions.learning: Cryptosporidium parvum is the most common cause of persistent, life-threatening watery diarrhea in patients with HIV/AIDS, especially when CD4 counts fall below 200 cells/mm3.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most common cause of consumptive coagulopathy in obstetrics?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Placental abruption

Placental abruption is the most common cause of severe consumptive coagulopathy in obstetrics.

Consumptive coagulopathy, also known as disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), is a pathologic disruption of hemostasis. It is characterized by systemic activation of blood coagulation, which results in thrombosis and fibrin deposition in the small blood vessels throughout the body.

Other causes of DIC in pregnancy:

* Amniotic fluid embolism

* Sepsis

* Preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome

* Acute fatty liver of pregnancy

* Postpartum haemorrhage.
questions.learning: Placental abruption Placental abruption is the most common cause of severe consumptive coagulopathy in obstetrics. Consumptive coagulopathy, also known as disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), is a pathologic disruption of hemostasis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A man sustains a perineal injury after falling into a manhole and subsequently develops difficulty in passing urine with blood seen at the urethral meatus. He is diagnosed with a bulbar urethral injury. In this condition, at which anatomical site would urine extravasation be least likely to occur?
questions.explanation: A fall-astride injury commonly causes a rupture of the bulbar urethra. When the urethra ruptures below the urogenital diaphragm, extravasated urine and blood are contained by Colles’ fascia. Colles’ fascia is continuous with Scrotal (Dartos) fascia and Scarpa’s fascia of the "anterior abdominal wall" (Option B), but it is firmly attached to the fascia lata of the thigh. Therefore, while urine can freely track into the "perineum" (Option A), "root of the scrotum" (Option D), and up the abdominal wall, it cannot track into the "medial portion of the thigh" (Option C). This creates a characteristic "butterfly" or "scrotal" swelling pattern. Diagnosis is confirmed via Retrograde Urethrography (RGU). Management usually involves the placement of a suprapubic catheter to divert urine, followed by delayed surgical repair of the urethra to avoid aggravating the injury or causing infection
questions.learning: A fall-astride injury commonly causes a rupture of the bulbar urethra. When the urethra ruptures below the urogenital diaphragm, extravasated urine and blood are contained by Colles’ fascia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the grip shown in the image below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lateral grip

The Leopold manoeuvre shown in the image is the lateral grip. It assesses fetal orientation.

Leopold's manoeuvres help assess the fetal pole, lie, presenting part, engagement, and attitude of the fetal head. They are as follows:

1. Fundal grip (first Leopold):

• Assesses the uterine fundus.
• Helps in identification of fetal lie and determination of fetal pole at the fundus.
• The breech is felt as a large, irregular mass.
• The head feels hard and round and is more mobile.

2. Lateral grip (second Leopold):

• Assesses the fetal orientation.
• The palms are placed on either side of the maternal abdomen, and gentle but deep pressure is exerted.
• The back is felt on one side as a hard, resistant structure.
• The fetal extremities are felt on the other side as numerous small, irregular, mobile parts are felt.
• Fetal orientation can be determined by noting whether the back is directed anteriorly, transversely, or posteriorly.
• The position of the anterior shoulder is mainly assessed by this grip.

3. Pawlik's grip / 1st pelvic grip (third Leopold):

• Assesses the presenting part.
• The thumb and fingers of one hand grasp the lower portion of the maternal abdomen just above the symphysis pubis.
• If the presenting part is not engaged, a movable mass will be felt, usually the head.

4. Deep pelvic grip / 2nd pelvic grip (fourth Leopold):

• Assesses the engagement and attitude of the fetal head.
• The examiner faces the mother's feet, and the fingertips of both hands are positioned on either side of the presenting part.
• They exert inward pressure and then slide along the axis of the pelvic inlet.

Leopold
Grip
Importance

First
Fundal
To know which fetal pole occupies the uterine fundus.

Second
Lateral/Umbilical
To know the fetal back and extremities

Third
Pawlik

To know the presenting fetal part in respect to the true pelvis

Fourth
Pelvic

To determine the degree of descent.

If the head has already descended into the pelvis, the anterior shoulder or the space created by neck may be differentiated readily from the head
questions.learning: Lateral grip — The Leopold manoeuvre shown in the image is the lateral grip. Leopold's manoeuvres help assess the fetal pole, lie, presenting part, engagement, and attitude of the fetal head.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The Lineweaver–Burk plot shown represents an enzyme inhibition mechanism. Which enzyme in the cholesterol synthesis pathway is inhibited by statins through this mechanism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. HMG-CoA reductase

• The Lineweaver–Burk plot shows competitive inhibition.
• In competitive inhibition, Km increases while Vmax remains unchanged.
• The inhibitor competes with the substrate for the active site.
• Increasing substrate concentration can overcome the inhibition.
• Statins are structural analogs of HMG-CoA and competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase.
• HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis.
• Inhibition decreases hepatic cholesterol synthesis.
• This increases LDL receptor expression on hepatocytes.
• More circulating LDL is removed from plasma.
• Statins are first-line drugs for hypercholesterolemia and prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glycogen storage

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is used to estimate relative risk (RR)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cohort study

Relative risk is best estimated in cohort studies.

Relative Risk:

* The ratio of incidence of disease or death among exposed to that among the non-exposed is called relative risk (RR).

* It is also called the risk ratio.

* It is the direct measure of the strength of association between suspected cause and effect in cohort studies.

* RR = 1 indicates no association.

* RR >1 indicates a positive association.

* RR of 2 or higher indicates a >/=100% increase in risk.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following accurately represents Bormann's classification for gastric carcinoma?
options: Type I: Polypoid tumor with a small ulcerated component
Type II: Ulcerated tumor with raised margins
Type III: Diffusely infiltrative tumor with linitis plastica appearance
Type IV: Mucinous carcinoma with extensive peritoneal metastases
questions.explanation: Bormann’s classification describes the gross morphological types of advanced gastric carcinoma. 1. Type I is a polypoid or fungating mass projecting into the lumen and is not typically defined by ulceration, so option (A) is inaccurate. 2. Type II is characterized by an ulcerated lesion with well-defined, raised margins, which matches option (B) correctly. 3. Type III refers to an ulceroinfiltrative tumor with poorly defined margins that infiltrates deeply into the gastric wall, not a diffusely infiltrative pattern, so option (C) is incorrect. 4. Type IV represents a diffuse infiltrative carcinoma, leading to linitis plastica (leather bottle stomach) due to widespread thickening of the stomach wall. It is not specifically defined as mucinous carcinoma with peritoneal metastasis, making option (D) incorrect. Thus, only option (B) correctly matches the Bormann classification
questions.learning: Bormann’s classification describes the gross morphological types of advanced gastric carcinoma. Type I is a polypoid or fungating mass projecting into the lumen and is not typically defined by ulceration, so option (A) is inaccurate.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Receptor used for the entry of HIV virus into the host cell is?
questions.explanation: To enter a host cell, the HIV virus must first bind its gp120 protein to the CD4 receptor on helper T cells, macrophages, or monocytes. However, successful fusion and entry require a second receptor known as a co-receptor. The primary co-receptors are CCR5 (found on macrophage lineage cells) and CXCR4 (found on T lymphocytes). CCR7 (Option A) is involved in lymph node trafficking, not HIV entry. CD6 (Option C) and CD8 (Option D) are other immune cell surface markers that do not serve as receptors for HIV. The importance of CCR5 is highlighted by the "CCR5 Delta 32" mutation; individuals who are homozygous for this mutation are resistant to HIV infection because the virus cannot gain entry to their cells
questions.learning: To enter a host cell, the HIV virus must first bind its gp120 protein to the CD4 receptor on helper T cells, macrophages, or monocytes. However, successful fusion and entry require a second receptor known as a co-receptor.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman was diagnosed with a large tumor in the right ovary and histopathology shows it has origin from all three germ layers. Which of the following is the most likely tumor she is having?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Teratoma

A cyst with all three germ layers is most likely to be a teratoma, also called a dermoid cyst(mature cystic).

Teratomas arise from pluripotent stem cells that differentiate into any of three germ layers forming tissues of all three germ layers.

A dermoid cyst is the most common germ cell tumor. It is also the most common benign tumor of the ovary in the reproductive age group and in pregnancy. It is bilateral in 10-15% of cases.

A dermoid cyst is derived from all three germ cell layers, but ectodermal derivatives are most common. Rokitansky’s protuberance is the most common site for the development of malignancy. It is seen as a projection covered by skin, sebaceous glands, sweat glands, teeth, and bones. Sometimes thyroid tissue can be seen on histopathological examination, known as struma ovarii.

The image below shows a dermoid cyst with Rokitansky protuberance.
questions.learning: Teratoma — A cyst with all three germ layers is most likely to be a teratoma, also called a dermoid cyst(mature cystic). Teratomas arise from pluripotent stem cells that differentiate into any of three germ layers forming tissues of all three germ layers.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Flask shaped ulcers in the colon are caused by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Entamoeba Histolytica

Flask shaped ulcers are classically seen in amoebiasis caused by Entamoeba histolytica.

In amoebiasis, amoeba attach themselves to the colonic epithelium, induces apoptosis, invade crypts, and burrow laterally into the lamina propria. This recruits neutrophils and causes tissue damage, resulting in flask-shaped ulcers with a narrow neck and broad base.

Clinical manifestations:

• Amebic Colitis

• Colicky abdominal pains and frequent bowel movements.
• Diarrhea associated with tenesmus and heme-positive stool.
• Trophozoites invade the intestinal mucosa, produce flask-shaped ulcers.

• Amebic Liver Abscess

• Fever is the hallmark of amebic liver abscess
• It is associated with abdominal pain, abdominal distention, and enlargement and tenderness of the liver.
• Changes at the base of the right lung, such as elevation of the diaphragm and atelectasis or effusion, may also occur.
• The most common finding is a single abscess in the right hepatic lobe, detected on ultrasonography,computed tomography, or magnetic resonance imaging.
questions.learning: Entamoeba Histolytica Flask shaped ulcers are classically seen in amoebiasis caused by Entamoeba histolytica. In amoebiasis, amoeba attach themselves to the colonic epithelium, induces apoptosis, invade crypts, and burrow laterally into the lamina propria.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 39-year-old man sustains significant chest trauma from a road traffic accident. After chest tube insertion, there is an acute blood loss of approximately 1800 mL within an hour. What is the most appropriate immediate step in managing this patient?
options: Conservative management for the next 6 hours
questions.explanation: In a patient with a massive hemothorax following chest trauma, the indications for an Emergency Thoracotomy are very specific. The most appropriate immediate step is surgery if there is an initial chest tube drainage of (as in this case with 1800 ml) OR a continuous drainage of per hour for 2 to 4 consecutive hours. Such massive blood loss suggests a major injury to a hilar vessel, the heart, or an intercostal artery that cannot be managed conservatively. Continuing resuscitation (Option C) alone without surgical control of the bleeding is insufficient. Options A and D (conservative management or waiting) are life-threatening delays in the face of active, high-volume hemorrhage. The goal of emergency thoracotomy is to control the source of bleeding, evacuate clots, and repair major structural damage. This is a critical trauma skill. Rapid assessment and immediate decision-making are necessary to prevent exsanguination and hypovolemic shock in these high-stakes trauma scenarios

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: 'Mount Fuji sign' is seen in _____________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tension pneumocephalus

'Mount Fuji sign' is seen in tension pneumocephalus.

Mount Fuji sign refers to the presence of air (pneumocephalus) between the tips of the frontal lobes giving the appearance of Mount Fuji.

Tension pneumocephalus occurs with subdural air causing a mass effect over the underlying brain parenchyma, often from a ball valve mechanism causing one-way entry of air into the subdural space.

The appearance of this sign often warrants immediate surgery to prevent permanent damage.

The CT image below shows the Mount Fuji sign.
questions.learning: Tension pneumocephalus 'Mount Fuji sign' is seen in tension pneumocephalus. Mount Fuji sign refers to the presence of air (pneumocephalus) between the tips of the frontal lobes giving the appearance of Mount Fuji.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with renal insufficiency presented with very low urine output, pedal edema, headache and BP 160/90. Which anti-hypertensive can be administered?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chlorthalidone

The antihypertensive that can be given in this case is chlorthalidone. The patient in this case is having renal insufficiency but there is no proteinuria mentioned in the question stem. So among the given options, the thiazide diuretic chlorthalidone can be administered as antihypertensive in this patient.

Management of hypertension in chronic kidney disease(CKD):

ACE inhibitors or ARBs are considered the first-line drugs in patients with proteinuria. These agents effectively reduce blood pressure, proteinuria and prevent kidney decline. Calcium channel blockers can be added if necessary.

For patients who do not have proteinuria, there is no established first-line therapy. One or two of the following drugs can be used:

• Thiazides/thiazide-like diuretics
• ACE inhibitors or ARBs
• Calcium channel blockers

In patients presenting with fluid retention or fluid overload, thiazide diuretics such as chlorthalidone and hydrochlorothiazide are recommended for management. In CKD stages 1 to 3 (GFR >=30ml/min), thiazides are recommended, while loop diuretics such as bumetanide, furosemide are used in stages 4-5 (GFR < 30ml/min).

Other options:

Option A: Aliskiren is a direct renin inhibitor. It effectively lowers blood pressure, reduces albuminuria, and limits left ventricular hypertrophy.

Option C: Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker. A common side effect of amlodipine is the production of peripheral edema.

Option D: Prazosin is a selective α1 antagonist. It is generally not used as an initial agent to treat hypertension, except in symptomatic prostatism or nightmares linked to posttraumatic stress disorder. Headache is one of the side effects of prazosin.
questions.learning: Chlorthalidone — The antihypertensive that can be given in this case is chlorthalidone. The patient in this case is having renal insufficiency but there is no proteinuria mentioned in the question stem.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient, 36 hours after cataract surgery, presents with complaints of pain and visual disturbance. His eye is as shown below. What is the management of this condition?
options: Bandage and padding of the eye
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Intravitreal antibiotics

A post cataract surgery patient presenting within 36 hours of surgery with inflammation, congestion and hypopyon as seen in the image, is suggestive of acute bacterial endophthalmitis. The treatment of acute bacterial endophthalmitis is intravitreal antibiotics.

Endophthalmitis is an intraocular inflammation affecting the inner structures of the eyeball. Acute postoperative bacterial endophthalmitis occurs within 1-7 days after cataract surgery and the most important factor to prevent it is preoperative administration of 5% povidone iodine. The cardinal features of endophthalmitis are pain, swelling of the lid, and a decrease in vision. The patient classically shows inflammation of the eye, corneal edema and a hypopyon due to the pouring of exudates in the vitreous cavity, anterior chamber, and posterior chamber.

Once the endophthalmitis sets in it is important to treat all the cases empirically with a combination of antibiotics and steroids from the beginning. The various drugs, routes and surgical management used to treat endophthalmitis are as follows:

1. The mainstay of treatment is intravitreal injections of antibiotics.

• First choice: Vancomycin 1 mg in 0.1 mL plus ceftazidime 2.25mg in 0.1ml.
• Second choice:Vancomycin 1 mg in 0.1 mL plus amikacin 0.4mg in 0.1ml.
• If there is no improvement, a repeat intravitreal injection should be given after 48 hours

2. Topical antibiotics are started immediately and used frequently.

• Vancomycin (50mg/ml) or cefazolin (50mg/ml)
• Amikacin (20mg/ml) or tobramycin

3. Systemic antibiotics have a limited role in the treatment but are commonly used in practice.
4. Steroid therapy includes:

• Intravitreal injection of dexamethasone (0.4mg in 0.1ml) which is started along with antibiotics.
• Topical dexamethasone (0.1%)

5. Oral steroids such as prednisolone are started after 24 hours of intensive antibiotic therapy.
6. Supportive therapy includes:

• Cycloplegics such as atropine 1%
• Anti-glaucoma drugs such as oral acetazolamide or timolol in patients with raised intraocular pressure

7. Pars plana vitrectomy is done if the patient does not improve with the above therapy in 48-72 hours or   when the visual acuity is reduced to hand movements near the eye

Other options:

Option A: Steroids are given in endophthalmitis to reduce the inflammation of the tissues. The preferred route of administration is either by intravitreal injections, topical concentrations or oral route. Intravenous route (option A) of administration of steroids is not used in endophthalmitis.

Option B: Systemic administration (intravenous) of antibiotics have a limited role in the treatment but are commonly used in practice as an add on.
questions.learning: Intravitreal antibiotics — A post cataract surgery patient presenting within 36 hours of surgery with inflammation, congestion and hypopyon as seen in the image, is suggestive of acute bacterial endophthalmitis.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old male was brought dead to the emergency after hanging. There was a dry, hard, parchment-like ligature mark 1.5 cm wide in the anterior middle third of the neck; the mark was directed posteriorly, upwards and laterally. The left eye was closed, while the right was open, and saliva drooling of saliva was present on the right side. Compression of which of the following structures explains the right eye opening?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cervical sympathetic chain

In hanging, characteristic findings include asymmetry of eye opening and salivary dribbling, which help determine the side of compression.

• Compression of the cervical sympathetic chain → loss of sympathetic supply on that side
• Leads to features of Horner’s syndrome:

• Ptosis (eye closed)
• Miosis
• Anhidrosis

Application to the case:

• Left eye closed → left sympathetic chain compressed
• Right eye open → right sympathetic chain intact
• Saliva dribbling on right side → indicates oblique ligature mark with pressure asymmetry

Why not others:

• ICA: Cerebral ischemia, not eye-opening changes
• IJV: Venous congestion, cyanosis
• Vagus nerve: Affects heart rate/voice, not eyelid position
questions.learning: Cervical sympathetic chain — In hanging, characteristic findings include asymmetry of eye opening and salivary dribbling, which help determine the side of compression. • Compression of the cervical sympathetic chain → loss of sympathetic supply on that…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Reservoir for Kala azar is ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Human

In India, humans are considered the main reservoir for kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis).

Kala azar or visceral leishmaniasis is a protozoal infection, mainly affecting the reticuloendothelial system. It is caused by the Leishmania donovani complex that includes L. donovani and L. infantum. These organisms are transmitted by sandflies.

Clinical features of kala-azar:

* Moderate- to high-grade fever with chills and rigors

* Splenomegaly and hepatomegaly

* Anemia

* Lymphadenopathy

* Pedal edema, ascites, due to hypoalbuminemia

* Epistaxis, gastrointestinal bleed, and retinal hemorrhages, due to thrombocytopenia

The gold standard test for the diagnosis is the demonstration of amastigotes in the smears of tissue aspirates. Another commonly used modality is the detection of antibodies to a recombinant antigen called rK39 by rapid immunochormatographic test.

Amphotericin B is the first-line drug used in India. Other drugs useful in treating the condition are sodium stibogluconate, meglumine antimoniate, paromomycin, and miltefosine.
questions.learning: Human — In India, humans are considered the main reservoir for kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis). Kala azar or visceral leishmaniasis is a protozoal infection, mainly affecting the reticuloendothelial system.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A female patient presented with a lesion as shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Malignant melanoma

An asymmetrical lesion, with an irregular border, with black/brown pigmentation points towards a diagnosis of malignant melanoma.

Types of melanoma:

* Lentigo maligna

* Superficial spreading

* Acral lentiginous

* Nodular

Histopathology of melanoma:

* Individual melanoma cells are larger than normal melanocytes

* They have large nuclei with irregular contours, chromatin is characteristically clumped at the periphery of the nuclear membrane with prominent red eosinophilic nucleoli

* All tumors have a vertical and radial phase of growth. The appearance of melanocytes is similar in both phases. The vertical growth has is often heralded by the appearance of a nodule.

* The possibility of metastasis correlates with the depth of invasion which is called the Breslow thickness.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a tributary of the inferior vena cava?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Left inferior phrenic vein

The inferior vena cava (IVC) directly receives the inferior phrenic veins, including the left one.

In contrast, the left suprarenal and left gonadal veins drain into the left renal vein, not directly into the IVC.

The ascending lumbar veins contribute to the azygos system, not the IVC.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following in IgA vasculitis warrants the use of corticosteroids?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. GI bleeding

IgA vasculitis is a small vessel vasculitis with IgA immune complex deposition.

Classic tetrad:

• Palpable purpura (skin)
• Arthralgia/arthritis
• Abdominal pain
• Renal involvement

Usually self-limiting, especially in children

Corticosteroids in IgA vasculitis are indicated for severe gastrointestinal involvement, especially GI bleeding, due to risk of complications like intussusception and perforation.

Skin rash, arthritis, and mild abdominal pain are usually self-limiting and managed with supportive care.

Steroids are reserved for organ-threatening disease, not routine symptoms.

| Arthritis | NSAIDs

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The following maternal infections or conditions are associated with certain characteristic fetal effects. Which of the following pair is not correctly matched?
options: Zika virus — microcephaly and cerebral malformations
Varicella infection — skin scarring and limb hypoplasia
Maternal SLE — congenital complete heart block
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. HIV infection — non-immune hydrops fetalis

• A. Zika virus → Microcephaly and cerebral malformations ✔️

Congenital Zika syndrome is characterized by severe microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, ventriculomegaly, and other CNS abnormalities.
• B. Varicella infection → Skin scarring and limb hypoplasia ✔️

Congenital varicella syndrome can cause cicatricial skin lesions, limb hypoplasia, ocular defects, and neurological abnormalities.
• C. Maternal SLE → Congenital complete heart block ✔️

Maternal anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB) antibodies can cross the placenta and cause neonatal lupus, particularly congenital complete heart block.
• D. HIV infection → Non-immune hydrops fetalis ❌

HIV is not a recognized cause of non-immune hydrops fetalis. Common causes include:

• Parvovirus B19 infection
• Fetal anemia
• Cardiac anomalies
• Chromosomal abnormalities
• Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the ideal time for umbilical cord clamping after birth?
questions.explanation: Current global and Indian clinical guidelines recommend delayed cord clamping (DCC), performed between 1 and 3 minutes after the birth of the baby. DCC allows for the transfer of approximately of placental blood to the newborn, which significantly increases neonatal iron stores and hemoglobin levels, reducing the risk of anemia later in infancy. Immediate clamping (Option A) or clamping within 30 seconds (Option B) is now reserved for specific emergencies where immediate maternal or neonatal resuscitation is required. Clamping more than 3 minutes after birth (Option D) does not provide significant additional benefit and may complicate the timing of active management of the third stage of labor. In preterm infants, DCC is particularly beneficial as it reduces the need for blood transfusions and decreases the incidence of intraventricular hemorrhage. Therefore, the "ideal" window for physiological benefit is the 1–3 minute mark

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is the probable diagnosis for a 38-year-old female who is experiencing substantial hair loss for 4 months and has a history of COVID-19 infection 8 months ago?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Telogen effluvium

Key clinical clues:

• Diffuse hair loss (not patchy)
• Duration \~4 months
• History of stressor (COVID-19 infection 8 months ago)

Pathophysiology:

• Hair prematurely shifts from anagen → telogen phase
• Triggered by physiological stress (e.g., infections like COVID)
• Hair shedding typically begins 2–3 months after the trigger, but can persist

| Condition | Key Features | Why NOT here

| --------- | ------------ | ------------

| Androgenetic alopecia | Gradual, patterned thinning (fronto-parietal/crown) | Chronic, not acute post-stress

| Alopecia areata | Well-defined patchy hair loss | Not diffuse

| Anagen effluvium | Rapid hair loss (days–weeks), usually chemotherapy | No chemo history

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the most effective treatment for a 3-year-old child diagnosed with 15-degree accommodative esotropia?
questions.explanation: Accommodative esotropia is a type of inward eye turn caused by excessive convergence that occurs when a farsighted (hyperopic) child tries to clear their vision. In a 3-year-old child, the most effective and standard first-line treatment is refractive correction (Option D) with full-cycloplegic spectacles. By correcting the underlying farsightedness, the need for excessive accommodation—and thus the associated convergence/crossing—is eliminated, often straightening the eyes immediately. Orthoptic exercises (Option A) may have a limited role in convergence insufficiency but are not the primary treatment for accommodative crossing. Surgery (Option B) is contraindicated as the primary treatment because the crossing is refractive; operating could lead to an outward turn (exotropia) later. Relieving prisms (Option C) are used for small paralytic deviations rather than primary childhood esotropia. Therefore, prescription glasses are the definitive and most appropriate clinical intervention for this condition. Early correction is essential to prevent permanent amblyopia and ensure the development of normal binocular vision
questions.learning: Accommodative esotropia is a type of inward eye turn caused by excessive convergence that occurs when a farsighted (hyperopic) child tries to clear their vision.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 45-year-old man is admitted with respiratory distress. CT imaging reveals a nasal polyp associated with fluid accumulation in a paranasal sinus. Obstruction of drainage from which structure is most likely responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation: The CT scan findings show a nasal polyp obstructing the drainage of the maxillary sinus. The maxillary sinus (Antrum of Highmore) is the largest paranasal sinus and drains into the middle meatus of the nose via the maxillary ostium. When a polyp grows in the middle meatus, it blocks this ostium, leading to secondary sinusitis and fluid accumulation. Regarding the distractors, the ethmoidal sinuses (Option A) are multiple small cells; the anterior ones drain to the middle meatus, but the large fluid collection shown is within the maxilla. The sphenoidal sinus (Option B) drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess. The frontal sinus (Option C) also drains to the middle meatus, but its obstruction would show fluid in the forehead region on CT. Thus, the anatomical location of the fluid collection confirms maxillary sinus involvement
questions.learning: The CT scan findings show a nasal polyp obstructing the drainage of the maxillary sinus. The maxillary sinus (Antrum of Highmore) is the largest paranasal sinus and drains into the middle meatus of the nose via the maxillary ostium.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman with a history of chronic cholecystitis recently underwent cholecystectomy and now presents with worsening digestive symptoms. What is the most common post-cholecystectomy complication that could explain her complaints?
questions.explanation: Following a cholecystectomy, the body no longer has a reservoir to store and concentrate bile. Bile now flows continuously and less efficiently into the small intestine. For some patients, this leads to malabsorption of fats, resulting in the most common long-term postoperative digestive complication: Steatorrhea (Option C). Steatorrhea is characterized by oily, foul-smelling stools and bloating. Acute kidney injury (Option A) and Osteoporosis (Option B) are unrelated to the removal of the gallbladder. While some epidemiological studies have suggested a very slight potential increase in the long-term risk of colorectal cancer (Option D), it is not a "common complication" that would explain immediate worsening of digestive issues after surgery. Therefore, the physiological loss of bile storage and its impact on fat digestion identifies steatorrhea as the definitive clinical consequence described. Management typically involves dietary modifications, such as consuming smaller, lower-fat meals to improve digestion
questions.learning: Following a cholecystectomy, the body no longer has a reservoir to store and concentrate bile. Bile now flows continuously and less efficiently into the small intestine.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient develops enophthalmos and periorbital ecchymosis after being struck by a ball. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Blunt trauma from an object like a ball causes a sudden rise in orbital pressure, often fracturing the thin orbital floor. This results in the herniation of orbital contents into the maxillary sinus, which causes enophthalmos (sunken eye). Patients also classically present with periorbital ecchymosis and potential infraorbital nerve anesthesia. Zygomatic fractures (Option B) typically present with cheek flattening and trismus rather than isolated enophthalmos. Nasal bone fractures (Option C) cause deformity and epistaxis but do not affect orbital position. Le Fort I fractures (Option D) are horizontal maxillary fractures involving the upper jaw and teeth. A classic radiographic sign for a blowout fracture is the "hanging drop" or "tear drop" sign on a Water's view X-ray or CT. Thus, the mechanism and enophthalmos confirm the orbital blowout diagnosis

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Treatment of ptosis caused by Horner’s syndrome is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fasanella servat operation

Fasanella servat operation is done for cases of mild ptosis (1.5-2 mm) with retained levator palpabrae superioris muscle function as seen in Horner’s syndrome.

Ptosis in Horner's syndrome is due to the loss of sympathetic supply to the muller's muscle of the lid and not due to levator muscle palsy. Fasanella servat operation is not done in patients with severe ptosis and poor levtaor function.

Option A:Levator resection is performed for moderate and severe grades of ptosis but with retained levator function. This operation is contraindicated in patients with poor levator function.

Option B: Frontalis sling also known as Brow suspension is done in patients with severe ptosis with poor or absent levator muscle function. Here, the lid is anchored to the frontalis muscle via a sling.
