questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: During a planned dilatation and curettage (D&C) procedure, a Sims’ uterine sound is introduced, but no resistance is encountered. Based on this finding, what should be the next appropriate step in management from the given options?
questions.explanation: During a D&C, a sudden loss of resistance while using a uterine sound or curette is a classic sign of uterine perforation. This is a serious surgical complication. The immediate priority is to stop the procedure and assess for injury to internal organs, such as the bowel or bladder. Immediate laparoscopy (Option C) is the gold standard for visualizing the site of perforation and checking for secondary damage or internal bleeding. Continuing the procedure (Option A) or proceeding with the planned evacuation (Option B) is extremely dangerous, as it can worsen the injury or cause a bowel pull-through. Mifepristone and Misoprostol (Option D) are medical management options that have no role in the acute management of a surgical perforation. If the patient is hemodynamically unstable, an emergency laparotomy might be required, but in a controlled setting, laparoscopy is the preferred diagnostic and potentially therapeutic next step to ensure patient safety
questions.learning: During a D&C, a sudden loss of resistance while using a uterine sound or curette is a classic sign of uterine perforation. This is a serious surgical complication.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: After gastric bypass/bariatric surgery, which deficiency is most commonly observed?
questions.explanation: Bariatric surgeries, particularly malabsorptive procedures like the Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, significantly alter nutrient absorption. The most common nutritional deficiency observed following these surgeries is Iron deficiency. This occurs because iron is primarily absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, which are "bypassed" during the procedure. Additionally, reduced gastric acid production impairs the conversion of dietary iron into its more absorbable ferrous form. Calcium (Option D) deficiency is also common and important, but statistically, iron storage depletion occurs more frequently and earlier in the postoperative period. Zinc (Option C) and copper (Option B) deficiencies are recognized but are much rarer than iron or Vitamin B12 deficits. Therefore, regular monitoring of hemoglobin and ferritin levels is a mandatory part of post-bariatric surgical follow-up. Patients are typically prescribed lifelong iron supplements to prevent chronic anemia
questions.learning: Bariatric surgeries, particularly malabsorptive procedures like the Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, significantly alter nutrient absorption. The most common nutritional deficiency observed following these surgeries is Iron deficiency.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 38-year-old man presents with a one-week history of fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, and myalgia. Examination shows multiple purpura and petechiae over the shoulder, trunk, and legs, and there is a history of increased mosquito breeding with similar cases reported in the area. What is the most common neurological complication associated with this condition?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms of retro-orbital pain, myalgia, and petechial rashes linked to mosquito breeding are classic for Dengue fever. Dengue encephalopathy is the most frequently encountered neurological complication of the dengue virus. It is primarily linked to Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever and Dengue Shock Syndrome and is often metabolic in nature rather than a direct brain infection. Guillain-Barré Syndrome (Option B), Stroke (Option C), and Encephalitis (Option D) are all recognized complications but occur less frequently than encephalopathy. Clinical features of dengue also include thrombocytopenia and plasma leakage leading to pleural effusion or ascites. Management of neurological symptoms is supportive, with a focus on fluid resuscitation and monitoring for shock, which can worsen metabolic brain dysfunction
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms of retro-orbital pain, myalgia, and petechial rashes linked to mosquito breeding are classic for Dengue fever. Dengue encephalopathy is the most frequently encountered neurological complication of the dengue virus.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 70-year-old man presents with low back pain and progressive pallor. Investigations reveal abnormal kidney function tests, normal liver function with preserved albumin levels, disproportionately elevated gamma globulins, and spinal X-rays showing multiple lytic lesions. Based on this clinical picture, what is the most likely cell of origin of the underlying disease?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of an elderly man with low back pain, anemia (pallor), renal dysfunction, and multiple lytic bone lesions on X-ray is classic for Multiple Myeloma. The biochemical hallmark—disproportionately increased gamma globulins (the "M-spike") with a normal albumin level—indicates the overproduction of monoclonal immunoglobulins. The cell of origin for this malignancy is the plasma cell. Multiple myeloma is a clonal proliferation of malignant plasma cells in the bone marrow. These cells secrete cytokines (like IL-6) that stimulate osteoclasts, leading to the "punched-out" lytic lesions and hypercalcemia. Lymphocytes (Option A) give rise to various lymphomas and leukemias. Histiocytes (Option C) and Monocytes (Option D) are involved in different types of proliferative disorders (like Langerhans cell histiocytosis) but do not produce the monoclonal protein spike seen in myeloma. Bone marrow biopsy showing clonal plasma cells is the definitive diagnostic step for this condition
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of an elderly man with low back pain, anemia (pallor), renal dysfunction, and multiple lytic bone lesions on X-ray is classic for Multiple Myeloma.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with bleeding from the ear following a fall. What is the investigation of choice in this scenario?

Correct answer: A. CT temporal bone

In a patient with ear bleeding following trauma, the investigation of choice is CT temporal bone, as it is the best modality to detect temporal bone fractures.

·  CT temporal bone (HRCT) provides detailed visualization of:

o    Bony structures of ear (external, middle, inner ear)

o    Fracture lines (longitudinal/transverse)

o    Ossicular disruption, facial canal involvement

·  Helps classify fractures and identify complications such as:

o    CSF leak

o    Facial nerve injury

o    Hearing loss

Why not other options:

·   MRI brain: Better for soft tissue and intracranial complications, not first-line for fractures

·   CBP: Irrelevant

·   X-ray skull: Low sensitivity, largely obsolete

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: All the following PFT findings in a child are suggestive of asthma except?
options: Increase in FEV1> 12% after salbutamol inhalation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Day- night variation of FEV1 > 15%

Day-night variation of FEV1 > 15% is not suggestive of asthma, variation ≥20% is suggestive of asthma.

• Spirometry showing airflow limitation: Low FEV1 (relative to the percentage of predicted norms) and FEV1:FVC ratio <0.80 (option B)
• Bronchodilator response (to inhaled β-agonist): Improvement in FEV1 ≥12% and ≥200 mL after inhalation of a short-acting beta agonist (option A).
• Exercise challenge: Worsening in FEV1 ≥15% (option D)
• Daily peak expiratory flow (PEF) or FEV1 monitoring: day to day and/or A.M.-to-P.M. variation ≥20%
• Exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO): A value of >20ppb (parts per billion) supports the clinical diagnosis of asthma in children.

Childhood asthma can be classified into two types: recurrent wheezing in early childhood, often triggered by respiratory viral infections and resolves during preschool/lower school years, and chronic asthma associated with allergies that persist into later childhood and adulthood.

questions.text: A 25-year-old woman presents with a breast lump with no skin changes or induration. On histology, there was a fibroadenoma appearance. Which of the following categories does it fall under?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. BIRADS 2

Fibroadenoma is a benign tumor in a 25-year-old woman with no skin changes and no indurations and is categorized as BIRADS 2.

Fibroadenoma is a form of aberrations of normal development and involution of the breast (ANDI), and it is the most common cause of a breast lump in women aged 15–25 years.

It arises from hyperplasia of a single lobule and presents as a well-circumscribed, smooth or lobular, firm, non-tender, freely mobile mass (mouse in the breast). The histopathology shows the proliferation of intralobular stroma, and the epithelium may be surrounded by stroma (pericanalicular pattern) or compressed and distorted (intracanalicular pattern).

USG is done to confirm the diagnosis. A biopsy is needed if USG shows atypical features or the age of presentation is above 25 years.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In which of the following situations is confidentiality upheld?
questions.explanation: Confidentiality is a foundational ethical and professional principle in healthcare, particularly in the context of Counseling. Counseling is an intimate, one-on-one relationship where the client shares sensitive personal information with the professional, under the strict understanding that this information will not be disclosed to others without consent. This trust is essential for the therapeutic process to be effective. In contrast, Group discussions (Option A), Panel discussions (Option C), and Seminars (Option D) are all public or semi-public forums intended for the open exchange of ideas and the collective learning of many participants; therefore, they do not provide or require an environment of individual confidentiality. Upholding confidentiality is a legal duty of a doctor, with rare exceptions such as reporting a contagious disease or preventing an immediate threat of harm. Maintaining privacy in counseling encourages patients to be honest about their health and lifestyle, facilitating accurate diagnosis and effective management. Recognizing where this principle applies is essential for professional medical practice

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 35-year-old patient with a history of bronchial asthma is planned for a minor surgical procedure. Which combination of induction agent and muscle relaxant would be the safest choice for anesthesia in this patient?
questions.explanation: For an asthmatic patient, the safest anaesthesia combination involves agents that do not trigger bronchospasm. Ketamine is the preferred induction agent because it is a potent bronchodilator. Vecuronium is the safest muscle relaxant as it does not cause significant histamine release, which is a major trigger for bronchial hyperreactivity. Regarding the distractors, Succinylcholine (Option A) and d-tubocurarine (Option B) can stimulate histamine release and are risky in asthma. Thiopental (Option D) may lead to respiratory depression and is generally avoided in unstable asthmatics. While Propofol is also a bronchodilator, the specific combination of Ketamine and Vecuronium is highlighted as ideal for its stability and lack of histaminergic effects. Therefore, this pairing minimizes the risk of intraoperative bronchospasm, ensuring airway safety for the asthmatic patient

Rinne’s test positive , Weber’s test lateralized to right ear
Rinne’s test negative , Weber’s test lateralized to left ear
Rinne’s test negative , Weber’s test lateralized to right ear

Correct answer: D. Rinne’s test negative , Weber’s test lateralized to right ear

Otosclerosis causes conductive hearing loss due to stapes fixation, leading to characteristic findings on tuning fork tests.

·         Rinne test: Negative (Bone conduction > Air conduction)

·         Weber test: Lateralizes to the affected ear (right ear in this case)

Why stapedectomy is advised:

·         Fixation of stapes footplate

·         Surgery restores ossicular chain mobility

Why other options are incorrect:

·         Rinne positive: Seen in normal or SNHL

·  Weber to opposite ear: Seen in SNHL

questions.text: Which is the best stain for biopsy during laryngoscopy for vocal cord examination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Supravital

Supravital staining is used during laryngoscopy for vocal cord examination to assess epithelial cell viability and early malignant changes in real time.

• Supravital stains (e.g., toluidine blue) are applied in vivo on mucosa
• They preferentially stain areas of high nucleic acid content → suspicious for dysplasia/malignancy
• Help in targeted biopsy by highlighting abnormal epithelium

Why not other options:

• H&E: Standard histopathological stain, used after biopsy, not during procedure
• Silver nitrate: Cauterizing agent, not a diagnostic stain
• Congo red: Used for amyloidosis, not for vocal cord lesions

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of these is not an essential feature for the diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder?
options: Restrictive patterns of behaviour and interests
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cognitive impairment

Cognitive impairment does not form part of the diagnostic criteria for autism spectrum disorder.

The DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for autism spectrum disorder are as follows:

• Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts, currently or by history
• Restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities, currently or by history
• Symptoms must be present in the early developmental period (but may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed limited capacities, or may be masked by learned strategies in later life).
• Symptoms cause clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning.
• These disturbances are not better explained by intellectual disability or global developmental delay. Intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder frequently co-occur; to make comorbid diagnoses of autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability, social communication should be below that expected for the general developmental level.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman in her third trimester presents to the emergency department after a fainting episode while lying down. She reports improvement after sitting up. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation: This patient is experiencing Supine Hypotensive Syndrome, a common occurrence in late pregnancy. When a pregnant woman lies flat on her back, the heavy gravid uterus can compress the Inferior Vena Cava (IVC). This obstruction reduces venous return to the heart, leading to a sudden drop in cardiac output and systemic blood pressure, which causes the fainting episode (syncope). The symptoms are immediately relieved by sitting up or turning onto the left lateral side, which shifts the uterus off the IVC. SVC compression (Option B) affects the upper body and is not related to uterine weight. While the patient has hypotension (Option C), "IVC compression" is the specific anatomical explanation for the symptom in this clinical context. Motion sickness (Option D) involves nausea and vertigo related to movement, not position-dependent syncope. Pregnant women should be counseled to avoid sleeping in the supine position and to always use a wedge or pillow to maintain a lateral tilt to ensure optimal placental and maternal circulation
questions.learning: This patient is experiencing Supine Hypotensive Syndrome, a common occurrence in late pregnancy. When a pregnant woman lies flat on her back, the heavy gravid uterus can compress the Inferior Vena Cava (IVC).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old male presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy. On examination, the right ear reveals conductive hearing loss with a dull tympanic membrane. A decreased mobility of the soft palate was also noted. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma

The given clinical condition is nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a malignant tumor of the nasopharynx. The theories for etiology include genetics, infection with Epstein-Barr virus, air pollution, and smoking. The commonest site of origin of nasopharyngeal carcinoma is the fossa of Rosenmuller.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma presents with the following symptoms:

* Cervical lymphadenopathy (most common)

* Nasal - obstruction, discharge, rhinolalia clausa, epistaxis

* Ear - eustachian tube obstruction leading to conductive hearing loss or recurrent otitis media.

* Ophthalmoneurologic - all the cranial nerves (CN) may be involved.

*

* CN VI - squint and diplopia, the most common cranial nerve involved

* CN III, IV, VI, - ophthalmoplegia

* CN V - reduced corneal reflex (Option B)

* CN II - exophthalmos (Option D)

* CN IX, X, XI - jugular foramen syndrome

* Horner’s syndrome

* Distant metastasis to the bone, liver, and lung.

Radiotherapy is the treatment of choice for nasopharyngeal cancer.

* Stage I and II are treated by radiotherapy alone.

* Stage III and IV require concomitant radiation and chemotherapy or radiation followed by chemotherapy.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In this scenario, what is the mode of transmission of the disease from the boy’s grandmother to his father and then to the boy?
questions.explanation: The inheritance pattern described involves a trait passed directly from a grandmother to her son, and then from that son to his own male child. The key diagnostic feature here is the presence of male-to-male transmission (father to son), which definitively excludes X-linked patterns. In X-linked dominant (Option A) or X-linked recessive (Option B) inheritance, a father contributes his Y chromosome to his son, not his X chromosome; therefore, he cannot pass an X-linked trait to male offspring. Autosomal recessive (Option D) typically presents with a "horizontal" pattern, often skipping generations and requiring both parents to be carriers. Autosomal dominance (Option C) is characterized by a "vertical" pattern where the trait appears in every generation, affecting both sexes equally and allowing for direct father-to-son transmission. Because the condition is passed directly through consecutive generations without gender restrictions, it follows the classic rules of autosomal dominant inheritance. This genetic knowledge is essential for accurate family counseling and risk assessment

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A pregnant woman with a prior mitral valve replacement is currently at 36 weeks of gestation. She has been on long-term warfarin therapy throughout pregnancy, and her INR is 3. In view of her advanced gestational age and cardiac history, which of the following is the most appropriate management approach at this stage?
options: Stop warfarin, start LMWH and aspirin
questions.explanation: In a pregnant woman with a mechanical mitral valve, continuous anticoagulation is essential to prevent valve thrombosis. However, at 36 weeks of gestation, continuing warfarin is unsafe because it crosses the placenta and increases the risk of fetal bleeding, especially intracranial hemorrhage during delivery. Therefore, warfarin must be discontinued at this stage. The preferred approach is to switch to low molecular weight heparin (LMWH). LMWH does not cross the placenta, making it safer for the fetus, and provides effective anticoagulation for the mother. It has a predictable dose-response and is widely used with anti-Xa monitoring in pregnancy. Other options are incorrect: (B) Unfractionated heparin is useful near delivery but is not the preferred option at this stage in stable patients. (C) Continuing warfarin poses significant fetal risk. (D) Adding aspirin is unnecessary and increases bleeding risk. Thus, at 36 weeks, the most appropriate management is to stop warfarin and initiate LMWH

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 17-year-old male presents with a painless swelling on the lateral aspect of his left knee. Based on the image shown, what is the most likely diagnosis among the following options?
questions.explanation: The X-ray finding of a bony, pedunculated outgrowth (exostosis) pointing away from the nearby joint is pathognomonic for an osteochondroma. It is the most common benign bone tumor and typically occurs in adolescents around the growth plates of long bones, like the distal femur. These lesions are usually painless unless they interfere with surrounding tendons or nerves. Ewing’s sarcoma (Option B) would show an "onion-skin" periosteal reaction and look highly aggressive. Giant cell tumor (Option D) is an expansile "soap-bubble" lesion that is located in the epiphysis (reaching the joint surface), not on a stalk projecting away. Enchondroma (Option A) is a benign cartilaginous tumor located inside the medullary cavity, often in the small bones of the hands. Therefore, the classic "stalk" or pedunculated appearance confirms the diagnosis of osteochondroma

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A virus exploits the neuron's intracellular transport machinery to travel from a peripheral nerve terminal back to the cell body, moving at approximately 200 mm/day along microtubules. Which motor protein mediates this movement, and which direction does it represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dynein — retrograde transport

Retrograde axonal transport carries materials from the nerve terminal back to the neuronal cell body along microtubules and is mediated by the motor protein dynein. This transport pathway is exploited by several neurotropic viruses, including Rabies, to reach the central nervous system after entering peripheral nerves.

Why not the other options?

• A. Kinesin — orthograde transport: Kinesin mediates anterograde (cell body → axon terminal) transport.
• C. Kinesin — retrograde transport: Kinesin does not mediate retrograde movement.
• D. Myosin — orthograde transport: Myosin functions primarily on actin filaments, not microtubule-based long-distance axonal transport.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: For testing blood clotting/ coagulation parameters, blood is collected in which color- coded vacutainer tube?
questions.explanation: For the assessment of coagulation parameters, such as Prothrombin Time (PT) and Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT), blood must be collected in a light blue vacutainer. This tube contains sodium citrate, which acts as a reversible calcium-chelating anticoagulant. Citrate is preferred because it preserves the fragile coagulation factors necessary for accurate laboratory testing. Red tubes (Option A) contain no anticoagulant and are used for serum studies. Green tubes (Option B) contain heparin and are utilized for arterial blood gases or osmotic fragility tests. Gray tubes (Option D) contain sodium fluoride to inhibit glycolysis for accurate blood glucose measurement. Therefore, the blue-coded vacutainer is the standard requirement for any clotting or intrinsic/extrinsic pathway study
questions.learning: For the assessment of coagulation parameters, such as Prothrombin Time (PT) and Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT), blood must be collected in a light blue vacutainer.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: During evaluation of PUO, a patient's chest X-ray is as seen below. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Miliary tuberculosis

The given chest radiography image shows miliary tuberculosis.

It is the widespread dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, via hematogenous spread.

Classic miliary TB is defined as millet-like (mean, 2 mm; range, 1-5 mm) seeding of TB bacilli with uniform size and distribution in the lung, as seen on chest radiography. This particular sign is called the miliary shadow which is also seen in sarcoidosis and histoplasmosis.

Sputum-smear microscopy is negative in most cases.

Physical findings include hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy

Bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial biopsy are used to provide bacteriologic confirmation

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A baby who was playing unsupervised now presents with difficulty swallowing for the past few hours. Based on the findings in the provided X-ray, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The provided X-ray illustrates a radio-opaque, coin-like foreign body lodged at the level of the upper esophagus . On a frontal view, an esophageal foreign body typically presents with its "flat" side facing forward (coronal plane), as seen here. The clinical history of a baby with sudden-onset difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) following unsupervised play is highly characteristic of accidental ingestion. A foreign body in the trachea (Option A) would classically appear on edge (sagittal plane) in the AP view due to the orientation of the vocal folds and would present with stridor or coughing rather than dysphagia. Objects in the lungs (Option C) or pleura (Option D) would be located more distally and laterally in the chest. Because the object is centered in the midline at the standard site of esophageal narrowing (cricopharyngeus), the esophagus is the definitive location. Immediate endoscopic removal is required to prevent aspiration or local necrosis

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: From which of the following structure does the saccule develop?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pars inferior

The saccule develops from pars inferior.

The development of the inner ear begins in the 3rd week of fetal life and is completed by the 16th week. The surface ectoderm on each side of the rhombencephalon thickens to form otic/auditory placodes, which then invaginate to form the otic vesicle (otocysts).

The cells of the otic vesicle differentiate to form ganglion cells, which later develop into the vestibulocochlear ganglia. Later each otic vesicle divides into a dorsal component called pars superior and a ventral component called pars inferior.

Pars superior gives rise to the utricle, semicircular canals, and endolymphatic ducts. Pars inferior gives rise to saccule and cochlear duct. The saccule is connected to the cochlea through a narrow duct called ductus reuniens.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Prominent occiput

Turner syndrome is a chromosomal disorder (45,XO) characterized by gonadal dysgenesis and distinctive somatic features, with absence of Barr body due to monosomy X.

• Common features include short stature, webbed neck, shield chest with widely spaced nipples, and streak gonads
• Other findings: coarctation of aorta, lymphedema at birth, primary amenorrhea
• Barr body is absent because there is only one X chromosome
• Prominent occiput is not a feature of Turner syndrome; It is seen in Edward syndrome.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The stage in vitamin D metabolism that requires exposure to sunlight is:
questions.explanation: Vitamin D synthesis begins in the skin and requires ultraviolet (UVB) radiation from sunlight. The specific photochemical reaction occurs when 7-dehydrocholesterol, found in the epidermal layers, is converted into cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3) upon exposure to sunlight. This is the only non-enzymatic step in the metabolic pathway. Subsequent steps involve enzymatic hydroxylation in the liver and kidneys. Cholecalciferol is converted to 25-hydroxycholecalciferol (Calcidiol) in the liver by 25-hydroxylase (Option C). The final activation step occurs in the kidney, where 25-hydroxycholecalciferol is converted to 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (Calcitriol) by 1-alpha-hydroxylase (Option D). Calcitriol is the active hormone responsible for calcium homeostasis. Option A is an impossible reverse reaction. Therefore, the initial dermal production of D3 is the definitive stage dependent on sunlight exposure

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Crypta magna is the remnant of:
questions.explanation: The embryological development of the pharyngeal apparatus is critical for forming structures of the head and neck. The second pharyngeal pouch is specifically responsible for the formation of the palatine tonsils. As the pouch endoderm proliferates into the surrounding mesenchyme, it forms the tonsillar crypts. The crypta magna (or intratonsillar cleft) is the largest and most prominent of these crypts and represents the original lumen or remnant of the second pharyngeal pouch itself. The first pouch (Option A) forms the Eustachian tube and middle ear. The third pouch (Option C) forms the thymus and inferior parathyroid glands. The fourth pouch (Option D) contributes to the superior parathyroid glands and the ultimobranchial body. Therefore, because the palatine tonsils are the direct derivative of the second pouch, the crypta magna is its definitive anatomical remnant

questions.text: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are implemented under the aegis of which international organization?

questions.explanation: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are a universal call to action consisting of 17 global objectives established by the United Nations in 2015. questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following parameters are true for anemia of chronic disease except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increased ferroportin

Anemia of chronic disease (anemia of inflammation) is mediated by increased hepcidin production from the liver in response to inflammatory cytokines (especially IL-6). Hepcidin inhibits ferroportin, reducing iron release from macrophages and intestinal absorption, leading to decreased serum iron despite normal or increased iron stores.

Typical findings include:

• ↑ Hepcidin
• ↓ Ferroportin activity
• ↓ TIBC
• Normal or ↑ ferritin (iron stores)

Thus, increased ferroportin is incorrect, as ferroportin is suppressed in anemia of chronic disease.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman presents with fatigue, weakness, and pallor, and investigations reveal a microcytic anemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The most common cause of microcytic hypochromic anemia worldwide, especially in a young female of reproductive age, is Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA). Clinically, IDA presents with symptoms of impaired oxygen delivery such as fatigue, generalized weakness, and visible pallor. The microcytosis occurs because hemoglobin synthesis is impaired due to a lack of iron, forcing red blood cells to undergo extra divisions to maintain concentration, resulting in smaller cells. Chronic kidney disease (Option B) typically presents with normocytic anemia due to decreased erythropoietin production. Hemolytic anemia (Option C) usually presents as normocytic or macrocytic with signs of increased cell destruction like jaundice. Alcoholism (Option A) is more frequently associated with macrocytic anemia due to folate deficiency or direct toxic effects. Diagnosis of IDA is confirmed by a low serum ferritin level, high total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), and low transferrin saturation. Management involves identifying the source of iron loss (such as heavy menstruation or GI bleeding) and providing oral or parenteral iron supplementation

questions.text: A 5-year-old child presented with a history of edema of the face which later progressed to generalised edema. Urine showed massive proteinuria and light microscopy was normal. Electron microscopy showed effacement of podocyte foot processes. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Minimal change disease

This case of nephrotic syndrome shows effacement of the podocyte foot processes which is characteristic of minimal change disease (MCD).

Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome. It is seen in ages 2-6 years with a clinical picture of nephrotic syndrome, that is, heavy proteinuria, oedema, hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. They may be asymptomatic or can present with peripheral oedema.

A renal biopsy is not required for confirmation and treatment can be initiated if the child fits the standard clinical picture of nephrotic syndrome. Light microscopy shows normal glomeruli and electron microscopy shows effacement of podocyte foot processes.

They show excellent response to steroid therapy with prednisone or prednisolone. A daily dose of 60 mg/m2/day for 6 weeks, followed by a single dose of 40 mg/m2 on alternate days for the next 6 weeks is the standard treatment.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following disease results in weakness of the levator palpebrae superioris, corneal anaesthesia, lagophthalmos, and ultimately blindness?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Leprosy

Leprosy could result in paresis of the levator palpebrae superioris, corneal anaesthesia, lagophthalmos, and ultimately blindness.

Lagophthalmos is the inability to close the eyelids. This can be due to the involvement of the zygomatic branch of the facial nerve (as in leprosy). Other causes of lagophthalmos include extreme proptosis and symblepharon. The decreased corneal sensation seen is due to the involvement of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve which innervates the cornea.

Leprosy or Hansen disease is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by infection with Mycobacterium leprae. Ocular features in leprosy occur due to bacterial invasion and include corneal anesthesia, lagophthalmos, corneal ulceration, episcleritis, and iris atrophy. Other features seen are:

• Keratitis with thickened, beaded corneal nerves, punctate subepithelial lesions, pannus, and vascularization
• Chronic low-grade anterior uveitis
• Miosis
• Iris atrophy
• Iris pearls
• Retinal pearls

Option B: The most common ocular manifestation in Lyme's disease is conjunctivitis. Other manifestations like keratitis, iridocyclitis, retinal vasculitis, choroiditis, optic neuropathy, and uveitis occurs very rarely.

Option C: Ophthalmia neonatarum also called neonatal conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva occurring in an infant <30 days after birth. The clinical features include conjunctival redness, eyelid edema, and ocular discharge (purulent or mucopurulent).

Option D: In trachoma, the symptoms include lacrimation, scanty mucoid discharge and foreign body sensation. Conjunctival congestion and follicles, papillary hyperplasia, Herbert follicles (seen in the limbal area), and progressive pannus are the characteristic features.
questions.learning: Leprosy Leprosy could result in paresis of the levator palpebrae superioris, corneal anaesthesia, lagophthalmos, and ultimately blindness. Lagophthalmos is the inability to close the eyelids.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A family is found dead in a closed room filled with smoke from a wood fire. Which of the following findings is most likely to be observed on their bodies?
questions.explanation: A wood fire in a closed, poorly ventilated room produces significant amounts of carbon monoxide (CO). CO has a much higher affinity for hemoglobin than oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin. A classic and pathognomonic post-mortem finding in CO poisoning is a bright, cherry-red discoloration of the skin and internal organs, known as cherry-red hypostasis. This occurs because carboxyhemoglobin is bright red and prevents the normal release of oxygen to the tissues. Cyanosis (Option B) is a bluish discoloration seen in deaths from typical hypoxia or heart failure where hemoglobin is deoxygenated. Blackish discoloration (Option C) might be seen in advanced decomposition or specific chemical poisonings. Brown pigmentation (Option D) can be seen in methemoglobinemia (e.g., from nitrates). Recognizing this cherry-red color is vital for forensic pathologists and emergency responders to immediately suspect CO poisoning as the cause of death in a fire scenario
questions.learning: A wood fire in a closed, poorly ventilated room produces significant amounts of carbon monoxide (CO). CO has a much higher affinity for hemoglobin than oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: If a person starts to serve a second employer, the new employer is responsible for his actions by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Borrowed servant doctrine

When an employee is being borrowed, the lending employer temporarily surrenders control over this worker and the borrowing employer temporarily assumes control. This is known as borrowed servant doctrine.

Vicarious liability is by which the employer is responsible for his employees’ negligence if such activity occurs in the course of the employment and within its scope.
questions.learning: Borrowed servant doctrine When an employee is being borrowed, the lending employer temporarily surrenders control over this worker and the borrowing employer temporarily assumes control.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a contraindication for the induction of labor?
options: History of lower transverse cesarean section in last three pregnancies
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Heart disease

Heart disease is currently not considered a contraindication for the induction of labor. Vaginal delivery is preferred in such patients.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young male professional trumpet player presents with a swelling on the left side of the neck that produces a gurgling sound on compression. An X-ray of the neck demonstrates characteristic findings. Based on the clinical presentation and imaging, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A laryngocele is an abnormal cystic expansion of the laryngeal saccule. The patient’s profession as a trumpet player is a classic risk factor because increased endolaryngeal pressure can force air into the saccule, causing it to dilate. The clinical sign of a "gurgling sound" or the sac emptying upon compression (Bryce’s sign) is highly suggestive. The provided X-ray confirms the diagnosis by showing a clear, air-filled radiolucent space in the neck. Option A (Pharyngeal pouch) is located lower in the neck and usually contains food/fluid rather than just air. Option C (Trachea-oesophageal fistula) presents with coughing and aspiration during feeding, not as a compressible neck mass. Option D (Tonsillar cyst) is a small, superficial lesion within the oropharynx. Laryngoceles can become infected or cause airway obstruction. They are also associated with laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma, which can obstruct the saccule opening. Surgical management is indicated for symptomatic or large lesions
questions.learning: A laryngocele is an abnormal cystic expansion of the laryngeal saccule. The patient’s profession as a trumpet player is a classic risk factor because increased endolaryngeal pressure can force air into the saccule, causing it to dilate.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old lady presented with a 1.5cm pigmented lesion on the face which is growing rapidly in size and associated with itching. The lesion is shown below. Which of the following is likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Malignant melanoma

The given clinical scenario of a >6mm pigmented lesion on the face which is asymmetrical, with an irregular border, made of black and brown pigments, and increasing rapidly in size, points towards a diagnosis of malignant melanoma.

Types of melanoma:

* Lentigo maligna

* Superficial spreading

* Acral lentiginous

* Nodular

Histopathology of melanoma:

* Individual melanoma cells are larger than normal melanocytes

* They have large nuclei with irregular contours, chromatin is characteristically clumped at the periphery of the nuclear membrane with prominent red eosinophilic nucleoli

* All tumors have a vertical and radial phase of growth. The appearance of melanocytes is similar in both phases. The vertical growth has is often heralded by the appearance of a nodule.

* The possibility of metastasis correlates with the depth of invasion which is called the Breslow thickness.

Type
Clinical features
Spread

Basal cell carcinoma

Nodule

Central ulceration with a pearly surface,

telangiectasia

local

Squamous cell carcinoma

Ulcer with thickened margins, keratosis

Papillomatous

Local,

lymph nodes

Malignant melanoma

>6 mm pigmented,

vascularization

inflammation

Local

vascular

lymph nodes

Other options:

Acquired melanocytic nevus (common mole) is rarely more than 1cm in size. It also does not show atypical network

Congenital melanocytic nevus may be small, medium or large size(>20cm). A large-sized mole may show an atypical network and have a risk of melanoma growth. But a history of being present since birth or infancy needs to be present.

A dysplastic nevus is formed at the dermo-epidermal junction. They are usually smaller in size than melanoma, have a fuzzy border, and more likely to show brown-tan pigmentation. Any blue-black pigmentation should raise suspicion of melanoma. The majority of them regress on their own

Pearl PF0159: Clinical findings suggestive of melanoma

The ABCDE of Melanoma consists of the rules for the examination of a nevus to assess its malignant potential:

A : Asymmetry

* Melanoma lesions are irregular, or not symmetrical, in shape.

B : Border irregular

* Melanoma lesions usually have irregular borders that are ill defined.

C : Color variegation

* The presence of multiple colors (blue, black, brown, tan, etc.) or the uneven distribution of color.

D : Diameter >6 mm

* Melanoma lesions are often greater than 6 millimeters in diameter (approximately the size of a pencil eraser).

E : Evolution

* There is a change in the size, shape, symptoms (such as itching or tenderness), surface (especially bleeding), or color of a mole.
questions.learning: Malignant melanoma — The given clinical scenario of a >6mm pigmented lesion on the face which is asymmetrical, with an irregular border, made of black and brown pigments, and increasing rapidly in size, points towards a diagnosis of malignant melanoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which among the following is correct regarding adequate thyroid FNAC sampling?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 6 follicular clusters with 10 cells each

6 follicular clusters each with 10 cells are considered adequate thyroid FNAC sampling.

There are different criteria for the adequacy of thyroid FNAC:

• Six groups with at least 10 cells in each group, or
• Ten groups with at least 20 cells in each group, are considered adequate.

Cystic goitre may not yield thyroid follicular cells, hence, the aspiration should be repeated under USG guidance.

FNAC is the investigation of choice in discrete thyroid swellings; it has excellent patient compliance, simple and quick to perform in the outpatient department and is readily repeated.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In a suspected tubal (ectopic) pregnancy with an inconclusive transvaginal ultrasound, what is the next step in management?
questions.explanation: In a clinically stable patient with a suspected ectopic (tubal) pregnancy and an inconclusive transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) (e.g., no pregnancy is seen in the uterus or adnexa), the mandatory next step is to obtain serial serum beta-hCG levels. The relationship between the hCG level and the TVS findings (the "discriminatory zone") is the cornerstone of diagnosis. If the hCG is above the discriminatory zone (typically ) and no intrauterine sac is seen, an ectopic pregnancy is highly likely. If it is below the zone, serial levels are monitored every 48 hours; a slow rise or plateau confirms an abnormal pregnancy. Methotrexate (Option B) is a treatment for ectopic pregnancy, not a diagnostic test. Laparotomy (Option C) and Diagnostic laparoscopy (Option D) are more invasive surgical steps reserved for when the diagnosis remains unclear after biochemical testing or if the patient becomes hemodynamically unstable. This biochemical-radiological correlation is essential for safe and effective early pregnancy management
questions.learning: In a clinically stable patient with a suspected ectopic (tubal) pregnancy and an inconclusive transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) (e.g., no pregnancy is seen in the uterus or adnexa), the mandatory next step is to obtain serial serum beta-hCG levels.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following parameters can be used to measure the rate at which the death is occurring from different causes in a given population, during a specified period?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Crude death rate

Crude death rate measures the rate at which the death is occurring from different causes in a given population, during a specified period.

Crude death rate = Number of deaths during the year X 1000/ Mid-year population

Other options:

Option B: The case fatality rate represents the killing power of the disease. Case fatality rate = Total number of deaths due to a particular disease X 100 / Total number of cases due to the same disease

Option C: Proportional mortality rate is used to know the proportion of total death due to any particular cause. It does not indicate the risk of contracting or dying from the disease.

Option D: Specific death rate is used to identify particular groups or groups "at-risk" for preventive action. They help in comparison between different causes of death within the same population.

Specific death rate due to cancer = Number of death from cancer during a calendar year X 1000/ Mid-year population
questions.learning: Crude death rate Crude death rate measures the rate at which the death is occurring from different causes in a given population, during a specified period.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Automatic implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (AICD) implantation is done for which of the following conditions?
options: Acute coronary syndrome with low ejection fraction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. All of the above

An Automated Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator (AICD) is a device placed in the chest or abdomen to detect arrhythmias and perform cardioversion, defibrillation, and pace the heart.

It is used in: -

• Brugada syndrome- refers to a sodium channelopathy with a high risk of arrhythmias that can lead to sudden cardiac death.
• Ventricular fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia.
• Acute coronary syndrome with a low ejection fraction.

ICDs are indicated for primary prevention in patients who had myocardial infarction >40 days ago (with Class II-III NYHA Heart failure with LVEF <35% and Class I NYHA with LVEF <30%). Cardiac resynchronization therapy for prevention of sudden cardiac death in heart failure. High-risk situations of sudden cardiac death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy with low ejection fraction.
questions.learning: All of the above — An Automated Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator (AICD) is a device placed in the chest or abdomen to detect arrhythmias and perform cardioversion, defibrillation, and pace the heart.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman is brought to the psychiatric outpatient department by a friend. She believes her boss is in love with her and is stalking her, but her friend denies these claims. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s belief that her boss is in love with her, despite a lack of evidence or direct interaction, is the defining symptom of Erotomania (also known as Clerambault syndrome) (Option D). This is a subtype of delusional disorder where the individual believes that another person, usually of higher social or professional status, is deeply in love with them. Megalomania (Option A) involves delusions of grandeur or extreme power. Delusion of reference (Option B) is the belief that neutral events or remarks have a special personal meaning. Delusion of control (Option C) is the belief that one's thoughts or movements are being directed by an external force. Because the patient’s fixed, false belief is specifically centered on a perceived romantic relationship with a person of higher status, erotomania is the definitive psychiatric diagnosis. Management typically involves antipsychotic medications and psychosocial interventions
questions.learning: The patient’s belief that her boss is in love with her, despite a lack of evidence or direct interaction, is the defining symptom of Erotomania (also known as Clerambault syndrome) (Option D).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
A patient presented with tendon xanthomas. His lipid profile showed serum cholesterol levels to be 283 mg/dL and serum LDL to be 202 mg/dL. He was started on lovastatin. What is the likely diagnosis?

LDL - Low density lipoprotein
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Familial hypercholesterolemia

The clinical presentation with tendon xanthomas and elevated serum LDL (low-density lipoprotein) and elevated serum cholesterol points to a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia (FH).

Familial hypercholesterolemia  (type IIa hyperlipoproteinemia) is an inherited disorder due to defects in LDL receptors. This defect causes a decrease in the uptake of LDL and cholesterol. As a result, the blood levels of both LDL and cholesterol are elevated. Such patients are at increased risk to develop atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease.

Features of FH:

• Painful polyarthritis and tendinitis are common.
• Physical findings seen are corneal arcus and tendon xanthomas over Achilles tendon and the dorsum of hands. Xanthomas are tumorous masses produced by foamy cell clusters (lipid-laden macrophages) found in the connective tissue of the skin and in tendons.

Diagnosis is done clinically based on hypercholesterolemia with

• LDL > 190 mg/dl,
• Family history of hypercholesterolemia and/or
• Premature coronary artery disease.

Treatment includes lifestyle changes, restriction of a fatty diet, and pharmacotherapy with statins in heterozygous FH patients.

Recent drugs for specific treatment of homozygous FH are:

• Lomitapide, a microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) inhibitor, and
• Mipomersen, an antisense oligonucleotide against apoB.

The image below shows Achilles tendon xanthoma and a plain lateral radiograph of both ankles showing bilateral symmetrical swellings (arrows) superior to the calcaneum respectively.

Other options

Option B: Tangier’s disease is a hypolipoproteinemia caused by a mutation of the ABCA1 gene. Enlarged orange tonsils are pathognomonic. Low HDL levels are seen. There is an increased risk for atherosclerosis.

The image below shows enlarged yellow-orange colored tonsils in Tangier's disease.

Option C: Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) deficiency causes type I hyperlipoproteinemia due to defects in LPL or apo C-II. Eruptive xanthomas are seen. Chylomicrons and VLDL are elevated. LDL and HDL are low. There is no risk for coronary disease.

Option D: Familial hyperchylomicronemia syndrome is caused due to either LPL deficiency, ApoC-II deficiency, ApoA-V deficiency, or GPIHBP1 mutation. Clinically, patients present with recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain due to acute pancreatitis. The retinal blood vessels may be opalescent and are called lipemia retinalis. Increased levels of triglycerides (mostly >1000 mg/dL) is seen. The risk of premature coronary heart disease is low.
questions.learning: Familial hypercholesterolemia — The clinical presentation with tendon xanthomas and elevated serum LDL (low-density lipoprotein) and elevated serum cholesterol points to a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia (FH).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The table below shows the results of ELISA test for HIV infection. Consider the following statements: 1. The sensitivity is 98%. 2. The specificity is 99%. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Both 1 and 2

Sensitivity and specificity are measures of the validity of a diagnostic test.

• Sensitivity = Ability of a test to correctly identify diseased individuals (true positives).
• Specificity = Ability of a test to correctly identify non-diseased individuals (true negatives).

From the table:

• True Positive (TP) = 4900
• False Negative (FN) = 100
• True Negative (TN) = 94,050
• False Positive (FP) = 950

Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN) × 100

= 4900 / (4900 + 100) × 100

= 4900 / 5000 × 100 = 98% ✓

Specificity = TN / (TN + FP) × 100

= 94,050 / (94,050 + 950) × 100

= 94,050 / 95,000 × 100 = 99% ✓

Hence, both statements are correct.
questions.learning: Both 1 and 2 Sensitivity and specificity are measures of the validity of a diagnostic test. • Sensitivity = Ability of a test to correctly identify diseased individuals (true positives). • Specificity = Ability of a test to correctly identify non-diseased…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old man presents with a painless, reducible swelling in the left inguinal region that appears on standing and disappears on lying down, with a positive cough impulse. Imaging confirms a left inguinal hernia. What is the most appropriate surgical treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation: In an adult male with a reducible inguinal hernia, the standard surgical treatment is hernioplasty. This procedure involves the reduction of the hernia sac followed by a tension-free repair using a prosthetic mesh (like the Lichtenstein repair). Mesh repairs significantly reduce the risk of hernia recurrence compared to older suture-only techniques. Herniotomy (Option A), which is the simple excision of the hernia sac without strengthening the abdominal wall, is the standard treatment for congenital hernias in children but is insufficient for adults. "Wait and watch" (Option C) might be considered for completely asymptomatic patients, but surgical repair is generally recommended for fit young adults to prevent future complications like strangulation. Emergency laparotomy (Option D) is only indicated if the hernia is strangulated and there is evidence of bowel necrosis, which is not the case for this reducible, painless bulge. Therefore, scheduled mesh hernioplasty is the most appropriate definitive management
questions.learning: In an adult male with a reducible inguinal hernia, the standard surgical treatment is hernioplasty. This procedure involves the reduction of the hernia sac followed by a tension-free repair using a prosthetic mesh (like the Lichtenstein repair).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common type of anorectal fistula?
questions.explanation: In the classification of anorectal fistulas (Parks classification), the inter-sphincteric type is the most common, accounting for approximately 45% to 70% of all cases. This type of fistula track begins at the dentate line and travels downward through the inter-sphincteric space (the plane between the internal and external anal sphincters) to open on the perianal skin. Trans-sphincteric fistulas (Option B) are the second most common (about 25-30%) and cross through both sphincteric layers into the ischiorectal fossa. Supra-sphincteric (Option C) and extra-sphincteric (Option D) fistulas are significantly rarer and often more complex to treat surgically due to their involvement of higher pelvic structures or the levator ani muscle. Accurate identification of the fistula type, often aided by Goodsall’s rule or MRI, is essential for surgical management. The high prevalence of the inter-sphincteric type makes it the standard expectation during clinical evaluation and surgical exploration for perianal fistula disease
questions.learning: In the classification of anorectal fistulas (Parks classification), the inter-sphincteric type is the most common, accounting for approximately 45% to 70% of all cases.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following symptoms does a patient with Reinke's edema classically present with?
options: Dysphagia of liquids more than solids
Dysphagia of solids more than liquids
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dysphonia

Dysphonia is the classic symptom that a patient with Reinke's edema presents with.

Reinke’s edema is a bilateral symmetrical swelling of the membraneous part of vocal cords. It is most commonly seen in middle aged smokers. It is also known as diffuse vocal polyposis or smoker’s larynx.

The classical symptom seen in this condition is hoarseness of voice (dysphonia). Patients can also present with a low pitched monotonous voice.

On examination of the larynx, the vocal cords appear swollen and edematous with a pale translucent look.

Treatment mainly consists of microlaryngoscopic stripping of the vocal cords. It should be done in two stages, taking one cord at a time to prevent anterior glottic web formation.

Other options

Option A - Diplophonia (double pitch) occurs when the vocal folds produce two distinct pitches simultaneously, often from uneven vibration. This can also be seen in Reinke’s edema.

Options C and D - Dysphagia is not a symptom of Reinke’s edema as it is a laryngeal pathology. Dysphagia of liquids more than solids is commonly seen in achalasia cardia. Tumors of the esophagus show dysphagia for solids more than liquids.
questions.learning: Dysphonia Dysphonia is the classic symptom that a patient with Reinke's edema presents with. Reinke’s edema is a bilateral symmetrical swelling of the membraneous part of vocal cords.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 41-year-old female patient presented with a tortuous swelling over the left side of the scalp and face as shown in the image given below. On local examination, the swelling was pulsatile. On auscultation, a bruit was heard. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cirsoid Aneurysm

The presence of a tortuous, pulsatile swelling over the scalp and face is suggestive of a cirsoid aneurysm.

Cirsoid aneurysm is a slow-growing, tortuous swelling that develops due to abnormal arteriovenous connections among the subcutaneous blood vessels. They are usually congenital. However, in some cases, they may be traumatic. The superficial temporal artery is most commonly involved.

Patients present with a tortuous, pulsatile swelling over the scalp or face. They are usually asymptomatic and present to the clinic due to cosmetic deformity. However, some patients may have headache, tinnitus, and/or bleeding. A loud bruit is heard on auscultation.

Angiography is the investigation of choice.

Treatment includes surgical resection, endovascular occlusion or injection of percutaneous sclerosing agents.
questions.learning: Cirsoid Aneurysm — The presence of a tortuous, pulsatile swelling over the scalp and face is suggestive of a cirsoid aneurysm. Cirsoid aneurysm is a slow-growing, tortuous swelling that develops due to abnormal arteriovenous connections among the…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman presents with a unilateral throbbing headache associated with nausea and vomiting. She has had similar episodes in the past where the headache usually lasts for 1-2 days. Bright light increases her discomfort and she prefers sitting in a dark room. Which of the following drugs can be used to decrease her headache episodes in the future?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Propranolol

Multiple unilateral throbbing headaches associated with nausea, vomiting, and photophobia suggest a diagnosis of migraine headaches and the drug used in the prophylaxis is propranolol.

Drugs used in the prophylaxis of migraine:
• Beta-blockers: propranolol
• Tricyclic antidepressants: amitriptyline
• Serotonergic: methysergide
• Anticonvulsants: valproate, topiramate
• Other classes: flunarizine
• Pizotifen

Sumatriptan is used in the treatment of an acute attack of a migraine.

Migraine:

The classic migraine is associated with an aura and can be:

a)Visual (most common)

* Zigzag lines

* Tunnel vision

* Scotoma

* Transient visual loss

b)Sensory

* Tingling sensation of hands, which spreads proximally

Note:

The most common negative visual aura is scotoma.
questions.learning: Propranolol Multiple unilateral throbbing headaches associated with nausea, vomiting, and photophobia suggest a diagnosis of migraine headaches and the drug used in the prophylaxis is propranolol.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old asymptomatic woman on USG shows a unilocular cyst in the ovary of 6 cm with negative serology. Treatment involves:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Follow-up after 1-2 cycles of OCPs

Follow up after 1-2 cycles of oral combined pills (conservative management) is the best treatment modality in the given scenario as it is most likely to be a functional cyst.

For conservative management of ovarian cysts, the following criteria should usually be met:

* Asymptomatic

* Unilocular

* Unilateral

* No solid areas

* Normal CA 125

* Less than 7cm

* Ultrasound re-examination after 3-6 months (no signs of increase in size or malignancy)

Features of a functional cyst:

* Related to temporary hormonal disorders

* Benign and rarely become complicated

* Usually 6-8cm in diameter

* Usually asymptomatic

* Unilocular

* Contains clear fluid, unless haemorrhage occurs

* Lining epithelium corresponds to the functional epithelium of the unit from which they arise

* Spontaneous regression occurs within 4-6 months

Treatment of functional cysts:

* Usually conservative; spontaneous regression occurs after 4-6months.

* Oral combined pills to hasten the regression of cyst.

* Laparotomy for tumours more than 7 cm to prevent complications or malignant transformation.
questions.learning: Follow-up after 1-2 cycles of OCPs Follow up after 1-2 cycles of oral combined pills (conservative management) is the best treatment modality in the given scenario as it is most likely to be a functional cyst.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The physician noticed the following finding in a patient that came to the OPD for an eye exam. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ptosis of right eye

The given image of the patient shows ptosis of the right eye. Ptosis is abnormal drooping of the upper eyelid to a level that covers more than 2mm of the superior cornea, it commonly occurs due to paralysis or defective development of the levator palpebrae superioris (LPS).

Types:

1. Congenital ptosis
2. Acquired ptosis

• Neurogenic ptosis is caused by innervational defects such as third nerve palsy, Horner’s syndrome.
• Myogenic ptosis occurs due to acquired disorders of the LPS muscle or the myoneural junction- Myasthenia gravis.
• Aponeurotic ptosis develops due to defects of the levator aponeurosis.
• Mechanical ptosis may result from the excessive weight on the upper lid as seen in patients with lid tumors, multiple chalazia, and lid edema.

Treatment of ptosis:

• The Fasanella–Servat operation is indicated for cases of minimal ptosis of  1.5 –2 mm with good function of the levator and a good lid fold.
• In moderate-to-severe ptosis with a moderate levator action, levator resection can be carried out.

Note: Pseudoptosis is apparent but not true drooping of the eyelid. Causes include lack of support of the lids by the globe(orbital volume deficit like an artificial eye, microphthalmos, or enophthalmos), contralateral lid retraction, ipsilateral hypotropia or brow ptosis.

Option A: Entropion is defined as inward rolling of the lid margin. The constant rubbing of the eyelashes onto the cornea can cause irritation, punctate corneal erosions and in severe cases ulceration and pannus formation. Weiss operation is done in senile entropion.

Option B: Lagophthalmos- in lagophthalmos there is incomplete closure of the palpable aperture when the patient attempts to close the eyes due to congenital deformity, paralysis of the orbicularis muscle, ectropion or contraction of the lid. Treatment includes the management of exposure keratopathy with frequent instillation of lubricants.

Option D: Exophthalmos- Although exophthalmos and proptosis are used interchangeably, the term exophthalmos is used to describe the protrusion/prominence of the eyes due to thyroid diseases while proptosis can be due to any other causes. Most common causes of proptosis:

Unilateral proptosis
Bilateral proptosis

In children: orbital cellulitis
Neuroblastoma & leukemia

In adults: Thyroid ophthalmopathy
Thyroid opthalmopathy

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A gym owner notices that individuals who consume iced tea during workouts appear to lose more weight. What type of relationship does this observation suggest?
questions.explanation: A spurious relationship is a mathematical relationship in which two variables have no direct causal connection, yet it may be wrongly inferred that they do, usually due to the presence of a third, unseen factor (a confounding variable). In this scenario, drinking iced tea doesn't cause weight loss. Instead, individuals who are disciplined enough to work out regularly (the real cause of weight loss) might also happen to prefer iced tea. The observed association between iced tea and weight loss is coincidental or influenced by the workout itself. A relative relationship (Option B) isn't a standard term in this context. A direct relationship (Option C) would mean iced tea chemically causes weight loss. An indirect relationship (Option D) would mean iced tea leads to another factor that then causes weight loss. Recognizing spurious correlations is vital in medical research to avoid drawing false conclusions about treatments or lifestyle habits. Researchers use randomized controlled trials to eliminate these confounding variables and establish true causality

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Pick from the following the usual cause of thyroid storm in thyroidectomy:
options: Rough handling of thyroid during surgery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inadequate patient preparation

The usual cause of thyroid storm in thyroidectomy is inadequate patient preparation before surgery. Patient preparation pre-operatively involves ensuring a euthyroid state.

Rough handling of the thyroid in thyroidectomy does not cause a thyroid storm. Though a significant amount of thyroglobulin is stored in the acinar cells, they are inactive unless converted to thyroxine (T3 and T4).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the characteristic feature of a fungal ulcer?
options: Dendritic ulcer on a fluorescien dye
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Satellite lesion

Satellite lesions are characteristic of fungal ulcer.

The signs of a fungal ulcer include:

• Irregular margins of the ulcer.
• Presence of satellite lesions surrounding the ulcer.
• An immune ring (Wesseley) may be seen around the ulcer due to deposition of the immune complexes.
• Slough is usually dry, with feathery borders surrounded by a yellow line of demarcation.
• Hypopyon may be present or absent. If present, it is thick, immobile due to the direct invasion of the fungal hyphae into the anterior chamber.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs are used to treat chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Granisetron i+ dexamethasone+ aprepitant

Granisetron i+ dexamethasone+ aprepitant is used to treat Chemotherapy-induced Nausea and Vomiting(CINV).

The combination of 5-HT3 receptor antagonists, NK1 receptor antagonists, and dexamethasone has decreased emesis and decreased the use of rescue medications for patients receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy during the acute and delayed phases.

5-HT3 receptor antagonists- Drugs are ondansetron, granisetron, dolasetron, and palonosetron. These agents are believed to prevent CINV by antagonizing 5-HT3 receptors either peripherally on vagal nerve terminals and/or centrally in the chemoreceptor trigger zone. The most common adverse effects are headaches and constipation.

NK1 receptor antagonists- They inhibit substance P in peripheral and central emetic pathways. Aprepitant was the first drug in this class to be approved by the FDA. The most common adverse effects include fatigue, headache, anorexia, diarrhoea, and increased transaminases.

Corticosteroids- They are now considered a mainstay of antiemetic regimens for the prevention of acute and delayed emesis. Dexamethasone is the recommended corticosteroid according to current guidelines.

Dopamine receptor antagonists were the primary antiemetics used for CINV, before the approval of the 5-HT3 antagonists. They have serious extrapyramidal side effects like akathisia, dystonia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. With the current availability of more effective preventive agents, dopamine receptor antagonists are mostly used in the management of breakthrough or refractory emesis.  This class includes prochlorperazine, haloperidol, droperidol, and metoclopramide.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the source of trauma in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bullet

Firearm (bullet) injuries produce characteristic wound patterns that help identify the source and type of trauma. Key features of entry wound (as seen in image):

• Small, circular/oval defect
• Inverted margins
• Surrounding abrasion collar (contusion ring)
• May show blackening/tattooing depending on range

High-velocity projectile causes:

• Penetrating injury
• Local tissue destruction
• Possible cavitation effect

Why not others:

• Scissor: Incised/stab wound with clean margins
• Rod: Blunt trauma → contusions/lacerations
• Axe: Chop wound → deep, gaping with bone cuts

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is pegloticase used for?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chronic gout

Pegloticase is used in the treatment of chronic gout.

Pegloticase is a pegylated uricase (urate oxidase). It catalyzes the enzymatic oxidation of uric acid into allantoin, which is a more soluble and inactive metabolite.

It is used in the treatment of severe, refractory chronic gout or in cases where other urate-lowering therapies are contraindicated.
